Once upon a time in a cozy little town, there lived a sweet puppy named Tilly. Tilly had gone through some tough times when she was just a baby pup, but now she was living happily with her new family - Mr. and Mrs. Smith and their young daughter, Emily. Even though Tilly loved her new home, sometimes she found it hard to trust people and get close to them because of what happened in her past.

One sunny day, Emily came running into the backyard where Tilly was playing. She held out a wiggly worm and said, "Look, Tilly! I found you a friend!" But Tilly got scared and ran away. Emily didn't understand; she thought maybe Tilly didn't like bugs. So, she asked her mom, Mrs. Smith, "Mommy, why doesn't Tilly want to play with my worm?"

With gentle eyes, Mrs. Smith explained, "Sometimes, dogs and even kids go through things called 'traumas,' which make them feel afraid. It takes time for them to learn that they are safe again."

"What does 'safe' mean?" Emily wondered aloud.

Her mother smiled and replied, "Being safe means feeling comfortable and secure so your body knows no harm is going to come its way."

Mr. Smith added, "And do you know how we help someone become safe? By being kind, understanding, and giving lots of love and patience. Just like we would if you ever felt sad or scared."

Emily nodded slowly and looked over at Tilly. Then, she picked up a soft toy dog and approached Tilly gently. "Here, Tilly," she whispered softly while placing the stuffed animal beside her. "You can be brave and strong like me. You don't need to be scared anymore."

Over time, Tilly saw that Emily and her parents were always caring towards her, never hurting or scaring her. With each passing day, she started to regain her confidence and learned to trust again. Soon enough, Tilly became Emily's best buddy, following her around everywhere and snuggling next to her during bedtime stories.

Whenever Tilly seemed frightened by loud sounds outside or sudden movements nearby, Emily hugged her tightly and reassured her saying, "It's okay, Tilly. We keep each other safe here." And soon, those fears faded too.

In their small town, everyone noticed the incredible bond between Tilly and Emily. They realized that helping others heal took kindness, patience, and understanding - that every creature needs support and love to overcome fear and build connections.

So whenever anyone asks why Tilly loves staying with Emily, they simply smile and say, "Because together, they built trust and created a space filled with warmth and resilience."

Mainz
Mainz ( or Meenz, () is a German city. It is the capital of the state of Rhineland-Palatinate.

Mainz is on the left side of the river Rhine, on the right side is the city Wiesbaden. Mainz has about 203,000 people. Its main economic product is wine. It has an oceanic climate (Cfb in the Koeppen climate classification).

Venn diagrams

To illustrate operations on sets mathematicians use Venn diagrams. Venn diagrams use circles to show individual sets. The universe is depicted with a rectangle. Results of operations are shown as colored areas. In the illustration of the intersection operation the left circle shows set and the right circle shows set .

Special sets
Some sets are very important to mathematics. They are used very often. One of these is the empty set.
Many of these special sets are written using blackboard bold typeface, and these include:
, denoting the set of all primes.
, denoting the set of all natural numbers. That is to say, = {1, 2, 3, ...}, or sometimes = {0, 1, 2, 3, ...}.
, denoting the set of all integers (whether positive, negative or zero). So = {..., -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, ...}.
, denoting the set of all rational numbers (that is, the set of all proper and improper fractions). So, , meaning all fractions where a and b are in the set of all integers and b is not equal to 0. For example, and . All integers are in this set since every integer a can be expressed as the fraction .
, denoting the set of all real numbers. This set includes all rational numbers, together with all irrational numbers (that is, numbers which cannot be rewritten as fractions, such as and 2).
, denoting the set of all complex numbers.

Each of these sets of numbers has an infinite number of elements, and .

Paradoxes about sets
The mathematician Bertrand Russell found that there are problems with the informal definition of sets. He stated this in a paradox called Russell's paradox. An easier to understand version, closer to real life, is called the Barber paradox.

The barber paradox
There is a small town somewhere. In that town, there is a barber. All the men in the town do not like beards, so they either shave themselves, or they go to the barber shop to be shaved by the barber.

We can therefore make a statement about the barber himself: The barber shaves all men that do not shave themselves. He only shaves those men (since the others shave themselves and do not need a barber to give them a shave).

This of course raises the question: What does the barber do each morning to look clean-shaven? This is the paradox.

If the barber shaves himself, he cannot be a barber, since a barber does not shave himself.
If he does not shave himself, he falls in the category of those who do not shave themselves, and so, cannot be a barber.

Welcome to our course unit all about designing and creating digital jewelry! That's right - we're going to use computers to design beautiful pieces of jewelry that you can wear or give as gifts to loved ones. Have you ever heard of surface modeling? It's a way of using computer software to create three-dimensional objects, like jewelry!

First, let's talk about why we would want to design jewelry on a computer instead of making it by hand. Well, there are lots of reasons! For one thing, once we create a piece of jewelry on the computer, we can easily make changes to the design until it's just perfect. We don't have to worry about cutting or shaping materials incorrectly, because we can adjust everything on the screen before we actually make the jewelry. Plus, if we want to make multiples of the same piece (like matching bracelets for a group of friends), it's much faster and easier to do so using computer software.

Now, I know what you're thinking - isn't working with computers boring? Not at all! With surface modeling, we get to be creative and hands-on while still using technology. We can choose from different shapes, colors, and textures to make our jewelry unique and eye-catching. And who knows - maybe we'll even discover a new style that becomes popular!

So how does surface modeling work exactly? Let me explain. When we start a new project, we first create a basic shape for our jewelry. This could be something simple like a circle for a ring or a rectangle for a pendant. From there, we add details like curves, edges, and holes to make the shape more interesting. Think of it like building a sculpture out of clay, but instead of physically molding the clay, we're adding and subtracting virtual shapes on the computer.

One important thing to remember when designing jewelry on the computer is to think about how the final product will look and feel. For example, if we're designing a pair of earrings, we need to consider whether they'll be heavy or lightweight, dangling or studded. If we're designing a bracelet, we need to think about whether it will fit comfortably around someone's wrist. By keeping these things in mind, we can create realistic designs that people will love wearing.

Before we finish up, I want to share a quick tip about taking care of any jewelry you create. Just like real jewelry, digital jewelry needs to be handled carefully. Avoid getting it wet or exposing it to harsh chemicals, which can damage the materials and cause them to lose their color or shine. Instead, treat your digital jewelry like a precious treasure and store it safely until you're ready to show it off!

I hope you're excited to learn more about surface modeling and digital jewelry design! Who knows - you may discover a hidden talent for creating stunning accessories that everyone wants to wear. Happy designing!

Ballarat
After World War II, Ballarat grew to the northwest. To ease the housing shortage a large estate was built by the Housing Commission of Victoria on the old Ballarat Common This area is now called Wendouree West. From 1951 to 1962, 750 houses were built, with another 300 added in the 1970s. This was matched by private housing built in Wendouree.

In the 1980s the areas of growth have been in the south and west of the city, as well as new building in the inner areas of the city. Through the 20th century Ballarat continued to grow at a steady rate. New public buildings have been built including the hospital, the library, the law courts and the police station complex. Ballarat is home to many schools, including Damascus College.

Super Smash Bros. Melee
Super Smash Bros. Melee, known in Japan as is a video game where players can choose from many people from famous Nintendo games and have them fight each other. Players can fight alone or team up with someone else against a friend. This game is a sequel to Super Smash Bros. for the Nintendo 64. Super Smash Bros. Melee is for the Nintendo GameCube. The subsequent game is Super Smash Bros. Brawl for the Wii.

Characters
Super Smash Bros. Melee takes 26 characters from many of Nintendo's series. It includes all 12 veteran characters from Super Smash Bros. 64, and adds 14 new characters, including Princess Peach and Bowser from the Super Mario Bros. series, Princess Zelda/Sheik and Ganondorf from The Legend of Zelda, and new characters like Ice Climbers from Ice Climber and Marth from Fire Emblem. Some characters seem to play more like other characters who were in the first game, like Ganondorf compared to Captain Falcon.

Sakurai planned to include more characters, including Diddy Kong, Meta Knight, King Dedede, Balloon Fighter, Urban Champion, Ayumi Tachibana, Sonic the Hedgehog, Bubbles, Excitebike, Solid Snake, and Lucas, but did not have time to fit them in. All of them except for Balloon Fighter made it into Super Smash Bros. Brawl.

Items
Items from different games can fall from the sky, like Pok Balls from Pokmon or Mushrooms from Mario. These items can be used in different ways. For example, Pok Balls can summon Pokmon, and Mushrooms can either grow the person whom touches it, unless it is a Poison Mushroom which makes them shrink.

Stages
Super Smash Bros. Melee has many stages that players can battle on. Most of the stages are based on Nintendo series like Mario, Pokmon, and The Legend of Zelda.

Tournament Play
Super Smash Bros. Melee has become very popular in tournaments. These tournaments do not use items or most stages, believing that these make the game unfair. In tournaments, however, a lot of characters are not strong enough to win. Some of the best characters for tournaments are Fox McCloud, Falco Lombardi, and Jigglypuff.

Once upon a time, long ago, when humans were just starting to form societies, something amazing happened. People began making decisions that would change the course of history! But have you ever wondered who got to make those important choices and why? That's where interpretation in history comes into play.

Imagine being one of the very first historians trying to figure out why things happened the way they did back then. Back in the day, many historians believed that only big shots like tsars, sultans, kings, and queens had any influence over historical events. This idea is called the Great Man Theory of history. It gives all the credit to powerful individuals for shaping our past.

But here's a little secret - modern historians know better now! They understand that everyone played their part in influencing history, from the mightiest king to the lowliest peasant. Still, even though early historians didn't always get it right, they sure knew how to spin a good yarn! Their stories might have been full of bravery, adventure...and maybe even a touch of embellishment. After all, politics and propaganda can sometimes sneak their way into the tales we tell about the past.

Now let's try a quick thought experiment: Imagine you're a historian investigating your own family tree. Think about your ancestors' lives and ask yourself questions like:

* Why did they move from place to place?
* How did they earn a living?
* Who influenced their most significant life decisions?

As you explore their stories, remember that each person has unique reasons behind the choices they make. Just like us, ancient folks acted based on factors like culture, beliefs, social status, and personal relationships. Understanding them will help bring the past to life!

So next time you dive into learning about history, keep in mind that interpreting the past means looking beyond famous figures and digging deeper into the lives of ordinary people too. And hey, if you find any exciting stories along the way, don't forget to share them - after checking for truthiness, of course!

Title: "The Amazing Adventures of Hormone Harry and Adrena Alice!"

Meet our two main characters today - Hormone Harry and his best friend Adrena Alice! They live right on top of your kidneys and work really hard every day to help you stay strong and healthy. Let's see what they do all day long!

Harry and Alice both come from a magical place called the Adrenal Glands. This special land has two parts - an outer part called the Cortex (which sounds like a cool spaceship) and an inner area known as the Medulla (that reminds us of delicious jelly). Even though they look tiny, these lands produce powerful chemicals called hormones which travel throughout your body using your bloodstream superhighway!

Let's start with Hormone Harry who lives in the yellow Cortex area. He loves making three important hormones named Aldosterone, Cortisol, and Androgens. Each one helps control something unique in your body.

* Aldosterone keeps watch over your salt and water balance so that you don't get too puffy or dried out. Imagine being a lifeguard at a beach party where everyone is having fun splashing around - cool job, huh?
* Cortisol controls how your body responds when it encounters stress. It's kind of like giving hugs during tough times, helping you feel better quickly.
* Lastly, there are those naughty but nice Androgens. You can think of them as secret agents because they quietly assist in growing muscles and hair. Shhh...don't tell anyone!

Now let's meet Adrena Alice who resides in the reddish-brown Medulla region. She makes just TWO types of hormones, but trust us, they're pretty exciting ones!

* Epinephrine, also known as Adrenaline, is her first creation. Think of it as rocket fuel for your body, preparing you for quick action whenever danger lurks nearby or even when playing games and sports!
* Norepinephrine comes next, acting like a helpful sidekick by working closely with epinephrine to prepare your heart and lungs for emergencies. Together, they make sure everything runs smoothly under pressure!

And guess what? Both Hormone Harry and Adrena Alice take turns working together to keep your body safe, happy, and ready for anything life throws at you! Isn't that amazing? So remember, deep inside, we all have these incredible heroes protecting us every single day!

Pokmon (video game series)
In 2005, Pokmon Emerald was released. It is a sequel to Ruby and Sapphire. It was the first "main" Pokmon game since Crystal where Pokmon had battle animations instead of static images. There was also a new place called the Battle Frontier where players could go after they beat the Elite Four. It was similar to the Battle Tower in Crystal, Ruby, and Sapphire, except it was eight different facilities, all with different rules. Players earned Battle Points which could be used to buy items for Secret Bases, items for Pokmon, and other things.

In 2007, Pokmon Diamond and Pearl were released. They take place in a new region called Sinnoh. They had 107 new Pokmon, which brought the total to 493. Another noticeable difference from the previous games was that Diamond and Pearl did not capitalize all the letters in names of Pokmon, people, towns, items, and other things that were important to the games. For example, Lugia would appear as "LUGIA" in previous games, but in Diamond and Pearl it would just say "Lugia." This cleared up a lot of players' confusion, because many thought that a sentence like "LUGIA is found in the WHIRL ISLANDS" looked unusual. A sequel to Diamond and Pearl, Pokmon Platinum was released in the United States in March 2009. In May 2009 it was released in the UK.

In 2010, Pokmon HeartGold & SoulSilver were released. They did not take place in a new region, or have any new Pokmon. They were simply remakes of Pokmon Gold and Silver. Like Pokmon Yellow, the player's Pokmon can follow them. The games come with a pedometer like device, called the Pok Walker, that can let players walk with their Pokmon, and gain Watts, which can be used to fight Pokmon, or dowse for items.

Later in 2010, Pokmon Black and White were released. They take place in a new region called Unova. They had 156 new Pokmon, bringing the total to 649. They introduced seasons, where areas appear differently depending on the season, and some areas can only be reached during certain seasons.

In 2012, Pokmon Black 2 & White 2 were released. They are sequels to Pokmon Black and White. They had a number of new areas and characters, as well as characters from Black and White.

In 2013, Pokmon X & Y were released. They are the first ever 3D games in the main Pokmon'' series. They take place in a new region called Kalos. There are many new features, including the Mega Evolution, where some Pokmon like Mewtwo, Blaziken, and Lucario are be able to evolve into stronger forms during a battle if they are holding a Mega Stone. There is also a new type called Fairy, which is strong against Dragon-type Pokmon.

in 2014, Pokmon Omega Ruby & Alpha Sapphire were released, which were remakes of ruby and sapphire. it added more mega evolutions, including the other hoenn starters, beedrill, Sableye, etc. tons of features were also added.

"Okay, okay! Let's study, but first, let's be aliens for five more minutes!" Leo said, feeling happy again. They bounced around and had fun. Later, they sat down to study, and Leo felt grateful for his friends.

"Even when I lose something, I can find joy," he thought, smiling. Math could wait. Friendship was more important!

Homelessness
Health care for the homeless is a major public health challenge. Homeless people are more likely to suffer injuries and medical problems from their lifestyle on the street. Quite a few drink or have addiction problems with drugs. Some have skin conditions from being out in the sun without sunscreen to protect themselves from UV radiation. It is hard to find places to wash up, and homeless people are exposed to extreme cold and hot sun. It is tough finding good food for many homeless people so they tend to suffer from medical conditions. This can include obesity if they eat a lot of poor quality food with empty calories. Homeless people also may have more severe dental problems than the general population due to lack of access to washrooms and in some cases excess intake of sweets, which may be the only food available. Diabetes and liver problems are not uncommon, as are diseases associated with cigarette smoking...

Vulnerability Index
The vulnerability index is a tool for finding out who among the street homeless population needs health care and housing the most.

The vulnerability index is from the work of Dr. Jim O'Connell of Boston's Healthcare for the Homeless. He was concerned about the causes of death of unsheltered homeless individuals living on the street. A national drive is underway by Common Ground to work with the HUD homeless count. Since communities are doing the count, he believes that is a good time to do the vulnerability index too. Its' people say that using it will help getting needy individuals off the street.

The vulnerability index has been tried out in a lot of other places not just the East Coast. These include New Mexico and Santa Monica

Main causes

The main reasons for homelessness have been studied in many reports and studies.
For example:
Lack of affordable housing
Low paying jobs
Addiction and lack of needed services
Mental illness and lack of needed services
Domestic violence
Unemployment or underemployment.
Social exclusion
Discrimination that lowers self-esteem.
Careless life style
Poverty, especially destitution (having no money at all).
Prison release and re-entry into society due to a criminal record that can cause recidivism.
Change and cuts in welfare
Natural disasters

Developing and undeveloped countries
The number of homeless people worldwide has grown steadily in the past few years. In some Third World nations such as Brazil, India, Nigeria, and South Africa, homelessness is a very big problem, with millions of children living and working on the streets. Homelessness has also become a problem in China, Thailand, Indonesia, the Philippines and Japan.

History
In the sixteenth century in England, the government first tried to give housing to vagabonds instead of punishing them. In the eighteenth century, these houses were replaced by workhouses. These were later replaced by dormitory housing ("spikes"). By the early 1930s in England, there were 30,000 people living in these places.

In most countries, many towns and cities had an area where all the poor, transients, and afflicted lived, such as a "skid row". In smaller towns, there were hobos, who camped near train tracks and hopped onto trains from place to place. Many places where loitering was once allowed (such as churches, public libraries and public atriums) became more strict as the number of homeless people grew.

Set
If you can count the elements of a set, it is called a countable set. Countable sets include all sets with a finite number of members. Countable sets also include some infinite sets, such as the natural numbers. You can count the natural numbers with . The natural numbers are nicknamed "the counting numbers", since they are what we usually use to count things with.

An uncountable set is an infinite set that is impossible to count. If we try to count the elements, we will always skip some. It does not matter what step we take. The set of real numbers is an uncountable set. There are many other uncountable sets, even such a small interval like .[3]

Subsets

If you look at the set and the set , you can see that all elements in the first set are also in the second set. We say: is a subset of
As a formula it looks like this:

In general, when all elements of set are also elements of set , we call a subset of :
.
It is usually read " is contained in ."

Example: Every Chevrolet is an American car. So the set of all Chevrolets is contained in the set of all American cars.

Set operations

There are different ways to combine sets.

Intersections
The intersection of two sets and is a set that contains all the elements that are both in set and in set at the same time.

Example: When is the set of all cheap cars, and is the set of all American cars, then is the set of all cheap American cars.

Unions

The union of two sets and is a set that contains all the elements that are in set or in set .
This "or" is the inclusive disjunction, so the union also contains the elements, that are in set and in set .
By the way, this means, that the intersection is a subset of the union:
.

Example: When is the set of all cheap cars, and is the set of all American cars, then is the set of all cars, without all expensive cars that are not from America.

Complements
Complement can mean two different things:

The complement of is the universe without all the elements of :

The universe is the set of all things you speak about.
Example: When is the set of all cars, and is the set of all cheap cars, then C is the set of all expensive cars.

The set difference of and is the set without all the elements of :

It is also called the relative complement of in .
Example: When is the set of all cheap cars, and is the set of all American cars, then is the set of all expensive American cars.

If you exchange the sets in the set difference, the result is different:In the example with the cars, the difference is the set of all cheap cars, that are not made in America.

Notation
Most mathematicians use uppercase ITALIC (usually Roman) letters to write about sets (such as , , ). The things that are seen as elements of sets are usually written with lowercase Roman letters.

One way of showing a set is by a list of its members, separated by commas, included in braces.
For example,
is set which has members 1, 2, and 3.

Another way, called the set-builder notation, is by a statement of what is true of the members of the set, like this:
{x | x is a natural number & x < 4}.

Alice: Hi Bob! Have you ever heard about the history of nightclubs in New York City?

Bob: Not really, Alice. I know what a nightclub is, but I don't know much about its history.

Alice: Well, did you know that nightclubs have played a significant role in shaping America's cultural landscape, especially when it comes to music and dance? For instance, many African American and black musicians found success performing in Harlem's nightclubs during the 1920s and 30s, which was known as the Harlem Renaissance.

Bob: Oh, like jazz music and stuff?

Alice: Exactly! Musicians such as Duke Ellington and Billie Holiday became famous after performing in popular clubs like the Cotton Club and Cafe Society. These venues provided a space where artists could express themselves and share their talents with the world.

Bob: That sounds cool! But why were nightclubs so important for African American and black performers?

Alice: At the time, there weren't many opportunities for these artists to showcase their skills in mainstream settings. Segregation laws and discrimination made it difficult for them to find work in other types of entertainment establishments. So, nightclubs became essential platforms for these talented individuals to gain recognition and succeed in their careers.

Bob: Wow, I see. It's kind of like when someone gets bullied at school, and they find a group of friends who accept them for who they are.

Alice: Yes, exactly! Just like those friends create a supportive environment for that person, nightclubs offered a safe space for African American and black artists to thrive and develop their craft. And because of that, they created incredible art that still influences us today.

Bob: I get it now. So, if someone isn't given a fair chance elsewhere, finding another place to show off their talent can make a huge difference.

Alice: Absolutely, Bob! And just think about how richer our lives are because of the contributions made by these pioneering artists. We can learn a lot from their experiences and understand the importance of creating inclusive spaces where everyone feels welcome and valued.

Bob: Yeah, that makes a lot of sense. Maybe one day, I can start my own club that supports underrepresented artists!

Alice: That sounds like a wonderful idea, Bob! By doing so, you'll be continuing the legacy of those groundbreaking nightclubs in New York City and helping to foster new talent along the way.

Leisure
Leisure (or free time) is when a person can choose what to do. During a person's leisure time, they do not have an obligation to be at school or work at a job. During leisure time, people can do fun activities, family activities, or other non-work activities, such as hobbies.

Common forms of recreation or leisure are:

Playing sports such as football or hockey
Playing games such as chess or cards
Exercising such as running or lifting weights
Watching television and movies
Listening to music
Hobbies such as playing piano or guitar, knitting, or sewing
Travelling
Reading
Drawing
Painting

A vacation or holiday is the setting aside of time specifically for leisure. During their vacation, some people travel to a different region or country, and stay at a hotel so that they can do things they could not do near home. Other people prefer to spend their vacation time at home in their own community.

In rich industrialized countries such as the US and Canada, as well as in most European countries, workers are allowed to stay home on the weekend (usually Saturday and Sunday), and use it as leisure time. People in poorer developing countries usually have less leisure time, as they have to work longer hours and more days per year.

Now that we have explored the surface areas of various three-dimensional figures such as triangular prisms, rectangular prisms, and boxes (also known as cuboids), it's time to delve deeper into finding the surface area of a box using its net. A net is a two-dimensional representation of a three-dimensional figure where all faces and edges are laid out flat. By understanding how to calculate the surface area using a net, students will gain a more comprehensive grasp of geometry and spatial reasoning.

Let us begin by examining what makes up a box (or cuboid). A box has six faces - the top, bottom, front, back, left, and right sides. Each face can either be a rectangle or square, depending on whether the box is a perfect cube or not. To find the surface area of a box using its net, we must first understand how to calculate the area of each individual face. The formula for the area of a rectangle is length  width. In this case, since every face of our box is a rectangle, we can apply this formula accordingly.

To construct a net for a box, follow these steps:

1. Draw a large square representing the bottom face of the box. Label one side 'l' for length and the other side 'w' for width. Calculate the area of this face by multiplying the length by the width. Record this value as 'A.'
* Area = l  w
* Example: If the length is 4 cm and the width is 3 cm, then A = 4  3 = 12 sq.cm.
2. Directly above the bottom face, draw a second square identical to the bottom face but do not label yet. This represents the top face of the box. Its dimensions should match those of the bottom face. Once calculated, record this value as 'B,' which should equal 'A' unless otherwise stated.
3. On the right side of the bottom face, draw a rectangle representing the vertical face adjacent to both the bottom and right faces. Label one short side 'h' for height and the other longer side 'w'. Determine the area of this face by multiplying the height by the width. Record this value as 'C.'
* Area = h  w
* Example: If the height is 5 cm and the width is 3 cm, then C = 5  3 = 15 sq.cm.
4. Repeat step 3 for the left, front, and back faces, ensuring their respective heights and widths correspond correctly within the context of the box. Label them D, E, and F, respectively. Remember, some lengths may differ between adjoining faces.

Now that we have labeled the individual areas of each face comprising the net, let us proceed to compute the total surface area of the box. Recall that surface area refers to the sum of all exposed outer surfaces. Thus, add together the values obtained from steps 1 through 4.

Total Surface Area (TSA) = A + B + C + D + E + F

Since A equals B, TSA simplifies to:

TSA = 2A + C + D + E + F

Returning to our previous example, suppose the length (l) measures 4 cm, the width (w) 3 cm, and the height (h) varies among the different faces as follows: Front Face - 5 cm; Back Face - 7 cm; Left Face - 3 cm; Right Face - 5 cm. Compute the Total Surface Area as shown below:

1. A = l  w
A = 4  3 = 12 sq.cm
B = A

Chapter 9: Introduction to Video Games and Coding

Have you ever played a video game? Of course, you have! They're super fun, right? But did you know that there are people out there who actually create those games? That's where coding comes into play!

Coding is like giving instructions to your computer or gaming console so it knows what to do next. Imagine if you were playing a game of hide and seek with your friends. You would need someone to tell you when it's time to start searching, where you can look, and when the game is over. In a video game, code tells the characters what they can do, how they move around, and even how they interact with other characters.

Let me give you an example using one of the most popular video games today - PUBG (PlayerUnknown's Battlegrounds). When you jump off the airplane in PUBG, code helps determine which direction you go, how fast you fall, and whether you land safely or end up splat! Code also controls things like inventory management, character interactions, and environmental factors such as weather conditions.

Now let's take another example from Overwatch 2. Say you want to try its free trial version but don't want any help from cheats. Well, guess what? Even creating something like a 'free trial' requires coding! People write specific sets of rules within the code to enable certain features only for limited periods. Similarly, avoiding getting detected while using hacks involves advanced techniques requiring deep understanding and manipulation of codes.

But why stop at just playing games? With coding skills, you could build your own basic game too! It might sound complicated now, but think about learning to ride a bike. At first, it seems impossible, but once you get the hang of it, it becomes second nature. Learning to code is similar; starting slow and practicing regularly makes all the difference.

So, ready to embark on this thrilling journey? Remember, every professional coder started exactly where you are now. Happy coding!

Jose wanted to help her, but his dad said, "We have our fishing line in the water."

Jose thought about the time, and he felt a pull in his heart. "Dad, what if she needs help?" he asked. His dad shrugged, saying it was not their business. But Jose could not ignore her. He stood up and waved at the woman. "Do you need help?" he called out, hoping she would say yes.

The woman looked up, her face brightening. "Oh, yes! My name is Anne, and I need to move this box to the shore before the sun sets!" Jose felt a rush of urgency. The sun was already low in the sky. He quickly ran over to help her. The box was large, but they managed to lift it together.

As they worked, Anne talked about her plans for the box. "It has food for the picnic I'm having later," she explained. Jose felt proud, thinking that they were saving a picnic. They laughed as they worked, and soon they reached the shore. "Thank you so much!" Anne exclaimed. Jose felt happy that he helped.

Just then, Jose's dad called out. "We should pack up soon!" he shouted. Jose looked at Anne and said, "I hope you have fun!" She smiled and invited him to the picnic. "There's enough food for everyone!" she said. Jose felt torn. He wanted to join but did not want to leave his dad alone.

In a moment of thought, Jose decided. "Dad, can we stay for a little while?" he asked. His father frowned but then agreed. They joined the picnic, where laughter filled the air. Jose saw how happy everyone was, and he felt warm inside.

As the sun dipped below the horizon, Jose realized he had made a new friend. Helping Anne was the best choice he could have made. The river, once a simple fishing spot, had turned into a place of joy and friendship.

Imagine you're walking down the street and you see a really cool gadget that you've never seen before! You wonder how it works and if you could make something similar. This is where reverse engineering comes into play.

So, what exactly is reverse engineering? Have you ever tried to put together a puzzle without looking at the picture on the box? That's kind of like reverse engineering! Basically, it means taking something apart and figuring out how it was made, what materials were used, and how all the pieces fit together. Then, using this information, you can create your own version of the same thing.

Why would someone want to do this? Well, maybe they found an old toy and want to fix it because the original manufacturer doesn't make replacement parts anymore. Or perhaps they want to recreate a vintage car accessory that's hard to find these days. Maybe they even came up with their own idea for improving a product and want to build a better version themselves!

Let me give you an example to help explain things more clearly. Say you love playing board games, and one day you come across an amazing game that everyone seems to enjoy. But unfortunately, after years of fun, the game starts falling apart, and new versions aren't being sold anywhere. What can you do now? With reverse engineering, you can take apart the broken game and study each piece carefully. By doing this, you learn about the type of wood used, the size of each piece, and other important details needed to rebuild the game. After gathering enough information, you can start creating your very own set! How awesome is that?

Another situation when reverse engineering might be helpful is when you encounter a problem while building something yourself. Let's say you're constructing a treehouse based on instructions you found online, but halfway through, you realize the plans just won't work for your specific backyard. Instead of giving up, you can examine the existing structure, figure out why certain elements weren't working, and modify the design accordingly. Just like magic, your treehouse will soon become functional again!

But remember, always ask permission before disassembling anything that belongs to others. We wouldn't want anyone getting upset! And sometimes, especially with electronic devices, reverse engineering may require special tools and skills beyond our reach right now. So let's focus on simpler projects we can handle ourselves.

Now go ahead and try observing objects around you with fresh eyes. Can you think of something you'd like to understand better or improve upon? Maybe it's time to break out those screwdrivers and get started on your first reverse engineering project!

"Who are you?" she replied, confused. The man smiled. "I am your brother! You have been gone for many years." She felt a knot in her stomach. "I don't remember anything. Why am I here?" He looked sad. "You lost your memory in a great storm. We searched for you everywhere."

As she walked through the village, faces and voices felt familiar but strange. "Why can't I remember?" she asked her brother. "The storm took more than your memories," he said quietly. "It took our home too. Our city sank into the sea." She gasped, "Sank? How?"

"We used to live in a bright city, full of life and joy," he began. "Then, one night, a great wave came. It swallowed everything." She felt a wave of sadness wash over her. "What can we do?" she whispered.

Her brother smiled gently. "We can rebuild. We can find the lost parts of our city. Maybe you will remember then." A flicker of hope sparked in her heart. "Let's do it!" she shouted. Together, they gathered the villagers. "We will find our home!"

Finally, she stood at the shore, looking out at the waves. "We will find a way to rise again," she said with courage. The ocean was big, but together they were strong. And with each new day, she knew she was home again.

Esperanto
In the first years of Esperanto's life, people used it only in written form, but in 1905 they organized the first (1st) World Congress of Esperanto in Boulogne-sur-Mer, France. This was the first notable use of Esperanto in international communication. Because of the success of the congress, it is organized each year (except years of the World Wars) to this day.

In 1912 Zamenhof resigned his leading position in the movement during the eighth (8th) World Congress of Esperanto in Krakw, Poland. The tenth (10th) World Congress of Esperanto in Paris, France, did not take place because of the start of World War I. Nearly 4000 people signed up for this congress.

Times of the World Wars
During World War I the World Esperanto Association had its main office in Switzerland, which was neutral in the war. Hector Hodler's group of volunteers with support of Romain Rolland helped send letters between the enemy countries through Switzerland. In total, they helped with 200,000 cases.

After World War I there was new hope for Esperanto because of the desire of people to live in peace. Esperanto and its community grew in those days. The first World Congress after the war took place in Hague, Netherlands, in 1920. An Esperanto Museum was opened in Vienna, Austria, in 1929. Today it is part of the Austrian National Library.

World War II stopped this growing of the language. Many Esperantists were sent into the battle. Nazis broke up Esperanto groups because they saw the language as a part of a worldwide Jewish conspiracy. Many Esperanto speakers died in concentration camps. The Soviet Union also treated Esperantists badly when Stalin was their leader.

After the wars

After World War II many people supported Esperanto. 80 million people signed a petition supporting Esperanto for use in the United Nations.

Every year they organize big Esperanto meetings such as the World Congress of Esperanto, International Youth Congress of Esperanto and SAT-Congress (meeting of Sennacieca Asocio Tutmonda - World Non-national Association).

In 1990, the Holy See published the document Norme per la celebrazione della Messa in esperanto, allowing the use of Esperanto in Masses without special permission. Esperanto is the only constructed language which received a permission like this one from the Roman Catholic Church.

Esperanto has many web pages, blogs, podcasts, and videos. People also use Esperanto in social media and online discussions and in their private communication through e-mail and instant messaging. Several (especially open source and free software) programmes have their own language version in Esperanto. Internet radio station Muzaiko has been broadcasting 24 hours a day in Esperanto since 2011.

Goals of the Esperanto movement

Zamenhof wanted to make an easy language to increase international understanding. He wanted Esperanto to be a universal second language. In other words, although he did not want Esperanto to replace national languages, he wanted a majority of people around the world to speak Esperanto. Many Esperantists initially shared this goal. General Assembly of UNESCO recognized Esperanto in 1954. Since then World Esperanto Association has got official relations with UNESCO. However, Esperanto was never chosen by the United Nations or other international organizations and it has not become a widely accepted second language.

Some Esperanto speakers like Esperanto for reasons other than its use as a universal second language. They like the Esperanto community and culture. Developing the Esperanto culture is a goal for that people.

Delft
Delft is a city in the province South Holland in the Netherlands. It is about halfway between Rotterdam and The Hague. It is famous for its Delft Blue pottery and the Delft University of Technology. It is the place where the royal family, the kings and queens, are buried. It has about 94,000 inhabitants.

Things to see
Delft is a city with typical Dutch canals, churches and large canal houses. The largest church in Delft is the Nieuwe Kerk (New Church).

Federal Ministry of Finance (Germany)
The Federal Ministry of Finance () (BMF) is a ministry of the Federal Republic of Germany. It is based in Berlin and Bonn. It is led by the Minister of Finance, whose office is in the Detlev-Rohwedder House in Wilhelmstrae, Berlin. This was the old Reich Air Ministry Building. The ministry is supported by a scientific advisory board.

Responsibility
The ministry works out how much the government can spend each year, and how to raise that money, in income tax and other taxes.

To help it do this, the ministry controls :
the Federal Forestry Commission, Bundesforstverwaltung
Federal Spirits Monopoly Administration, Bundesmonopolverwaltung fr Branntwein
Federal Portfolio Management, Bundesvermgensverwaltung, and

Federal Ministers of Finance since 1949

Between 1990 and 1993, the senior civil servant () was Horst Khler (CDU) who went on to become Federal President in, 2004.

I have a meal to plan!" he insisted. The fairy fluttered her wings and laughed. "You should try to enjoy a snack in the woods! What about berries?"

Alex shook his head. "I need to know the right amount!" The fairy rolled her eyes. "You will never know unless you taste them!" Curious, he followed her to a bush full of shining berries. The bright red color tempted him, but he hesitated. "What if they are sour?" he thought.

"Just take one!" the fairy urged. So, with a deep breath, he picked a berry and popped it into his mouth. It burst with sweetness. Alex was shocked. "It's delicious!" he exclaimed. "See?" the fairy smiled. "Life is full of surprises!"

Feeling brave, he picked more berries and shared them with the fairy. They laughed and ate until their bellies were full. Suddenly, he forgot about his list and his meal plan. He was just enjoying the moment.

As the sun set, the fairy said, "Now you know! You can plan, but don't forget to play!" Alex nodded. He realized that sometimes, being spontaneous brought the greatest joy.

From then on, he would take time to wander in the enchanted forest. He would try new foods and share laughter. Each trip brought a new adventure, and Alex learned that hunger was more than just a meal.

Legislature
Legislature is a word that comes from the Latin language, meaning "those who write the laws." A legislature is therefore a group of people who vote for new laws, for example in a state or country.

Each person in the legislature is usually either elected or appointed. The constitution of that state or country usually tells how a legislature is supposed to work.

In many countries, the legislature is called a Parliament, Congress, or National Assembly. Sometimes there are two groups of members in the legislature. This is called a "bicameral" legislature. A unicameral legislature has only one group of members.

A country, district, city, or other small area may also have something like a legislature. These are often called councils, and they make smaller laws for their areas.

Welcome to our E-Learning Module all about Housing and Other Tangible Assets! Today we will explore how people can invest their money in things they can touch and see, just like your favorite teddy bear or toy car!

Meet Sammy the Squirrel. Every autumn, Sammy collects acorns from the park to store for winter. This way, he knows he has enough food to last him until springtime. By saving his acorns now, he is investing in his future comfort and well-being.

One day, Sammy meets Mr. Rabbit who tells him about other ways to invest his acorns. Instead of just storing them underground, Sammy could also buy a cozy treehouse or even build an apple farm! These are examples of tangible assets - something you can physically own and benefit from.

Let's talk more about these two types of investments.

A house (or treehouse!) is called real estate. It provides shelter and security. Plus, if Sammy ever decides to move out, he might be able to sell it for more than what he paid initially. That difference is known as capital gain.

An apple farm, on the other hand, is a business investment. Sammy needs seeds, soil, water, and sunlight to grow delicious apples which he then sells at the market. After covering costs such as labor and equipment, whatever remains is profit. However, there's always some risk involved because weather conditions, pests, or low demand can affect sales.

Just remember, every type of investment comes with its own level of risk and return. The higher the potential reward, often the greater the risk. But don't worry too much; over time, many investments tend to increase in value due to inflation. So, holding onto them for longer periods usually pays off.

That's all folks! Now you know about housing and other tangible assets. Investing isn't only about keeping money safe but also making it work harder so that you can enjoy bigger rewards in the future. Happy learning!

Chapter 10: Unlocking Your Mind - Understanding and Analyzing Your Dreams

Have you ever woken up after a wild night of adventures, only to realize that it all happened while you were fast asleep? That's right, we're talking about DREAMS! Dreams are fascinating and strange stories that play out in your mind when you're snoozing away. Let's explore this mystical territory together!

What are dreams?
------------------

Imagine having a movie theater inside your head that plays different scenes every time you go to sleep! Cool, huh? Well, dreams are exactly that! They are collections of thoughts, pictures, and even sounds that pop up when you're catching Zzz's. Sometimes these stories might seem silly or scary, but other times they can feel incredibly real.

Why do dreams matter?
---------------------

You might think dreams are nothing more than weird tales cooked up by your brain at night. But did you know that decoding your dreams can help you learn more about yourself? Yep! Those nocturnal narratives can sometimes reveal what's hiding deep within your heart - your secret hopes, fears, and big ol' pile of emotions! So let's become dream detectives and start solving some mysteries!

How do I analyze my dreams?
---------------------------

Now comes the fun part! To figure out what your dreams want to tell you, follow these simple steps:

Step 1: Write 'em down!

As soon as you wake up, grab a notebook (or use your phone) and scribble down everything you remember about your recent adventure in Dreamland. Don't worry if it seems confusing; just get those details on paper before they vanish like morning mist!

Step 2: Identify symbols

Remember how movies use things like hearts, cars, or monsters to symbolize certain ideas? Dreams work similarly! For example, seeing water often means emotion because it flows like feelings. Or maybe heights suggest ambition since climbing high takes effort and determination. Try guessing what each strange thing from your dream represents.

Step 3: Reflect on YOU

This step is crucial! Think about what each symbol might mean specifically for *you*. If you hate spiders and had one crawl all over you last night, perhaps there's something causing anxiety in your daily life. Be honest with yourself here - no judgment allowed!

Let's look at a quick example:

Suppose you dreamed about losing teeth. What does that mean? Teeth falling out can represent various things depending on context. Maybe you're worried about getting older or looking less attractive (hello, peer pressure). Perhaps you're concerned about saying something wrong and embarrassing yourself. Whatever the reason, try connecting the dots between your dream symbol and YOUR personal experiences.

A Short History Lesson
--------------------

People have always been curious about their dreams! Ancient folks thought they were messages from gods or glimpses of the future. Even today, people believe similar things. The famous biblical tale of Joseph interpreting Pharaoh's ominous dreams demonstrates how powerful understanding dreams can be. Who knows? You might end up saving someone from trouble someday too!

Your Turn!
----------

Now that you've learned the basics of unraveling your nighttime narratives, give it a shot! Start paying attention to your dreams and see what secrets they share. Remember, everyone has unique dreams so don't compare yours to others'. Happy dream analyzing!

Welcome to Derivative Pricing Models! Have you ever heard of stocks, bonds, or options before? If so, have you wondered how people determine their prices? That's where derivative pricing models come into play! These are mathematical formulas that help us understand what these securities are worth based on different factors.

Let's start with something simple like apples. Imagine your friend sells apples for $1 each. Now imagine you want to buy some apples next week instead of today. How much would you pay then? Well, it depends. Will there still be plenty of apples available, or will they become scarce due to bad weather? This concept applies to stocks too - just replace 'apples' with shares of stock.

Now let's take this idea further by introducing derivatives such as options. Options give buyers the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell an asset at a specific price within a certain period. So, if I think Apple Inc.'s share price will go up soon, I might buy a call option - giving me the right to purchase Apple Inc. shares later at a fixed price.

But how do we know what to pay for this option? We use a model called the Black-Scholes Model. It uses variables like current stock price, strike price (the set price), volatility (how much the stock changes over time), risk-free interest rate (what banks charge for loans), and time until expiration. By plugging these numbers into the formula, voila! We get a fair value for our option.

Here's an example using fake numbers: Suppose Apple Inc.'s stock trades at $100 today, my call option has a strike price of $110, its annualized volatility is 30%, the risk-free rate is 2%, and there are three months left until expiration. Plugging these values into the Black-Scholes equation gives me an estimated option price of around $7.48.

Remember, though, while these models are helpful tools, they aren't perfect because they cannot predict unexpected events affecting markets, like pandemics or natural disasters. Nonetheless, understanding them provides valuable insights into how professionals analyze and trade complex financial instruments. And who knows, maybe someday YOU could use these skills when managing money or investing wisely!

Welcome to our exploration of Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT)! You might be wondering what that even means - well, let's break it down together! 

Imagine you really want to buy the newest video game that just came out, but your parents say you need to save money for something more important. You feel disappointed and frustrated because you can't have the game right now. That feeling inside you when things don't go as planned - that's where we start with ACT.

Now, imagine instead of getting upset about not having the game, you think about how much fun you had playing previous games and look forward to saving up so you can enjoy this new one too. This shift in thinking helps us deal with life's challenges better. And guess what? That's exactly what ACT aims to do! It teaches us ways to handle difficult emotions by accepting them and committing to actions that align with our values.

Let me explain further using another example. Have you ever felt super nervous before giving a presentation at school? I know I did! Instead of letting those nerves take over, ACT encourages us to accept that being anxious is natural sometimes. Once we acknowledge that feeling, we can focus on why the presentation matters to us, like sharing cool facts about space or impressing our teacher. By doing this, we commit ourselves to give it our best shot despite feeling nervous.

Here are some key points about ACT:
1. **Acceptance:** Learning to welcome all feelings, good or bad, rather than pushing them away or fighting against them.
2. **Cognitive Defusion:** Understanding that thoughts aren't always reality; they come and go like clouds in the sky.
3. **Mindfulness:** Paying attention to the present moment without judgment.
4. Values Clarification:** Identifying what truly matters to us in life.
5. Committed Action:** Setting goals based on our values and working towards achieving them consistently.

By learning these skills, we become more resilient and able to navigate any bumps along our journey called life. So next time you face a challenge, remember acceptance and commitment can lead you closer to happiness and success!

MTR
The Mass Transit Railway or MTR (in Chinese, , literally "Hong Kong Railway Company"; or  for short) is the main rapid transit railway system in Hong Kong. Since the MTR service first opened in 1979, the network has grown to more than 150 stations. Built and run by MTR Corporation Limited, the MTR system is a very popular mode of public transport in Hong Kong, with around 2.46 million passengers riding each day.

Construction
Hong Kong's growing economy and the quick increase in population created a lot of traffic problems. The Hong Kong government made a study of these problems. The first line was opened in 1979. The MTR was quickly popular with the people of Hong Kong, so later they built more lines to cover more ground. People are still deciding how and where to expand the MTR network next.

Network

History of the MTR

Initial proposal
During the 1960s, the government of Hong Kong thought they need to accommodate increasing road traffic that growing Hong Kong's economy would bring. British transport consultants Freeman, Fox, Wilbur Smith & Associates were appointed to study the transport system of Hong Kong. The consultants released the Hong Kong Mass Transport Study in September 1967, which proposed the construction of a mass transport underground railway system in Hong Kong.

In 1970, an underground network with four lines was laid out and planned as part of the British consultants' new report, Hong Kong Mass Transit: Further Studies. The four lines were to be the Kwun Tong Line, Tsuen Wan Line, Island Line, and East Kowloon Line. However, the lines that were eventually constructed were somewhat different compared with the lines that were originally proposed by the "Hong Kong Mass Transport Study".

In 1972, the Hong Kong government authorised construction of the Initial System, a 20-km system that roughly translates to the Kwun Tong Line today (except the line now extends to Tiu Keng Leng). Negotiations with four major construction consortia started in 1973. The government's intention was to tender the entire project, based on the British design, as a single tender at a fixed price. A consortium from Japan signed an agreement to construct the system in early 1974, but in December of the same year it pulled out from the agreement, stemming from fears of the Arab oil crisis.

Modified Initial System (Kwun Tong Line / Tsuen Wan Line)
Several weeks later, in early 1975, a government agency known as the Mass Transport Provisional Authority was established to take charge of the project. It announced that the Initial System would be slightly reduced to 15.6 kilometres, and renamed it the Modified Initial System. Plans for a single contract were also abandoned in favour of 25 engineering contracts and 10 electrical and mechanical contracts.

In addition, the government-owned Hong Kong Mass Transit Railway Corporation (MTRC) was established to replace the Mass Transport Provisional Authority. (This was the company succeeded by the MTR Corporation Limited on 30 June 2000)

Construction of the Modified Initial System (now part of Kwun Tong Line and Tsuen Wan Line) commenced in November 1975. After almost four years, the northern section was completed on 30 September 1979. On 1 October 1979, the northern section was opened, with trains running from Shek Kip Mei to Kwun Tong. The route from Tsim Sha Tsui to Shek Kip Mei was opened in December of the same year.

Chapter 1: Introduction to Electric Circuits and Logic Gates

Have you ever wondered how your video game console, tablet, or even a simple flashlight works? Well, behind all those gadgets are tiny electronic components working together to create magic! Today, we'll embark on an exciting journey through the world of electric circuits, logic gates, andBoolean algebra - cornerstones of electronics! So grab your safety goggles and let's dive right in!

Section A: What are Electric Circuits?

Imagine setting up a train track for your miniature trains to run around. Now think about electricity as if it were the toy train moving along the tracks. An electric circuit functions similarly; it's like a pathway where electrical energy flows from its source (like batteries) to perform various tasks before returning to the source. To build our own simple circuit, we need three main components:

1. Power Source: This provides juice to our circuit, just like how a power station supplies electricity to your home. Batteries are common portable power sources used in everyday devices.
2. Conductor: Copper wires act as conductors, allowing current to flow effortlessly from one component to another within the circuit.
3. Load: Finally, this part does something useful with the electrical energy. For example, a light bulb shines brightly when current passes through it!

Let's try a fun activity! Using a battery, some copper wire, and a small light bulb, can you set up a functioning circuit? Remember, safety first - ask an adult for help if needed!

Section B: Introducing Logic Gates

Now imagine having a secret language that only your friends understand, enabling you to communicate messages discreetly among others. Similarly, logic gates serve as building blocks for digital communication using binary code (only zeros and ones). They manipulate and process information based on specific rules. Let me introduce you to the most common types of logic gates: AND, OR, and NOT.

AND Gate: Think of this gate as a bouncer outside a club who allows entry only if both conditions are met. It outputs '1' (true) if input values A and B are true ('1'), otherwise, it outputs '0' (false).

Example: If I have enough money (A = true) and my parents give permission (B = true), then I can go to the movies. Otherwise, no movie time!

OR Gate: Imagine ordering food at a restaurant; you get what you want whether you choose soup or salad. That's exactly how an OR gate behaves. Outputting '1', if either A or B is true, else outputting '0'.

NOT Gate: Consider this the grumpy older sibling constantly contradicting everything you say. Whenever there's an input value, the NOT gate flips it to the opposite state. Thus, if A=1, NOT(A)=0; while if A=0, NOT(A)=1.

Activity Time: Can you figure out which type of logic gate best fits each situation below?
a. When playing soccer, I wear my lucky socks if it's sunny or raining.
b. My alarm goes off only if it's morning and mom remembers turning it on.
c. At a fast-food drive-thru, order fries or they'll forget to give them to you.

Intriguing, isn't it? You've now learned about fundamental concepts of technology and engineering, specifically understanding electric circuits and logic gates. With practice and patience, soon you'll master more complex topics such as Boolean algebra and design amazing projects! Happy experimenting, future engineers!

There is a special pattern in wood called curly. It can be seen in all types of wood, but it is most common in red and silver leaf maple. Sometimes, a piece of wood can be a little bit wavy or very wavy. This wave can make the wood bend or break more easily.

There's a kind of wood we call "brash wood". This kind of wood doesn't have a lot of rings if you look at it closely, or it might be starting to rot. This wood is easy to break and it often cracks if you try to bend it. Cherry wood is often this kind of wood.

There are also woods that bend really well. One of these is called "white ash". It's not too heavy and it's pretty hard. It can handle a lot of weight without breaking. When it dries, it can shrink a little bit. The outer part of the wood, called the sapwood, is almost white. The inside part, called the heartwood, is light brown and sometimes it can be darker. It's sometimes hard to tell the sapwood from the heartwood because they look very similar.
This wood changes to a light orange color if it's not dried quickly. It has lines in it like a red oak tree, and these lines are usually straight. It bends very well and is strong for how much it weighs. It's also good at not breaking when hit hard. That's why it's often used for baseball bats.

A bug called the emerald ash borer came from Asia to North AM city in the 1990s. This bug digs into the living part of the tree, which is between the bark and the wood. This hurts the tree so much that it dies. When the tree dies, it becomes weak quickly. This weak or dead wood is called brash wood. When brash wood is bent, it breaks.

As of some time ago, we stopped buying this type of wood because too much of it was brash or dead. We think that 80% of the last batch of wood we got was brash or dead, so we didn't take any of it. Right now, we don't know anyone who can promise to give us wood from living trees. When we run out of the wood we have now, we won't get more. The harm done by the emerald ash borer might be like the harm done by other tree diseases.
This is about two types of trees. The first one is often called Cherry tree. It's a strong tree with a hardness level of 950. The wood from this tree starts off a pale yellow color, but as it gets older and sees more sunlight, it turns a golden brown. The grain of the wood can be a bit uneven, which can make it tricky to bend. But people have liked using this wood to make things like cabinets for a long time because it turns a nice reddish-brown color.

The second tree is often known as the Hard Maple tree. The wood from this tree is almost white if it's cut in the winter. But, the inside part of the tree, called the heartwood, is a darker reddish-brown. If this wood isn't dried quickly, it can turn orange. The grain of the wood is very smooth, which can make it shine in the light.

Chapter 1: Introduction to Coding Adventures

Imagine being able to create your own video games, design amazing websites, or even build robots that can do cool tasks! Well, guess what? With coding, all these things are possible, and much more!

So, what exactly is coding? Think of it like giving instructions to your computer or robot, just like how you follow a recipe to bake a cake or directions to find a new place. By using special languages called programming languages, we tell computers or robots what to do step-by-step. And when they follow our instructions correctly, magic happens!

Why is coding important? Coding helps us understand how technology works, and gives us the power to shape the world around us. It also allows us to express ourselves creatively while solving real-world problems. Just think about it - if you could build a website that teaches others about taking care of pets, or develop an app that helps people learn math facts faster, wouldn't that be awesome? That's the kind of impact coding can have!

Now, let's talk about why protecting creative work, like code, is essential. Imagine spending hours creating a beautiful piece of art or writing a fantastic story, only to have someone else take credit for it. Not fair, right? That's where copyright comes in. Copyright ensures that creators get recognized and rewarded for their original ideas. When you see a little symbol like '', it means that someone has claimed ownership over their creation and asked others to respect their rights. So always remember to appreciate and admire other people's creations instead of copying them.

German-speaking Community of Belgium
The German-speaking Community of Belgium (, short DGB) is one of the three federal communities in Belgium. It is the main part of the so-called East Cantons () of Belgium. It has an area of , and a population of over 73,000, of which almost 100% are German speaking (traditionally Ripuarian-speaking).

Its capital is Eupen; it is part of the province of Lige and borders on the Netherlands, Germany, and Luxembourg.

The area was known as Eupen-Malmedy, and is now called the East Cantons. It is made up of the German-speaking Community and the municipalities of Malmedy and Waimes (Weismes), which belong to the French-Speaking Community of Belgium.

The East Cantons were part of the Rhine Province of Prussia in Germany until 1920 but were annexed by Belgium following Germany's defeat in World War I and the subsequent Treaty of Versailles. Thus they also became known as the cantons rdims, "redeemed cantons". The peace treaty of Versailles demanded the "questioning" of the local population about their political status.

This was not a secret vote, and anyone who did not want to become Belgian had to register their full name and address. Many locals feared reprisals or even expulsion after enlisting.

In the mid-1920s the kingdom of Belgium seemed to want to sell the region back to Germany. The French government told the Belgians to stop the Belgian-German talks about the deal.

In 1940 the new cantons were retaken by Germany in World War II. They had only been in Belgium for 20 years, so the majority of people of the east cantons still thought of themselves as German. Following the defeat of Germany in 1945 the cantons were once again taken over by Belgium.

In the early 1960s Belgium was divided into four language areas, the Dutch speaking Flemish area, the French speaking area, the bilingual capital of Brussels, and the German speaking area of the east cantons. In 1973, three communities and three regions were established and granted internal autonomy. The legislative Parliament of the German-speaking Community, Rat der Deutschsprachigen Gemeinschaft, was set up. Today the German-speaking Community has a degree of self government, especially in language and cultural matters, but it still part of French speaking Wallonia.

Some people want the German-speaking Community to be its own region. One of these is the current Minister-President Karl-Heinz Lambertz.

Government
The German-speaking Community has its own government, which is appointed for five years by its parliament. The Government is headed by a Minister-President, who acts as the "prime minister" of the Community, and is assisted by the Ministry of the German-speaking Community. The government currently formed by four Ministers:
Karl-Heinz Lambertz, Minister-President and Minister for District Authorities
Bernd Gentges, Deputy Minister-President and Minister for Vocational Training and Employment, Social Policy and Tourism
Oliver Paasch, Minister for Education and Research
Isabelle Weykmans, Minister for Culture and Media, Monuments and Sites, Youth and Sport

Course Unit: Understanding State Courts in the United States

Welcome, future lawyers and judges! Today, we will explore the fascinating world of state courts in the United States. You might be wondering, what exactly are state courts? Well, imagine if you had a disagreement with your friend about who gets to use the swing set at recess. To solve this problem, you could ask a teacher to help you figure things out. In much the same way, when people in a state disagree on something, they can take their case to a state court. These special places help settle arguments and keep our communities running smoothly.

Now, let's dive into the details of how these state courts work. There are different types of state courts across the country, but most follow a similar structure. Some states might call them slightly different names, but there are usually trial courts, appellate courts, and supreme courts. Let's break down each one:

1. Trial Courts: Imagine being back in your classroom again, where you first raised your hand to tell your teacher about the playground dispute. This initial stage, where you share your side of the story and bring evidence, is like a trial court. It's the place where legal battles begin. Judges listen to witnesses, examine physical proof, and hear opening statements and closing arguments. After considering all the information presented, trial court judges make decisions based on the laws of their specific state. If anyone involved in the case isn't happy with the outcome, though, they can appeal to higher courts - just like asking another grownup for help after talking to your teacher.
2. Appellate Courts: Now, think about going up one more grade level. At this point, you get to talk to someone who wasn't involved in your original discussion. An appellate court works similarly. When parties aren't satisfied with a trial court decision, they can request a review from an appellate court. A panel of judges examines the record from the lower court, looking closely at any mistakes made during the trial process. They won't rehash old evidence or testimony; instead, they focus solely on whether errors occurred along the way. If so, appellate court judges can change parts of the ruling or even send the case back to the trial court for further action.
3. Supreme Court: Finally, let's say your principal wants to weigh in on the playground conflict. That would be like taking your case to the highest court in the land - the state supreme court. Typically, only a small number of cases reach this stage because losing parties must prove significant problems with previous rulings. Once heard, supreme court justices issue final judgments that cannot be challenged elsewhere within the state's judicial system.

One interesting fact about state courts is that no two systems look alike! Each state designs its own unique court framework according to local needs and preferences. So while many aspects remain consistent throughout the nation, every state offers its distinct flavor of justice.

Now you know all about state courts and how they operate. Just remember: next time you find yourself in a disagreement, consider resolving it peacefully through conversation and compromise. But if you do end up needing a judge's assistance someday, now you understand what happens behind those courthouse doors!

Mrkischer Kreis
The Mrkischer Kreis is a district (Kreis) in central North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany.

The district was created in 1975 as part of the reorganisation of North Rhine-Westphalian districts.

Twinning
The district is twinned with
, Wrexham County Borough. This was started in 1970 by Iserlohn.
, Elbe-Elster. This started as a twin with Finsterwalde before Finsterwald became a part of Elbe-Elster.
, Racibrz district.

Coat of arms

Towns and municipalities

Politics and administration
The district is led by a Landrat. The headquarters of the government of the county are in Ldenscheid, but there are county halls with parts of the administration in Iserlohn and Altena, too. The police headquarters of the county are in Iserlohn.

The county council meets in the county hall in Iserlohn. Its last election was on September 26 2004.

In the middle of the garden stood an old tree, its roots deep in the ground. She sat beneath its branches, feeling the cool shade wrap around her. What stories had the tree heard? What secrets did it keep? She thought about love and how it could grow like the plants around her, sometimes wild and sometimes gentle.

Days passed, and she returned often, sharing her thoughts with the flowers. They listened quietly, their blooms nodding as if they understood. She believed that in this place, everything was alive with dreams. Each day was a new chance to find beauty, to uncover more wonder in her heart.

As the sun set one evening, painting the sky with orange and pink, she felt a connection to it all. The flowers, the tree, and the sky became one big poem of love. She smiled and knew that wonder was everywhere. Perhaps, dear reader, you too can find such magic in your garden.

Abu Dhabi
Abu Dhabi (, 'Ab aby) is the capital city of the United Arab Emirates. It is in the emirate of Abu Dhabi. Abu Dhabi is one of the seven emirates which form the United Arab Emirates(UAE). The city is on a T-shaped island going into the Persian Gulf from the central western coast. The city is 972 km2 in size. The city had a population of 1.45 million people in 2022. Abu Dhabi is also the capital of UAE and is the largest emirates in UAE.

History
People started to live in the area and call it Abu Dhabi about 300 years ago. In the 1970s, the Bani Yas tribe made Abu Dhabi their capital city. Shakhbut bin-Dhiyab Al Nahyan became the leader of the city in 1818. People found oil in 1958 in Abu Dhabi. They started to sell the oil in the 1960s. In 1971 December the 2nd, Abu Dhabi joined the United Arab Emirates and became the capital city.

Weather
Abu Dhabi is in a desert and has a desert climate. There is not a lot of rain but it does rain a little in the winter months. The average rainfall per year is 51 cm. It can also be very hot. In the daytime, the average summer temperature is 42 C. The average daytime temperature in the winter is more comfortable at 23 C.

Tourism
Abu Dhabi has many tourist attractions such as the Sheikh Zayed Mosque, Abu Dhabi Louvre Museum, Mangrove Kayaking Tours, Ferrari World, the Emirates Palace, Qasr Al-Hosn, bout towers, Abu Dhabi According to the Department of Culture and Tourism. The usual amount of people that come in Abu Dhabi is 10 million per year. Abu Dhabi also has Jabal Hafeet, which is the tallest mountain in the UAE.
