Judiciary
The judiciary or judicial system is the system of courts that administers (or makes decisions about) justice. This kind of system, does its work in the name of the state (or country) or the sovereign. A judicial system is used to resolve disputes.

The term is also used to refer collectively to the judges and magistrates who form the basis of the judiciary, as well as the other people who help keep the system running properly.

Separation of powers
Separation of powers causes separate branches of government that each has a different purpose. The judiciary is the branch of government that interprets the law. Such systems may have three branches: Legislature, Executive and Judiciary. Often the judiciary branch has courts of first resort, appellate courts, and a supreme court or constitutional court. Decisions of the lower courts may be appealed to the higher courts.

Judiciary in the USA

In the United States the federal Judicial Branch is an integrated system of courts headed by the Supreme Court of the United States. Each state also has a judicial system.

Law occupations
Courts (law)

Ardennes (department)
Ardennes is a department in the Grand Est region of northeastern France named after the Ardennes forest. Its prefecture is the city of Charleville-Mzires.

History
Ardennes is one of the original 83 departments created during the French Revolution on 4 March 1790 with Mzires as is capital. It was formed with the former province of Champagne, the principalities of Sedan and Argonne and other territories.

It was divided in six districts: Charleville, Grandpr, Rethel, Rocroi, Sedan and Vouziers.

In 1800, with the creation of the arrondissements in France, the six districts were changed into five arrondissements: Mzires, Rethel, Rocroi, Sedan and Vouziers.

On 10 September 1926, the arrondissements of Rocroi and Sedan were eliminated but in 1942 Sedan was made again an arrondissement.

The communes of Charleville and Mzires are joined to form the new commune of Charleville-Mzires; it was named the capital of the department.

Geography
Ardennes is part of the Grand Est region. It has an area of .

The department borders with Belgium (Namur and Luxembourg provinces) and 3 other departments in 2 regions:
Hauts-de-France region
Aisne (west)
Grand Est region
Marne (south)
Meuse (east)

The highest point of the department is Croix-Scaille () with an altitude of high.; it is found between the French commune of Hautes-Rivires and the Belgian commune of Gedinne.

The lowest point is on the Aisne river in Brienne-sur-Aisne, high.

Several rivers flow through the department; the main rivers are the Meuse, in the north, and the Aisne, in the south.

Climate
The Kppen climate classification type for the climate at Charleville-Mzires is an "Oceanic climate" (also known as Marine West Coast Climate) and of the subtype "Cfb".

The average amount of precipitation for the year in Charleville-Mzires is . The month with the most precipitation on average is November with of precipitation. The month with the least precipitation on average is June with an average of .

The average temperature for the year in Charleville-Mzires is . The warmest month, on average, is July with an average temperature of . The coolest month on average is January, with an average temperature of .

Administration
Ardennes is managed by the Departmental Council of Ardennes in Charleville-Mzires. The department is part of the Grand Est region.

Administrative divisions
There are 4 arrondissements (districts), 19 cantons and 452 communes (municipalities) in Ardennes.

Now, how does Ollie, who doesn't have kidneys like we do, manage to do this? Well, meet his trusty helpers - Contractile Vacuoles! These special parts of Ollie's cell work hard to remove extra water and waste products so that Ollie stays healthy and balanced.

When Ollie takes in too much water (maybe after playing in the rain), his Contractile Vacuoles come into action! They fill up with the excess water and then gently squeeze, pushing the water out of Ollie's cell, preventing him from bursting. It's like when you drink too much juice and need to visit the bathroom!

But Contractile Vacuoles aren't only about squeezing out water. They also help eliminate waste substances that could be harmful to Ollie if they build up inside him. By working together, these powerful little helpers keep Ollie's insides clean and functioning properly!

So remember, even the tiniest creatures have unique ways to take care of themselves. And although Ollie might look different from you and me, deep down, we all share something in common - the need to stay clean and healthy!

Trialeti culture
The Trialeti culture was seen around the 2nd millennium B.C. In the late 3rd millennium B.C. settlements of the Kura-Araxes culture began to be replaced by early Trialeti culture sites. The Trialeti culture was the second culture to appear in the Caucasus, after the Kura-Araxes culture. The Trialeti culture shows close ties with the highly-developed cultures of the ancient world, particularly with the Aegean.

Chapter 9: Keeping Safe on the Streets - Making Smart Decisions
=============================================================

Imagine walking home from school one day when suddenly, you see two people arguing loudly up ahead. As you get closer, the argument starts to turn physical, with punches being thrown. What do you do?

Most people would want to help or at least watch what's happening. But sometimes, getting too close to danger can lead to trouble. This chapter will teach you about making smart decisions when faced with potentially risky situations like this. It might just keep you out of harm's way!

The Art of Walking Away
-----------------------

Have you ever heard the phrase "discretion is the better part of valor"? It means that knowing when to walk away from a dangerous situation is often the wisest choice. Our first tip for staying safe is learning how to recognize potential dangers and avoiding them altogether.

For example, if you come across a heated argument between strangers, it may be best to cross the street or take another route rather than sticking around to see what happens next. While your instinct might tell you to stay and observe, remember that things could escalate quickly, leading to violence. By simply removing yourself from such a scenario, you greatly reduce any chance of becoming accidentally injured.

Think Before You Act
-------------------

Now let's consider another hypothetical situation. Suppose someone approaches you while you're waiting for the bus and demands your phone. Your heart rate spikes, adrenaline pumps through your veins - what do you do now?

First, take a deep breath. Try not to panic; instead, think clearly. If possible, hand over your phone quietly without resisting. Remember, material possessions aren't worth putting yourself in harm's way. Afterward, report the incident to authorities immediately so they can handle the situation appropriately.

However, if you believe the person intends further harm after taking your belongings, yelling or running away might alert others nearby who can assist. Use good judgment here because each situation is unique.

Know When To Seek Help
----------------------

It's crucial to understand that no one should face threatening circumstances alone. Whether it's calling the police, seeking assistance from a trusted adult, or confiding in friends, never hesitate to ask for help when needed. Safety always comes first!

Remember, our aim isn't to instill fear but to empower you with knowledge. Being aware of these strategies can boost your confidence and equip you to navigate life's challenges more effectively. Stay vigilant, stay informed, and most importantly, stay safe!

New York City Subway
The fare is $2.75. Riders must pay with MetroCards or OMNY. The subway started using MetroCards in 1994. At subway stations, riders can buy MetroCards from the station booth or from vending machines. Riders can also buy MetroCards from many places in New York City, like convenience stores and newspaper sellers. ONMY later came out in 2019 as a testing fare for credit/debit cards on the 4/5/6 lines, to use for another way to pay for your subway fare. Once it succeeded, it expanded all throughout the NYCTA. Currently, it is planning to replace the MetroCard by 2024.

Rider safety

Riders are allowed to take pictures using cameras, but are not allowed to take pictures with cameras that flash or with cameras that are on tripods.

Subway police can search riders to make sure they do not have weapons or other items that could be used to hurt other people.

When riders get hurt, usually it is because they slip when they are getting on or off the train. This is because there is a gap between the train and the platform. In recent times, workers have made the gaps smaller to prevent people from slipping. Often messages are played from loudspeakers that say "Please watch the gap when entering and exiting the train".

Train safety
The MTA makes sure that New York City Subway trains run without accidents. There are railroad switches, railroad signals, and speed limits on the subway. All tracks also have a stopper on the side. If the train passes a red signal, the stopper will stop the train.

A black-and-white striped board hangs above the middle of each platform. The conductor has to point to the board in front of him or her. After the conductor points to the board, the train doors will open.

The subway has had over 56 train accidents since 1918. The Malbone Street Wreck on November 1, 1918 was the most deadly. That crash killed 93 people.

Since the late 1990s and early 2000s, the MTA has experimented with Automatic train operation. New York City Subway trains normally run with a train conductor and a train operator. In 2006, the L train was the first route to be run by computers. The 7 train is becoming the second route to be run by a computer. There are computers both on the train and along the side of the tracks. The computer does the engineer's job by driving and stopping the train.

White House
The second floor family residence includes the Yellow Oval Room, East and West Sitting Halls, the White House Master Bedroom, President's Dining Room, the Treaty Room, Lincoln Bedroom and Queens' Bedroom, as well as two additional bedrooms, a smaller kitchen, and a private dressing room. The third floor consists of the White House Solarium, Game Room, and a Linen Room.

West Wing
The West Wing holds the Oval Office and offices of his senior staff, with room for about 50 employees. It also includes the Cabinet Room, where the president conducts business meetings and where the Cabinet meets, as well as the White House Situation Room, James S. Brady Press Briefing Room, and Roosevelt Room.

East Wing
The East Wing, which contains additional office space, was added to the White House in 1942. Among its uses, the East Wing has intermittently housed the offices and staff of the first lady and the White House Social Office. Rosalynn Carter, in 1977, was the first to place her personal office in the East Wing and to formally call it the "Office of the First Lady". The East Wing was built during World War II in order to hide the construction of an underground bunker to be used in emergencies. The bunker has come to be known as the Presidential Emergency Operations Center.

Grounds
The White House and grounds cover just over . Before the construction of the North Portico, most public events were entered from the South Lawn, the grading and planting of which was ordered by Thomas Jefferson. Jefferson also drafted a planting plan for the North Lawn that included large trees that would have mostly obscured the house from Pennsylvania Avenue.

During the mid-to-late 19th century a series of ever larger greenhouses were built on the west side of the house, where the current West Wing is located. During the Kennedy administration, the White House Rose Garden was redesigned by Rachel Lambert Mellon.

The Rose Garden borders the West Colonnade. Bordering the East Colonnade is the Jacqueline Kennedy Garden, which was begun by Jacqueline Kennedy but completed after her husband's assassination. Michelle Obama planted the White House's first organic garden and installed beehives on the South Lawn of the White House, which will supply organic produce and honey to the first family and for state dinners and other official gatherings.

Jay-Z
In 2003, Jay-Z stopped rapping, because he found that there were not enough good rappers to compete with him. He said that the game was too easy for him. He decided to concentrate more on his producer career than his rap career. He became the president of Def Jam Recordings. He signed a lot of great artists such as Rihanna, Ne-Yo and Kanye West. He also became a businessman by creating his own clothing company, Rocawear, and owning a part of the Brooklyn Nets, an NBA basketball team.

Present
After a step back in his career, he made a decision in 2006 to come back into the game. He created the albums "Kingdom Came" and the year after "American Gangster". In 2009, he released Blue print 3, but in 2011 he teamed up with Kanye West to do an LP called Watch the Throne. This album went triple hit, made the top rap charts for August and also nominated for the Grammy for the best rap Album. Now, he is known to be one of the best rappers of all time. In April 2011 Jay-Z started a website called Life+ Times. He also took part in Barack Obama's last elections. Jay-Z's twelfth album, Magna Carta Holy Grail, was released in July 2013. The album topped the chart to number one. It was nominated for Album of the Year at the 2013 BET Hip Hop Awards. The first single on the album, "Holy Grail", features Justin Timberlake singing in it. It reached number four on the US Billboard 100. In South Korea it reached number one. Jay-Z's wife Beyonc sings on "Part II (On the Run)". In December 2013 Jay-Z was nominated for nine Grammy Awards. This was more than anyone else that year. He rapped on his wife Beyonc Knowles' fifth album Beyonc.

Together with Beyonc, Jay-Z has three children: daughter Blue Ivy (born 2012) and twins Rumi and Sir Carter, who were born in June 2017.

Under the old tree, a boy sat quietly. He watched as the leaves danced in the wind. This boy wanted to explore the world but felt too scared. One day, a wise turtle crawled by. The turtle was on a secret mission to find a lost flower that could make anyone brave. The boy saw the turtle and felt curious.

"Why do you move so slowly?" asked the boy. The turtle replied, "Slow and steady wins the race. I am looking for a special flower." The boy felt a spark of excitement. "Can I help you?" he asked. The turtle smiled and said, "Yes, but remember, it takes time."

As they traveled, the boy learned from the turtle. They walked through thick grass and crossed small streams. The turtle shared stories of bravery. The boy listened and began to feel stronger. They searched for many days, meeting other animals and learning from them.

One day, they found a clue. A colorful butterfly fluttered by and pointed to a hidden valley. "The flower is there!" it said. They hurried to the valley, but it was far. The boy felt tired and wanted to give up. The turtle said, "Do not rush. Take a moment to breathe."

They took a break under a shady tree. The turtle encouraged the boy to think of all they had seen. The boy felt proud of their journey. He realized he was growing braver. After resting, they continued to the valley. Finally, they spotted the lost flower glowing in the sunlight.

The boy approached the flower. As he touched it, he felt a wave of courage. "I am ready to explore!" he shouted. The turtle smiled, proud of the boy's growth. They picked the flower and celebrated their mission together. The boy learned that bravery comes from inside.

With the flower in hand, they returned home. The boy shared his adventure with his friends. He showed them the flower and told them the turtle's wisdom. Now, the boy felt confident to try new things. He understood that it was okay to be scared sometimes.

Chapter 1: Introduction to Foreign Languages

Have you ever wanted to learn another language? Speaking a different language can open up new worlds! You could travel to a faraway country and communicate with people there. Or maybe you just think it would be cool to understand what your friend's parents are saying when they talk in their native tongue. Whatever your reason, learning a foreign language can be fun and rewarding.

In this chapter, we will introduce three popular languages: German, Spanish, and French. Each one has its own unique sound, grammar rules, and vocabulary. But before we dive into those details, let's first explore why learning a foreign language is important and exciting.

Why Learn a Foreign Language?
-------------------------------

Imagine being able to watch a movie without subtitles or read a book in its original language. Learning a foreign language allows us to appreciate art, literature, and culture on a deeper level. It also helps us connect with others who speak that language. By understanding someone else's perspective and way of life, we become more empathetic and open-minded citizens of the world.

Moreover, knowing a second language can give you an advantage in many fields such as business, healthcare, tourism, and education. For example, companies often look for employees who can speak multiple languages because they can interact with international clients more effectively. Similarly, doctors and nurses need to communicate with patients who may only speak their native language. And teachers who know more than one language can teach abroad or work with diverse groups of students.

The Joy of Learning Languages
-----------------------------

Learning a foreign language is like solving a puzzle. Every word you learn is a piece that fits into the bigger picture. Once you put enough pieces together, you start seeing patterns and making connections. Suddenly, words flow smoothly, sentences make sense, and conversations happen naturally.

But don't worry if it seems hard at first. All new things require effort and practice. Think about when you learned how to ride a bike or play a video game. At first, it might have felt impossible. But after several tries, you got better and enjoyed the process. The same applies to learning a foreign language. With patience, curiosity, and determination, you too can master a new language.

------------------

Hide Your iPod's Dirty Music from Your Parents: A Comprehensive Guide

Are you worried that your parents might discover some explicit or otherwise inappropriate music on your iPod? Fear not! This detailed guide will walk you through the process of hiding your mature content from prying eyes and ears. By following these steps, you can ensure your privacy while maintaining access to all of your tunes.

**Step 1: Create Playlists**

Create playlists for different types of music, separating clean tracks from potentially questionable ones. Organize them based on genre, mood, artist, or any other criteria that make sense to you. This way, when you want to listen to more sensitive material, you won't have to sift through family-friendly songs first.

Key Tip: Use vague names for your risqu playlists, such as "Study Tunes" or "Workout Mix," so they don't raise suspicion if found.

**Step 2: Restrict Access with Guided Access (iOS)**

If you share an iTunes account with your parents or they have physical access to your device, consider using Guided Access, a built-in feature in iOS devices. It allows you to restrict certain apps and features, preventing others from accessing specific parts of your iPod.

1. Open Settings > General > Accessibility.
2. Scroll down and tap on Guided Access.
3. Turn on Guided Access and set a passcode.
4. Open the Music app and triple-click the home button to enable Guided Access.
5. Circle the areas of the screen you want to disable (e.g., explicit lyrics warning).
6. Tap Start at the top right corner.

Now, only the allowed functions within the Music app will be accessible until you enter the correct passcode to exit Guided Access.

**Step 3: Disable Explicit Lyrics**

To prevent explicit lyrics from appearing during songplay, follow these steps:

1. Connect your iPod to a computer and open iTunes.
2. Select your iPod from the Devices list.
3. Click Summary, then Options.
4. Uncheck "Show explicit lyrics."

This action hides explicit lyrics but doesn't remove them entirely; you can still view them by manually selecting "View Explicit Lyrics" within the Now Playing window. However, this reduces the likelihood of accidentally displaying offensive language.

**Step 4: Encrypt Backups (Mac Only)**

Encrypting backups adds another layer of security by protecting your data with a password. If someone gains unauthorized access to your computer or backup files, encrypted backups ensure they cannot view your hidden content without entering the correct password.

1. Connect your iPod to your Mac.
2. Open iTunes and select your iPod from the Device list.
3. Under the Summary tab, check "Encrypt iPhone Backup."
4. Enter a memorable yet secure password when prompted.

Keep in mind that forgetting this password means losing access to your backed-up data forever. Store it somewhere safe or use a password manager like LastPass or 1Password for added protection.

**Step 5: Hide iTunes Library on Computer**

Hiding your entire iTunes library folder keeps nosy individuals from stumbling upon your less savory selections. Note that this method works best on macOS systems since Windows users may need additional software to hide folders effectively.

1. Close iTunes completely.

Course Unit: Understanding Prayer in Christianity

Welcome to our exploration of prayer in Christianity! You might have heard the word "prayer" before, but what does it really mean for Christians? Let's dive into this fascinating world together!

Imagine having a pen pal - someone you can share your secrets, dreams, and worries with, knowing they care about you and want the best for you. For many Christians, that's what prayer feels like! It's their special way of communicating with something much bigger than themselves: God. Through prayer, they build a relationship with the divine and grow spiritually.

Now, let's meet the VIPs of Christian prayer: the Holy Trinity. This term represents the heart of Christian belief and includes three unique parts - God the Father, Jesus Christ the Son, and the Holy Spirit. When Christians pray, they often address any of these divine beings because they believe all are part of the same loving force looking out for them.

You might wonder when and where such conversations take place. Well, there aren't strict rules! Many Christians choose different times during the day for prayer, while others find specific places like churches or quiet corners at home to connect with God. Some even talk to God throughout their daily activities!

Ever noticed how people use gestures while speaking? Similarly, certain prayer positions hold significance in Christianity too. Although not mandatory, some prefer bowing their heads, folding hands, or kneeling down to show respect and focus during prayer. Again, these actions vary among individuals based on personal preferences and cultural backgrounds.

How long should prayers last? There isn't a set time limit either! Just like talking to a friend, Christian prayer could be short or lengthy depending on what one wants to discuss with God. What matters most is sincerity and openness in sharing feelings and thoughts.

But why bother praying? Good question! Christians see numerous benefits in regular prayer. Besides strengthening their bond with God, it brings peace, comfort, guidance, and gratitude into their lives. Also, by sharing concerns through prayer, they experience support from both God and their religious community.

Finally, did you know that tools exist to enhance this spiritual journey? Things like prayer books, candles, crosses, or rosary beads serve as reminders of God's presence and help maintain focus during prayer. These objects become symbols of faith, adding depth and meaning to Christian liturgical practices.

So here we are, wrapping up our look into Christian prayer! Remember, every person has their own unique style of prayer influenced by individual beliefs, traditions, and experiences. Embrace curiosity and respect towards diverse approaches, celebrating the beauty of diversity found within religions worldwide. Happy exploring!

1500
Year 1500 (MD) was a leap year starting on Wednesday (link will display the full calendar) of the Julian calendar. The year 1500 wasn't a leap year in the Proleptic Gregorian calendar.

The year was seen as being especially important by many Christians in Europe, who thought it would bring the beginning of the end of the world. Their belief was based on the phrase "half-time after the time", when the apocalypse was due to occur, which appears in the Book of Revelation and was seen as referring to 1500. This time was also just after the Old World's discovery of the Americas in 1492, and therefore was influenced greatly by the New World.[1]

Historically, the year 1500 is also often identified, somewhat arbitrarily, as marking the end of the Middle Ages and beginning of the Early Modern Era.

The end of this year marked the halfway point of the 2nd millennium, as there were 500 years before it and 500 years after it.

Breezy and Drizzle were two best friends who lived on Windy Willow Farm. One sunny day, they noticed that all the plants in their garden had wilted and turned brown! They were so sad and didn't know what to do.

Breezy said, "Drizzle, I think we need to ask Farmer Flo for help." So, they went to find her. When they did, Breezy exclaimed, "Farmer Flo, our beautiful garden has become sick!"

With a concerned look, Farmer Flo asked them to describe what happened. After hearing their concerns, she reassured them by saying, "Dear friends, let's stay positive. We can fix this together. First, let's figure out what might have caused this problem."

They observed that the soil was dry and hard due to lack of water. Farmer Flo explained, "Plants drink water from the ground. Without enough water, they cannot make food for themselves and begin to wilt." She then showed them how to use a rain gauge to measure the amount of rainfall they receive each week. This way, they would know exactly when their plants needed extra watering.

Together, they started taking care of the garden again. But even after several days of regular watering, some plants still looked weak. Breezy wondered aloud, "Why aren't these plants getting better?"

To answer his question, Farmer Flo decided to teach them about photosynthesis - the process by which plants convert sunlight into energy. "You see," she began, "plants absorb light through their leaves. If they don't get enough sunlight, they won't produce enough food either." With new knowledge in hand, they moved their struggling plants closer to the windowsill to provide them with plenty of natural light.

Unfortunately, despite their efforts, those few plants never fully recovered. However, both Breezy and Drizzle learned valuable lessons about gardening, resilience, and the importance of caring for nature. Through patience, determination, and scientific curiosity, they knew they would create an even healthier garden next season.

Title: Guided Imagery for Kids: A Journey into Mindfulness and Meditation

Have you ever heard about magic carpets that can take you on incredible adventures? Or maybe imagined what it would be like to swim under the ocean surrounded by colorful fish and coral reefs? What if I told you there's a way to actually go on those journeys using something called guided imagery?

Guided imagery is a form of meditation where someone helps you visualize peaceful scenes or situations to calm your body and mind. It's like going on an imaginary trip! You don't need any special tools or equipment; all you need is your imagination. By practicing guided imagery regularly, you can learn how to relax, reduce stress, and even improve focus.

Let's try a simple guided imagery exercise together right now:

1. Find a comfortable place to sit or lie down, somewhere quiet where you won't be disturbed. Close your eyes gently.
2. Take three deep breaths. Breathe in slowly through your nose, hold it for a moment, then breathe out slowly through your mouth. Feel your chest rise and fall as you fill your lungs with air and let it go.
3. Now, imagine yourself sitting at the edge of a beautiful lake. The sun is setting, casting warm colors across the sky. Can you see the ripples on the water as fish swim beneath the surface?
4. Listen carefully. Hear the gentle lapping of the waves against the shore, birds singing their evening songs, and perhaps even the distant sound of leaves rustling in the breeze.
5. Smell the fresh scent of pine trees nearby and feel the cool grass under your feet. Dip your toes into the refreshing water - notice how good it feels.
6. Stay here for a few moments, just enjoying this peaceful scene. If thoughts pop up, acknowledge them but then return your focus to the lake.
7. When you're ready, take another deep breath and bring your awareness back to your surroundings. Slowly open your eyes.

Congratulations! You just experienced guided imagery. Did you notice how relaxed and calm you felt during the exercise? That's because when we use our imagination to create peaceful scenarios, our brains release chemicals that help us feel happy, safe, and less stressed. With practice, you can become better at guiding yourself on these imaginative trips whenever you want.

Incorporating guided imagery into daily life has many benefits for kids. Here are some ways you can do this:

1. Bedtime Relaxation - Before falling asleep, spend five minutes visualizing a calming environment (like the lake) to help clear your mind and prepare for rest.
2. Test Anxiety Reduction - During study breaks, close your eyes and imagine a successful testing experience. Picture yourself confidently answering questions and finishing the test early.
3. Coping with Emotions - Whenever you feel overwhelmed or upset, take a moment to picture a serene place where you feel completely safe and secure. This will help soothe strong emotions and give you time to think clearly.

So go ahead, explore the world of guided imagery and discover its amazing power. Happy travels!

Chapter 9: Empty Nest Syndrome - When Kids Leave Home

As kids grow older and more independent, they eventually leave home to start their own adventures. For many parents, this can bring about mixed emotions. On one hand, they're proud of their children for becoming responsible adults; on the other hand, it can feel lonely and strange once the house is quieter. This feeling is called Empty Nest Syndrome.

Imagine you have spent years caring for your little birdies (your children), teaching them important life skills and nurturing them with love and attention. One day, those birds fly off to build their own nests, leaving you with an empty nest at home. You might find yourself asking questions such as, "What do I do now?" or "Who am I if not just a parent?" These feelings are completely normal during midlife transitions.

Midlife is an essential stage where people redefine themselves beyond parenthood and discover new passions and interests. Lucy's story mentioned at the beginning serves as a great example of someone experiencing empty nest syndrome but still finding purpose and fulfillment. After her children left home, she decided to focus on herself and started volunteering for the Pink Berets. Her dedication led her to become their volunteer Wellness Lead and later even the Chief Operating Officer. By involving herself in meaningful activities, she transformed her experience into something positive.

Here are some tips that could help anyone dealing with empty nest syndrome:

1. Stay connected with your children. Even though they aren't living under the same roof anymore, technology allows us to communicate easily. Regular phone calls, video chats, or visits will keep your bond strong. Remember, just because your kids moved out doesn't mean they don't want or need your guidance and support.
2. Pursue hobbies and personal goals. Use this time to explore what makes YOU happy. Always wanted to learn painting? Sign up for a class. Interested in gardening? Build your dream garden. Now is the perfect opportunity to try new things and meet new people.
3. Volunteer in your community. Giving back feels good! Find organizations or causes near you that resonate with your values and offer your assistance. Whether it's helping at local schools, food banks, animal shelters, or hospitals - there are countless opportunities waiting for volunteers like you.
4. Seek professional advice. If feelings of sadness persist over a long period, consider speaking with a mental health expert. They can provide strategies and tools to cope with the changes brought about by empty nest syndrome.
5. Reconnect with friends and family members. Spend quality time with old friends or distant relatives. Attending social gatherings and catching up can remind you that you have a wide network of loved ones ready to share laughter and joy.
6. Take care of your physical health. Make sure to eat well, exercise regularly, and get enough sleep. Taking charge of your overall wellbeing plays a significant role in maintaining emotional stability.

Remember, everyone experiences transition differently, so there isn't a 'one size fits all' solution. Be patient with yourself, embrace the process, and know that growing and evolving is all part of being human.

Welcome to our math journey where we'll explore a concept that might seem complex at first glance but is actually quite simple once broken down into smaller parts. Today, we're going to learn about Function Operations and Composition! Don't worry if these words sound intimidating - by the end of this lesson, they won't anymore.

Let's start with functions. Imagine you have a vending machine that takes coins as input and gives out snacks as output. If we represent each type of coin with different numbers (a penny as 1, nickel as 5, dime as 10, etc.), then every time we put money into the machine, we get a specific kind of snack back. We could say that our vending machine follows a certain rule or pattern - this is what mathematicians call a function.

Now let's take this one step further. Suppose there are two vending machines side by side: Machine A which doubles whatever amount you insert (so if you give it $3, it returns $6), and Machine B which adds $2 to any amount given (if you give it $3, it returns $5). How would you find out how much change either machine will give you if you combine them? That's exactly what function operations do!

Function operations involve performing arithmetic calculations like addition, subtraction, multiplication, or division on functions. For example, if we want to add the outputs of Machines A and B together for every dollar we feed them, we create a new function called C(x)=A(x)+B(x). So when x=1 ($1 bill), C(1) = A(1) + B(1) = 2*1 + 2+1 = 4. Our new machine C now tells us that feeding it a $1 bill gets us $4 in total!

But wait, there's more! What happens when instead of just adding or subtracting functions, we apply one function after another? Say, first using Machine A, then Machine B? Or vice versa? Well, my friend, that brings us to function composition!

In function composition, we chain two or more functions together such that the output of one becomes the input of another. Using our previous example, composing Functions A and B means creating a third function D(x) = B(A(x)). To break it down: First, we calculate A(x); next, we use its result as the input for calculating B(x). Let's see what happens when we compose Functions A and B. When x=1 again, D(1) = B(A(1)) = B(2*1) = B(2) = 2+2 = 4. Cool, huh? Even though we performed the same operation (+$2), doing it through function composition gave a slightly different outcome than simply adding the functions together.

As you can see, functions aren't scary monsters waiting to confuse us. With some friendly interpretation and clever manipulations, they become powerful tools that help solve real-world problems. Just remember: Keep calm and trust the functions!

Let's dive into our next 2-step word problem, this time set in a movie theater!

Imagine you've been saving up money from doing chores around the house and you finally have enough to go see a movie with some friends at the local theater. The ticket prices vary depending on whether it's a matinee showing or an evening showtime. You also want to buy snacks during the movie, but you know that those can add up quickly. To make sure you don't overspend, you decide to plan out how much everything will cost beforehand.

The regular ticket price for an evening showtime is $10, but matinees only cost $7.50. Your favorite type of candy costs $4 per box and drinks are priced at $3 each. With these details in mind, let's consider some scenarios and solve them using 2-step arithmetic.

Scenario 1: You want to take three friends to a matinee showing, and everyone wants their own box of candy and drink. How much will the tickets and snacks cost?

Step 1: Calculate the total cost of the tickets by multiplying the number of people attending (you + 3 friends) by the cost of a single matinee ticket ($7.50). This gives us a total of 4 * $7.50 = $ >30.

Step 2: Add the cost of four boxes of candy ($4 each), which totals $16, and the cost of four drinks ($3 each), which comes to $12. So, the combined cost for all the tickets, candies, and drinks is $30 + $16 + $12 = $ >58.

Scenario 2: Now imagine that instead of going to a matinee, you choose to watch an evening show, still taking three friends along. However, one friend decides they don't need any snacks. What would the new total cost be?

Step 1: First, calculate the cost of the four evening tickets by multiplying the number of attendees minus one person who doesn't want snacks (3 people) by the cost of a single evening ticket ($10): 3 * $10 = $ >30.

Step 2: Next, find the combined cost of the remaining snacks. Since there are three people getting both candy and a drink, plus one additional box of candy, we first sum the cost of the required items: $4 (candy) + $3 (drink) = $7 per person; then multiply that amount by the number of people buying snacks, which is 3: 3 * $7 = $ >21. Therefore, the updated total cost including tickets and snacks is $30 + $21 = $ >51.

By working through these real-world problems involving a trip to the movies, you'll gain valuable practice setting up and solving multi-step arithmetic problems - a crucial skill as you continue learning math!

War in Afghanistan (20012021)
The War in Afghanistan was a war fought by the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, The Netherlands, Australia and other countries against the Taliban and Al-Qaeda, after the terrorist attacks against the US on September 11, 2001.

On 31 August 2021 (local time), the war ended as the last coalition soldiers (from foreign countries), left Afghanistan.

History
The war started when the US invaded Afghanistan in 2001. The US and its allies forced the Taliban and Al-Qaeda to hide. In December 2001, the US and its allies founded a new government for Afghanistan. Its president was Hamid Karzai.

By February 2002, 5,000 soldiers from ISAF (or International Security Assistance Force) were in Afghanistan. That military force was led by United States. ISAF's soldiers were on loan from the militaries of NATO countries and allied countries. In 2012 ISAF was at its maximum: 130,000 soldiers (in Afghanistan).

In 2004 Hamid Karzai started as the first president of the Islamic Republic of Afghanistan. Even though the Taliban had lost power, they formed a "shadow government". Taliban insurgents, or fighters, controlled many parts of Afghanistan, and enforced their own laws.

Osama bin Laden was killed in Pakistan, May 2011.

British troops left Afghanistan in 2015, after 5 years of training the Afghanistan police to deal with threats from the Taliban.

After security deteriorated, American soldiers returned and over 10,000 were in the country at the end of 2017. In 2020, the US and NATO allies promised to leave Afghanistan as long as the Taliban agreed to certain things: not allowing terrorists to operate in its area, and starting peace talks with the Afghanistan government. In mid-2021, the Taliban began a military offensive to enlarge their territory as US and allied forces began to leave. By August 15, 2021, the Taliban had recaptured Kabul and defeated the Afghan government.

An anti-Taliban front took control of the Panjshir Valley, in August 2021.

During the 2021 evacuation from Afghanistan, over 150,000 people chose to to be taken out of Afghanistan; They were diplomats, other civilian staff, other civilians, and military staff.

The last military airplanes of the United States, left the airport in Kabul, one minute before 31 August 2021.

On 31 August 2021 (local time), the war ended.

Deaths and injuries
More than 15,000 Coalition soldiers were wounded: 6,773 US, 3,954 UK, 1,500 Canadian and over 2,500 other Coalition soldiers. 5,500 Afghan army soldiers and 200 Northern Alliance militants were killed in this war. 378 US civilian contractors were killed and 7,224.

Aftermath

An anti-Taliban front has control of the Panjshir Valley, as of 2021's third quarter.

Let's dive into our next topic: finding a missing value in a data set when we know the mean! This skill is important because it allows us to make sense of incomplete data by using what we know about the overall pattern of the data.

Imagine that you are conducting a survey of students in your school to find out how many siblings they have. You collect data from 20 students and calculate the mean number of siblings to be 1.5. However, one student fails to provide their sibling information. Can you figure out how many siblings this student has?

To solve this problem, let's follow these steps:

Step 1: Add up all the known values in the data set. Suppose the number of siblings for the other 19 students are: 2, 1, 1, 0, 2, 1, 2, 1, 0, 1, 2, 1, 0, 1, 2, 1, 0, 1, 2. The sum of these numbers is 18.

Step 2: Subtract the sum of the known values from the product of the total number of data points and the mean. In this case, the calculation would look like this: (20 \* 1.5) - 18 = 30 - 18 = 12.

Step 3: Since there are 20 data points in total, with 19 of them accounted for, the remaining value must correspond to the unknown sibling count. Therefore, the missing value is equal to the result obtained in Step 2 divided by the number of unaccounted-for data points, which is 1. So, the missing value is 12 / 1 = 12.

In summary, when presented with a data set where some values are missing but the mean is provided, you can determine the missing value(s) through the following process:

1. Sum the known values in the data set.
2. Calculate the difference between the product of the total number of data points and the mean, and the sum found in step 1.
3. Divide the result from step 2 by the number of missing values to obtain the missing value(s).

Now try solving the following problems using the same method:

Problem 1: A group of friends measures their heights in inches. They add up their heights and divide by the number of people to get a mean height of 64.25 inches. One friend forgets to report her height. If the other friends' heights are 65, 66, 62, 68, 63, 67, 61, and 64 inches, what could the forgotten height be?

Problem 2: Ten employees at a small company earn monthly salaries ranging from $2,000 to $5,000. Their average salary is calculated to be $3,400 per month. Unfortunately, due to a clerical error, one employee's salary was left blank in the records. Given that the other nine employees earn $2,500, $2,800, $3,100, $3,200, $3,700, $4,000, $4,200, $4,800, and $4,900 respectively, what should the missing salary be to maintain the correct mean salary?

Esperanto
Esperanto is a constructed auxiliary language. Its creator was L. L. Zamenhof, a Polish eye doctor. He created the language to make international communication easier. His goal was to design Esperanto in such a way that people can learn it much more easily than any other national language.

At first, Zamenhof called the language , which means "The International Language" in Esperanto. Soon, people began calling it by the simpler name , which means "one who hopes". That name comes from ("Doctor who hopes"), which is what Zamenhof called himself in his first book about Esperanto.

There are people who speak Esperanto in many countries and in all the major continents. No one knows exactly how many people now speak Esperanto in the world. Most sources say that there are between several hundred thousand and two million Esperanto speakers. A few people grew up speaking Esperanto as their first language. There may perhaps be around 2,000 of these people. Therefore, Esperanto is the most-used constructed language in the world.

A person who speaks or supports Esperanto is often called an "Esperantist".

History

Zamenhof's childhood
L. L. Zamenhof created Esperanto. He grew up in Biaystok, a town that was in the Russian Empire, but is now in Poland. People in Biaystok spoke many languages. Zamenhof saw conflicts between individual ethnic groups living there (Russians, Poles, Germans and Jews). He thought that lack of a common language caused these conflicts, so he began creating a language people could share and use internationally. He thought this language should be different from national languages. He wanted it to be culturally neutral and easy-to-learn. He thought people should learn it along with national languages and use Esperanto for communication between people with different native languages.

First attempts
First, Zamenhof thought about bringing Latin back into use. Although he learned it in school, he realized it was too difficult for normal use. He also studied English and understood that languages did not need to conjugate verbs by person or number. Once he saw two Russian words:  (reception, derived from  - receptionist) and  (confectionery, derived from  - confectioner). These words with the same ending gave him an idea. He decided that regular prefixes and suffixes could decrease the number of word roots, which one would need for a communication. Zamenhof wanted the root words to be neutral, so he decided to use word roots from Romance and Germanic languages. Those languages were taught in many schools in many places around the world at that time.

Creation of the final version

Zamenhof did his first project Lingwe uniwersala (Universal Language) in 1878. But his father, a language teacher, regarded his son's work as unrealistic. So, he destroyed the original work. Between 1879 and 1885 Zamenhof studied medicine in Moscow and Warsaw. In these days he again worked on an international language. In 1887 he published his first textbook ("The International Language"). According to Zamenhof's pen-name ("Doctor who hopes"), many people started calling the language as Esperanto.

First attempts to change
Zamenhof received a lot of enthusiastic letters. In the letters, people wrote their suggestions for changes to the language. He noted all of the suggestions. He published them in the magazine La Esperantisto. In this magazine, Esperanto speakers could vote about the changes. They did not accept them. The magazine had many subscribers in Russia. It was eventually banned (stopped) there because of an article about Lev Nikolayevich Tolstoy. Publishing of the magazine ended after that. The new magazine Lingvo Internacia replaced it.

Quietly, in the shadows of a grand city, a man named Samuel walked alone. His heart was filled with dark thoughts. He moved through the busy streets, watching people laugh and smile. They seemed so happy, while he felt empty. Samuel had lost his way, consumed by his own anger and pain. The world had turned its back on him, and he was filled with regret.

Once, Samuel had a family. They were his light, his reason to live. But one fateful night, a terrible accident took them from him. He could not forget the sound of the crash, the screams, the chaos. In his grief, he pushed everyone away. Friends stopped calling, and neighbors stopped visiting. He became a ghost in a world full of life.

Samuel wandered through the city, his heart heavy with sadness. He saw families together, children playing. With each happy face, he felt his heart grow colder. He wanted to scream at the world, to make them understand his pain. But he only watched in silence, a dark cloud over him.

One evening, while walking past a park, he saw a young girl sitting alone. She was drawing with chalk, her small face full of joy. Samuel felt a strange pull to her. In that moment, he remembered his own daughter. The laughter they shared echoed in his mind. The memory stung like a knife, and he turned away, afraid of what he might feel.

As the days passed, Samuel noticed the girl return to the park. She would sit for hours, drawing and smiling. Each time, he felt a tug at his heart. He wanted to go to her, to speak, but fear held him back. What could he say to a child? Would she understand the darkness he carried? The thought made him shiver.

One night, he stood in the shadows, watching her as she drew. The girl suddenly looked up and smiled, as if she felt his gaze. In that moment, Samuel felt a flicker of hope. Maybe she could bring some light into his dark world. But just as quickly, he felt a wave of doubt. Could he let her in? Could he face the warmth of her smile?

Finally, he took a step forward, ready to speak. But the girl gathered her things and left, her laughter fading into the night. Samuel felt a heavy weight in his chest. He had lost his chance. Standing alone in the dark, he realized that the world had moved on without him. In that moment, he knew he was lost forever, trapped in his own sadness, unable to reach for the light.

Malcolm X
El-Hajj Malik El-Shabazz (Arabic:   , romanized: al-jj Mlik ash-Shabzz, May 19, 1925 - February 21, 1965) also known as Malcolm X was an African American nationalist and civil rights activist. Before he became Malcolm X, his original name was Malcolm Stuart Little. Malcolm X's father was a Baptist minister whose skin was very dark, whilst his mother's skin was of a much lighter tone. His parents taught him to be proud of being black in an openly anti-black society. Malcolm X's father died when Malcolm was only six years old, leaving his mother in poverty.

In 1946, Malcolm was arrested at the age of 20 for armed robbery, but was released from jail 8 years later. He was introduced to the Nation of Islam and Islam while he was in jail, joining the Nation after he was released.

Actions
At first, Malcolm X's actions and speeches were mostly inspired by the beliefs and teachings of the Nation of Islam. He taught that all white people were bad. Once he learned that the leader of the Nation of Islam was in relationships with many women, he quit the group and changed his religion to Sunni Islam. He went on a pilgrimage to see the Islamic holy city of Mecca in Saudi Arabia. At this point, his opinions of white people got better, and he began to believe that white people could be good people, too. Malcolm X believed that black people should fight for their civil rights in any way they could, even if they had to become violent. He also thought that black people should support one another by shopping in stores owned by black people. He was critical of the civil rights movement.

Personal life
Malcolm X had six children with Betty Shabazz. He had six grandchildren. Malcolm Shabazz was killed in May 2013. He also has two great-grandchildren.

Death

On February 21, 1965, he was shot to death in New York City after preaching about black rights. Three members of the Nation of Islam had a part in his murder.

Welcome back to our exploration of rational numbers! In this sub-unit, we will dive into the world of number opposites. If you've been with us since the beginning of this chapter, you'll recall that we started by discussing positive and negative numbers and their placement on the number line. We then moved on to exploring how both decimals and fractions can also be represented on the number line. Now, it's time to take things one step further and investigate the relationship between opposite numbers.

To begin, let's consider two points on the number line: 3 and -3. While these numbers appear quite different at first glance, they actually share a special connection. Specifically, they are opposites of each other. This means that if we were to add 3 and -3 together, we would get zero as a result. Zero, of course, represents the absence of any value - a sort of "neutral" point on the number line.

This idea of oppositeness extends beyond just whole numbers, however. Consider the decimal numbers 0.5 and -0.5, for instance. Once again, these numbers are opposites - adding them together results in zero. The same holds true for fractions such as 1/2 and -1/2, which are also opposite pairs.

So what exactly makes two numbers opposites? At its core, the concept of opposition hinges on the idea of addition. Specifically, two numbers are considered opposites if their sum equals zero. Using this definition, we can see why pairs like 3 and -3, 0.5 and -0.5, and 1/2 and -1/2 are all opposites - when we add them together, we always end up with zero.

Now that we understand what makes two numbers opposites, let's explore some of the properties of opposite pairs. One interesting property is that every non-zero number has exactly one opposite. This means that there is only one number that can be added to a given non-zero number to produce zero. For example, the opposite of 4 is -4, and no other number shares this distinction.

Another important property of opposite pairs is that they lie symmetrical to zero on the number line. To visualize this, imagine placing a mirror along the zero point of the number line. Any pair of opposites will reflect perfectly across this mirror, meaning that their distance from zero is equal but in opposite directions. For instance, the opposite of 7 lies seven units to the left of zero, while the opposite of -7 lies seven units to the right of zero.

Let's try out some practice problems to solidify our understanding of opposite numbers:

1. Find the opposite of the following numbers:
a. 9
b. -1.2
c. 13/5
d. -sqrt(2)
2. Determine whether the following pairs are opposites:
a. 2 and -2
b. 0.8 and 0.6
c. -3/4 and 3/4
d. sqrt(3) and -sqrt(3)
3. Plot the following pairs of opposites on the number line:
a. 5 and -5
b. -0.7 and 0.7
c. -pi and pi

As we continue to delve deeper into the world of rational numbers, understanding the concept of opposites will prove crucial. By recognizing the connections between seemingly disparate numbers, we gain valuable insights that help us make sense of complex mathematical ideas. So keep practicing those opposite pairs, and stay tuned for more exciting adventures in the land of ratios!

Delitzsch (district)
Delitzsch is a former rural district in the Free State of Saxony, Germany.

History
After the Congress of Vienna in 1815 Saxony had to give a lot of its land to Prussia, including the region of Delitzsch. The Prussian government made the district of Delitzsch.

Prussia was dissolved after the end of the Nazi era. Delitzsch was made a part of the new state of Saxony-Anhalt. In 1953 the East German government dissolved the states. After the German reunification in 1990, the states were made again, but now Delitzsch and Eilenburg (two districts made of the former Delitzsch district) were given to Saxony instead of Saxony-Anhalt. The two districts were joined in 1994 and gave the district in its present borders. In 2008 Delitzsch Rural district was merged with Torgau-Oschatz Rural District to Nordsachsen Rural District.

Geography
The district is in the triangle between the big cities of Leipzig, Halle and Bitterfeld. It is mostly countryside, and used for farming. The Mulde River runs through the east part of the district. On the eastern banks there is the Dben Heath (Dbener Heide) nature park.

Chapter Title: Taking Care of Your Intimate Areas: A Guide to Good Hygiene

Introduction:
Hey there! Let's talk about something important - taking care of your intimate areas. You might have heard some whispers about it, but don't worry; we will keep things simple, fun, and easy to understand. By the end of this chapter, you will know why good hygiene down there matters and how to maintain it like a pro!

Section 1: What are Intimate Areas?
Imagine putting on tight clothes after playing outside all day long - yikes, that doesn't sound comfortable at all, right? Our bodies have special places where our skin folds together, creating warm and moist environments. These parts need extra attention because germs love those conditions! We call these regions our "intimate areas," which include spots like our underarms, groin, and buttocks.

Activity Time!
Can you think of other body parts that could be considered "intimate areas"? Write them down here: _______________. Compare with a friend and discuss why they might require special care.

Section 2: Why Is It Important To Keep Intimate Areas Clean?
Just like how we brush our teeth every morning and night, keeping our intimate areas clean helps prevent bad smells, rashes, and infections. When we sweat, bacteria can grow quickly in these warm and damp areas, leading to problems if left unattended. So, let's learn how to take proper care of them!

Section 3: How Can I Maintain Good Intimate Area Hygiene?
Here comes the big question: How exactly do we practice good intimate area hygiene? Follow these steps for a happy and healthy downstairs region:

Step 1: Wash regularly. Use mild soap and warm water when bathing or showering. Be sure to gently wash your intimate areas daily, just as you would with the rest of your body. Don't forget to clean between the folds!

Step 2: No harsh chemicals allowed! Harsh soaps, douches, and perfumes can irritate sensitive skin and upset the natural balance of bacteria found in our intimate areas. Stick to gentle products made specifically for delicate skin.

Step 3: Dry thoroughly. After washing, pat yourself dry using a soft towel. Make sure everything is completely dry before getting dressed, especially during hot and humid weather. Moisture leads to bacterial growth, remember?

Step 4: Choose breathable fabrics. Opt for cotton undies instead of synthetic materials that trap heat and moisture. Change into fresh clothing after activities that cause sweating, such as sports or dance class.

Fun Fact! Did you know that certain types of fabric can help keep your intimate areas cool and dry throughout the day? Cotton is one example, but there are many others to explore too!

Conclusion:
Congratulations! Now you know more about taking care of your intimate areas and maintaining good personal hygiene. Remember, everyone deserves to feel confident and comfortable in their own skin. Share your newfound knowledge with friends and family members so they can join in on practicing great habits for a healthier lifestyle!

Story
A story can be different things:
when we tell others about a thing that happened, or a thing we thought of: Bob read the children a story; Mary told John the story of her life.
a report in a newspaper or on the television news: Did you see the story about George Bush on page 12?
a thing we tell others that is not real: Little Johnny said he was a millionaire, but he's not, it was only a story. See fiction
in US English, a level of a building: The house has eight stories. (In British English this is a storey).

Course Unit: Turkish Sufi Mysticism

Welcome, young explorers! Today, we will embark on an incredible journey into the world of Turkish Sufi Mysticism. This form of mysticism comes from Turkey, but its roots reach far back into history, all the way to ancient Persia and the birth of Islam. So what exactly is Sufi Mysticism? Well, imagine you have a secret garden inside your heart where only you can go to talk to God. That's kind of like Sufism! It's a pathway to connect with the Divine using love, devotion, and poetry. Let's explore this fascinating concept together!

First, let's understand who these Sufis are. They are people just like you and me, seeking answers about life, love, and their connection with something greater than themselves. But instead of finding those answers in books or teachings alone, they look within - exploring their hearts and minds to discover the beauty that lies beneath. By doing so, they believe one can achieve self-realization and inner peace. Doesn't that sound amazing?

Now, let's dive deeper into how Sufis practice their beliefs. One popular aspect is the use of whirling dervishes (yes, you read that right!) during ceremonies called "Sama." Dressed in white robes symbolizing death to the ego, they spin around and around while listening to beautiful music. As they twirl, they focus on feeling close to Allah (God). Imagine being able to express yourself and worship through dance - wouldn't that be fun?

Another essential element of Turkish Sufi Mysticism is poetry. Poetry helps Sufis convey deep emotions and thoughts in a simple yet powerful way. For instance, Rumi, arguably the most famous Sufi poet ever, wrote poems filled with wisdom and guidance. His words inspire many still today because they speak straight to our souls. Reading his poem below, see if any lines resonate with you:

The Guest House
This being human is a guest house.
Every morning a new arrival.
A joy, a depression, a meanness,
some momentary awareness comes
as an unexpected visitor.
Welcome and entertain them all!
Even if they're a crowd of sorrows,
who violently sweep your house
empty of its furniture,
still treat each guest honorably.
He may be clearing you out
for some new delight.
The dark thought, the shame, the malice,
meet them at the door laughing,
and invite them in.
Be grateful for whoever comes,
because each has been sent
as a guide from beyond.

Finally, let's remember why Sufis choose this unique path. Love is at the core of everything they do. Loving God unconditionally allows them to appreciate every small detail of creation, spreading kindness and compassion throughout society. Think about someone special in your own life - maybe a friend or family member. How does loving them change the way you interact with others? Can you imagine expanding that warm feeling towards everyone and everything else too?

In conclusion, Turkish Sufi Mysticism offers us a chance to reflect upon ourselves, build stronger connections with those around us, and embrace love wholeheartedly. Through practices such as meditation, dancing, and poetry, anyone can follow this spiritual tradition and find harmony between mind, body, and spirit. Now isn't that worth exploring further?

Now that we've learned how to multiply fractions using the fraction model, let's explore another way to understand this concept: by using a number line. A number line is a visual representation of numbers that can help us better understand mathematical concepts, including multiplication of fractions.

Let's start with a simple example: multiplying the fraction 1/2 by the fraction 3/4. To do this using a number line, follow these steps:

1. Draw a number line labeled from 0 to 1, divided into fourths (since we're working with the fraction 3/4). This will give us five equally spaced points on the number line, each representing a value between 0 and 1: 0, 1/4, 1/2, 3/4, and 1.
2. Locate the point on the number line that represents 1/2. We know this should be halfway between 0 and 1, at the third mark on our number line.
3. Starting from this point, draw a segment equal in length to one quarter of the distance between 1/2 and 1. This will take us to a new point on the number line that represents 3/8 (three quarters of the way between 1/2 and 1).
4. The resulting point on the number line is where 1/2 times 3/4 falls. In other words, it represents the product of the two fractions.

This process may seem complicated at first, but with practice, it becomes second nature. Let's try another example, this time with larger numbers: multiplying 5/6 by 7/8.

1. Start by drawing a number line labeled from 0 to 1, divided into eighths. This will give us nine equally spaced points on the number line, each representing a value between 0 and 1: 0, 1/8, 2/8, 3/8, 4/8, 5/8, 6/8, 7/8, and 1.
2. Find the point on the number line that represents 5/6. Since six parts make up the entire interval from 0 to 1, and we want to find the point corresponding to five sixths of that interval, we divide the interval into six equal segments and then move along those segments until we reach the fifth one.
3. From this point, draw a segment equal in length to seven eighths of the remaining distance between the current position and 1. This will bring us to a new point on the number line that represents the product of 5/6 and 7/8.

By using the number line method, students gain a deeper understanding of what it means to multiply fractions together and see visually how the values relate to each other. It also helps them develop their spatial reasoning skills and provides yet another tool they can use when solving complex problems involving fractions. With continued practice and repetition, students will become proficient at multiplying fractions both through the fraction model and the number line approach.

As the kids swung their clubs, Alex pointed out their mistakes. "You missed again!" he laughed, feeling a cruel pleasure. But inside, he felt scared. What if they learned? What if they beat him? He was afraid of losing his power, so he stayed on the sidelines.

One day, a girl named Lily joined the game. She swung her club with precision, sending the ball soaring. Alex felt his heart race. "I can't let her win," he thought, scheming to distract her. But every time he opened his mouth, she just smiled, her confidence growing.

Finally, during a big match, Lily scored a hole-in-one. The crowd erupted in cheers, lifting her up. Alex stood frozen, feeling the emptiness wrap around him. The absence of cheers for himself was like a heavy fog. Maybe true power was about lifting others up, not tearing them down...

We also want to talk a bit about circles. If you're not sure about the difference between a circle's radius and diameter, here's a simple way to remember. The radius is half the diameter. We need to know the length of the outer edge of the bend to figure out how long our starting piece of wood should be. If we're making a bend that covers a quarter of a circle (like a piece of pie), we'll need four pieces to go all the way around a table. A three-part circle is like cutting a pizza into three equal pieces. Each piece is 1/3 or 120 degrees of the whole pizza. This is just like putting a border around a round table using only three parts.

When there's less water in the air, things made by steam bending lose water and get smaller. Steam bending makes the inside of the bend tighter (like squeezing a sponge) than the outside. So, when the inside loses water and gets smaller, the ends move closer. But, when there's more water in the air, the wood absorbs it and the ends move farther apart. This moving is called clamming.

Here are some things that can make clamming happen faster or slower:

- Wood loses or gains water faster when it's hot.
- If there's a lot of water or very little water in the air, the wood can change faster. But it usually takes at least a week.
- Some types of wood dry slowly, so they change shape slowly. Some types dry fast, so they change fast.
- Smaller bends move more than bigger bends.
- Very flat bends, like a very big circle, usually just get flatter.
- Long bends move more than short bends.

But, you can slow down these changes by keeping the wood in the right place. The best place is where it's not too hot or too cold (between 65 and 75 degrees), and not too dry or too wet (30 to 40% humidity).
Lots of places that make things add water to the air in winter. This stops the wood from getting too dry. Putting water in the air when it's cold and we use heaters can stop the wood from splitting.
Some places spend more money to take water out of the air in summer. This is good for the place where they keep the wood parts. Keeping the air and temperature just right can stop well-dried wood from getting clammy.
When we bend wood and then dry it, the ends might not be in the same place. So, we should not trust the ends when we put the wood in the machine. The first thing we should do is mark the ends and cut the bends to the right length before putting them in the machine.
Putting sticks on the ends can help, but the bends might move in or out when we take the sticks off. It's best to do most of the machine work before we take the stick off.
There is more about water and wood in another part of this website. For someone who works with wood, it's very important to know how water affects wood.

Game Boy line
The Game Boys are a group of handheld video game consoles made by Nintendo that ran from 1989 to 2009.

Game Boy

The first Game Boy was released in 1989. It had a small screen, a D-pad, Start and Select keys, and an A and B button. To play games, there were small objects called cartridges that you put into the Game Boy to play the game in the cartridge. The game that made it popular, and the system's launch title, was Tetris. The Game Boy had a link cable and a link port which let it connect with other Game Boys to play games in multiplayer mode.

Game Boy Pocket
After the Game Boy, Nintendo released the Game Boy Pocket, which was a smaller Game Boy more convenient to carry around. It had a better, sharper screen and it only needed two AAA batteries instead of four AA. The link port was smaller than the Game Boy's, so the Game Boy and Game Boy Pocket could not connect with the original connector cable; a newer model cable with double-sided ends was needed to do this.

Game Boy Light
The Game Boy Light was only released in Japan and had a front-light (the blue light used on old watches) so people could see better. It is very rare - only about 12,000 of them were manufactured. Because it is rare, it sells for more money than other Game Boys.

Game Boy Color

The Game Boy Color was the first Game Boy in color. It was also able to play Game Boy cartridges, which helped it sell better. This also helped other Game Boy models after the Game Boy Color. It is sometimes called the GBC.

Game Boy Advance

The Game Boy Advance is a handheld that had better color and smaller cartridges. It could play more advanced games than the previous Game Boys. It is sometimes called the GBA. It came out in March 2001.

Game Boy Advance SP

The Game Boy Advance SP was an improved version of the original GBA. It has a clamshell design, which means you can fold it to make it smaller when you're not using it. It has a front-lit screen (better than the one on the Game Boy Light), which the Game Boy Advance did not have. It can play Game Boy and Game Boy Color games, along with the new cartridges introduced with the GBA. A newer model, labeled the AGS-101, was released which had an even better backlight and very good contrast; some people say it is the best way to play Game Boy, Game Boy Color and Game Boy Advance games.

Game Boy Micro

The Game Boy Micro is a smaller variation of the GBA. It has a smaller link port than the Game Boy Advance. Its backlight and contrast are as good as the 101 model of the Game Boy Advance SP. Unlike its predecessors, it cannot play GB or GBC games.

Succesors
The Nintendo DS line is the successor to the Game Boy line. It consists of the Nintendo DS and the Nintendo 3DS.

Nintendo DS


Homelessness
Homelessness means people who do not have a place to stay. The word "homelessness" also includes people who sleep in warming centers, homeless shelters, or in abandoned buildings, parking garages, or other places not meant for humans to live in. Homelessness occurs for many reasons. It may happen when people or households are unable to buy or maintain housing they can afford. International human rights law includes the right to housing.

Homeless people live in many parts of the world including: San Francisco in California, Dublin in Ireland and Tallinn in Estonia.

Homeless people

In academic articles and government reports, these people are called "homeless people". You may hear different words to describe homelessness and homeless people. Some of these words apply to people who might not be homeless. Sometimes they are based upon stereotypes. For instance, in slang, a vagabond is someone who travels without the money necessary to stay in good hotels. Such a person may or may not have a home somewhere. Sometimes police reports use the word "transient" to describe people from out of town or who are passing through. Many times these words confuse the issues because someone just passing through might own a mansion somewhere or might not.

There are tough questions in sorting out homeless people even when trying to create programs and services to help them. Homeless counts are required by the government agencies that deal with homelessness.

In the US, the United States Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) agency requires a homeless "enumeration" or count every two years. They classify "homeless" in a careful way and that way is very influential and a lot of other agencies and church groups copy it. In Metro Vancouver homeless people are counted by the British Columbia (B.C.) Non-Profit Housing Society which conducts the homeless count with the help of about 1,200 volunteers.

HUD definitions
Housing and Urban Development of the United States spreads information about what does and does not work when providing shelter for homeless people. That information about the things that seem to work is called "best practices". HUD defines homeless as 1. somebody who lacks a fixed, regular, and decent place to sleep at night or 2. somebody who sleeps at night in A.a supervised shelter (including welfare hotels, homeless shelters, warming centers and transitional housing) ; B. a place that provides a temporary residence for people waiting for space in a place like a hospital, jail or hospice; or C. places not designed for human beings to sleep, such as parks or public sidewalks.

A new interest: people who live outside
The "C" part of the HUD definition is now getting more attention. It is called "chronic homelessness". (HUD) defines a "chronically homeless" person as "an unaccompanied homeless individual with a disabling condition". There are other conditions to that definition. It has to be someone who has either been homeless for a year or more, or has been homeless four times in the past three years.

People who study these things believe that "chronic" homelessness costs a lot more than the rest. A new approach is to seek information on those folks who are considered chronically homeless. They are using what is called a vulnerability index system. It was invented by a doctor in Boston who works with a New York organization called Common Ground. These "Vulnerability Index's" code for things like bad liver, kidney disease, HIV-AIDS, age, and visits to the hospital.

Health care

The Guardian
The Guardian is a British newspaper. It is published every day, except on Sunday. It is owned by the same company as The Observer, which only publishes on Sunday. The Guardian is edited by Katharine Viner.

History

The newspaper was founded in 1821. It was founded by textile traders and merchants. The Guardian was seen as "an organ of the middle class", or, in the words of C.P. Scott's son Ted, "a paper that will remain bourgeois to the last". In 2005, Sir Max Hastings stated that he writes for The Guardian "because it is read by the new establishment", reflecting the paper's growing influence.

Until 1959 The Guardian was called The Manchester Guardian.

Three of the four people who wrote leaders for the Guardian joined the Social Democratic Party on its foundation in 1982. The paper supported Tony Blair when he wanted to lead the Labour Party and to become Prime Minister.

In 1999 theguardian.com started. At the time it was a website called Guardian Unlimited.

Characteristics
The Guardian describes itself as centre-left.
