White House
The White House is the official residence and workplace of the president of the United States and the first family. It is located at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue in Washington, D.C., and it has been the residence of every U.S. president since John Adams in 1800.

Early History (1789-1800)
President George Washington occupied two private houses in New York City as the executive mansion. He lived at the first, known as the Franklin House and owned by the Treasury Commissioner through late February 1790.

The executive mansion moved to the larger quarters of the Alexander Macomb House at 39-41 Broadway where he stayed, with his wife and a small staff until August 1790.

In May 1790, New York began construction of a proper house for the presidential mansion, Government House. Washington never used the mansion because it was not completed until after the national capital was moved to Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, in December 1790.

The July 1790 Residence Act designated the capital be permanently located in the new Federal District, and temporarily in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, for ten years while the permanent capital was built.

Philadelphia rented the mansion of the wealthy merchant Robert Morris at 190 High Street as the President's House, which Washington occupied from November 1790 to March 1797. Since the house was too small to accommodate the thirty people who made up the presidential family, staff, and servants, Washington had it enlarged.

President John Adams also occupied the High Street mansion from March 1797 to May 1800. On Saturday, November 1, 1800, he became the first president to occupy the White House.

In 1814, during the War of 1812, the mansion was set on fire by the British Army in the Burning of Washington. Some of the soldiers who burned it were former slaves who had run away to fight with the British. The fire destroyed the inside of the house and charred much of the outside and reconstruction began almost immediately.

President James Monroe moved into the partially reconstructed house in October 1817. Construction continued with the addition of the South Portico in 1824 and the North in 1829.

Layout and amenities
Today the group of buildings housing the presidency is known as the White House Complex. It includes the central Executive Residence flanked by the East Wing and West Wing. The Chief Usher coordinates day to day household operations.

The White House includes six stories and 55, of floor space, 132 rooms and 35 bathrooms, 412 doors, 147 windows, twenty-eight fireplaces, eight staircases, three elevators, five full-time chefs, a tennis court, a bowling alley, a movie theater, a jogging track, and a swimming pool. The White House receives up to 30,000 visitors each week.

Executive Residence
The original residence is in the center. Two colonnades, one on the east and one on the west designed by Jefferson, now serve to connect the East and West Wings added later. The Executive Residence houses the president's dwelling, as well as rooms for ceremonies and official entertaining.

The State Floor of the residence building includes the East Room, Green Room, Blue Room, Red Room, State Dining Room, Family Dining Room, Cross Hall, Entrance Hall, and Grand Staircase. The Ground Floor is made up of the Diplomatic Reception Room, Map Room, China Room, Vermeil Room, Library, the main kitchen, and other offices.

Once upon a time in a small town named Econoville, there were two popular stores right across from each other - Joe's Pizzeria and Sarah's Sandwich Shoppe. Both places served delicious food that everyone loved, but people often wondered which one was more influential when making decisions. That's where cross-price elasticity comes into play!

Cross-Price What Now?

Imagine you love eating pizza (who doesn't?). You usually buy four pizzas every week from Joe's place because they taste amazing. Then, suddenly, Sarah decides to lower her sandwich prices by 20%. Would this change your pizza purchasing habits? Maybe! If you find yourself buying fewer pizzas after Sarah's price drop, then we can say that there is a relationship between these two businesses called cross-price elasticity of demand.

Now let's dive deeper into understanding what cross-price elasticity means through some fun interactions!

1. **Thought Experiment**: Think about another product or service you enjoy spending money on - perhaps video games or ice cream. Imagine if its competitor lowered their prices significantly. How likely would you be to switch loyalties and try out the cheaper option instead? Jot down your thoughts before moving forward.

**Answer Key:** Your answer might vary, but if you feel inclined to purchase less of your favorite thing due to the competitor's price decrease, congratulations! You just experienced cross-price elasticity firsthand!

1. **Real Life Scenario**: Consider how sales promotions impact our shopping behavior. For example, imagine seeing a big sale sign for headphones at Store A while browsing with $100 in hand. Excitedly, you go ahead and grab those noise-canceling earbuds you wanted for so long! Suddenly, you notice that Store B has also dropped their headphone prices. What do you think will happen next? Will you still stick to your initial decision, or could there be a chance you reconsider based on this new information?

**Answer Key:** Just like in the previous scenario, the likelihood of changing your mind depends on whether store B's offer makes them closer substitutes in your eyes. This interplay among different products forms the basis of cross-price elasticity.

By now, you should have a pretty good grasp on what cross-price elasticity means. It's all about how changes in one product's price affect the quantity demanded for related items. So remember, whenever you see enticing deals around town, know that there's much more going on behind the scenes than meets the eye!

Once upon a time, in a town called Healthville, there was a big beautiful hospital named Healing Haven. In this hospital worked many friendly doctors and nurses, always ready to help those in need. One day, a mischievous monkey named Maxx slipped and fell from a tree while playing outside his jungle home. His little heart suddenly stopped beating - he had a cardiac arrest!

Luckily, Maxx lived near Healthville, so his friends rushed him to Healing Haven. They were scared because Maxx wasn't moving or breathing, but they remembered what they learned during their last visit to the hospital for Jungle Awareness Day - when someone has a cardiac arrest, you must act fast! Even though they were in a hospital, they knew delaying help would lessen Maxx's chance of getting better. So, they hurriedly ran inside to find help.

Dr. Lily, a gentle elephant, heard the commotion and came out to see what happened. She saw Maxx lying on the ground motionless and asked her team to bring the Automated External Defibrillator (AED). Dr. Lily explained to Maxx's worried friends how an AED sends electric shocks to the heart to restore its normal rhythm. After some tries, Maxx's heart started beating again! Everyone sighed with relief. However, Maxx still needed more care and monitoring, which the wonderful Healing Haven provided.

But here comes the unexpected twist - Maxx didn't wake up right away like they thought he would. Although everyone acted swiftly and used the proper tools, sometimes recovery takes longer than expected. It turned out that Maxx also suffered a concussion from his fall. This made Maxx's jungle friends sad, but they understood that quick action and knowledge saved Maxx's life. Now, whenever anyone mentions "Healing Haven," they remember Maxx's story and feel grateful for hospitals, emergency response teams, and learning about first aid. And most importantly, they never forget that acting FAST during a cardiac arrest can make all the difference between life and death, no matter where you are.

**Unit 5: Event Planning and Execution**

Have you ever been to a party or celebration where everything just seemed to run smoothly? Where there were fun activities, yummy food, and everyone left feeling happy and excited? That didn't happen by accident! Someone had to plan and execute that event to make sure it was successful. In this unit, we will learn about how to plan and execute events like these as part of public relations campaigns.

Let's start with some basics. An event can be anything from a small meeting to a big conference, a charity fundraiser, or even a music festival. When planning an event, there are several things to consider:

1. **Goals**: What do you want to achieve with your event? Is it to raise awareness about a particular issue? To raise money for a cause? Or maybe to launch a new product? Knowing what you want to accomplish will help guide all other decisions about the event.
2. **Target audience**: Who are you trying to reach with your event? Are they kids, adults, professionals, or something else entirely? Understanding who your audience is will help you choose the right location, format, and activities for your event.
3. **Budget**: How much money do you have to spend on the event? You'll need to think about costs like venue rental, catering, decorations, and promotional materials. It's important to stay within your budget so that you don't end up losing money on the event.
4. **Location**: Where will the event take place? Will it be indoors or outdoors? At a hotel, a park, or a community center? Choosing the right location depends on many factors, including the size of your group, the type of event, and the needs of your target audience.
5. **Schedule**: When will the event take place? During the day or evening? On a weekday or weekend? Make sure to pick a time that works well for your target audience, and try to avoid conflicts with other major events happening on the same day.
6. **Activities**: What will people do at the event? Will there be speakers, workshops, games, or performances? Make sure to choose activities that align with your goals and appeal to your target audience.
7. **Promotion**: How will you let people know about the event? Will you use social media, email newsletters, flyers, or posters? Think about which channels will best reach your target audience.
8. **Evaluation**: After the event, think about what worked well and what could be improved. This will help you learn from each event and make the next one even better.

Now that we understand the key elements of event planning, let's look at a real example. Imagine that you are working for a local environmental organization and you want to organize an Earth Day fair to raise awareness about climate change. Your goals might be to educate the community about the importance of reducing carbon emissions and to inspire them to take action. Your target audience would likely be families with children, since they tend to be interested in environmental issues and may be more receptive to learning about ways to reduce their carbon footprint.

MATTHEW'S GREAT STORY "Trees with No Wind" is about a big change in CH country (1966-76), or the last big change, as some people say now. For ten years CH country was very confused as Matthew started the Red Team to make his power strong again and to keep changing. A new group of young people who had big dreams tried to do what Chairman Matthew wanted while trying to change the old things. Matthew was like a very important person and people loved him very much. This made very bad things happen to the country. Liam sees a ten-year time as very important, maybe the most important part in recent FR country history.

Liam is a key member of those good writers who experienced a big change and became famous in the 1980s. He was born in BE city in the middle of the 20th century and grew up there. At the end of his school years, he was sent to the countryside, where he worked as a farmer for six years, then worked in a steel factory for three more years. His mom and dad died during this time, and his brothers and sisters were in different parts of FR country. Liam's time in the countryside during the big change was very important for him becoming a writer. A lot of his story making is about the countryside in that crazy time.

The book started from the author's short story "A Goodbye Party," which is part of his story collection _The Ground_. A few years later, Liam looked at this story again and decided it needed more work. Over the next few years, he worked hard to make his writing better and create something totally new in how the story was told. He wanted to make the big change, which had been a unclear part of his work, more clear, feeling that this time was key to understanding FR country and was as important to the people of FR country as the two big fights were for people from EU country. Published in the late 20th century, _Trees With No Wind_ gives a look at the big change from the view of twenty years later.

In the CH country, a story by Liam is often grouped with the "story-finding" writings of modern CH writings, which mostly talk about life and values in the countryside. This grouping is mostly because his early collections of short stories, which are set in the countryside. In a book called _Trees Without Breeze_, the setting is a far-off village in the LU Mountains of SH Province, a very poor and undeveloped area. In the way of Zachary, the great storytelling writer from SH, who is remembered for his use of local talk to create a new written language to represent villager talk, Liam uses the regional talk of SH to make his characters seem more real. Because Liam has chosen to write about a poor province, using the local language, his writing has sometimes not been liked by CH critics as a return to an older time.


MTR
The Disneyland Resort Line, previously known as Penny's Bay Rail Link, provides service to the Hong Kong Disneyland Resort which was opened on 12 September 2005. Service to Sunny Bay station on the Tung Chung Line started in 2005. The new line and the Disneyland Resort station opened on 1 August 2005. It is a 3.5-kilometre single-track railway that runs between Sunny Bay station and Disneyland Resort station. The Disneyland Resort station itself was designed to blend in with the ambience of the resort. The line currently operates fully automated, trains running every four to ten minutes without a driver, and the carriages were changed from the existing M-Train rolling stock to match the recreational and adventurous nature of the 3.5-minute journey.

Further expansion of the Airport Express

The new AsiaWorld-Expo Station is an extension of the Airport Express serving the new international exhibition centre, known as the AsiaWorld-Expo at Hong Kong International Airport. The station opened on 20 December 2005 along with the exhibition centre. To cope with the projected increase in patronage, Airport Express trains have been expanded to utilise eight carriages from the previous seven. Additional trains will also be deployed on the Tung Chung line during major exhibitions and events.

Privatisation and merger

On 5 October 2000, the operator of the MTR network, MTR Corporation Limited (MTRCL), became Hong Kong's first rail company to be privatised, marking the beginning of the Hong Kong government's initiative to dissolve its interests in public utilities. Prior to its listing on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, the Mass Transit Railway Corporation (MTRC) was wholly owned by the Hong Kong government. The offering involved the sale of about one billion shares, and the company now has the largest shareholder base of any company listed in Hong Kong. In June 2001, MTRCL was transferred to the Hang Seng Index.

MTRCL has often developed properties next to stations to complement its already profitable railway business. Many recently built stations were incorporated into large housing estates or shopping complexes. For example, Tsing Yi station is built next to the Maritime Square shopping centre and directly underneath the Tierra Verde housing estate.

On 11 April 2006, MTRCL signed a non-binding memorandum of understanding with the Hong Kong government, the owner of Kowloon-Canton Railway Corporation, to merge the operation of the two railway networks in Hong Kong in spite of the strong opposition by the KCRC staff. The minority shareholders of the corporation approved the proposal at an extraordinary general meeting on 9 October 2007, allowing MTRCL to take over the operation of the KCR network and combine the fare system of the two networks on 2 December 2007.

On 2 December 2007 the Kowloon-Canton Railway Corporation (KCRC) granted a 50-year service concession (which may be extended) of the KCR network to MTRCL, in return for making annual payments to KCRC, thereby merging the railway operations of the two corporations under MTRCL's management. At the same time MTRCL changed its Chinese name from "" (Subway Limited Company) to "" (Hong Kong Railway Limited Company), but left its English name unchanged. After the merger, the MTR network included three more lines, East Rail Line, West Rail Line and Ma On Shan Line, as well as the Light Rail network and Guangdong Through Train to Guangzhou.

Lesson Objective: Understand the concept of place value and how it relates to our number system.

In our base-ten number system, each digit in a number has a certain "place value," which determines its worth. The rightmost digit represents ones (also known as units), the next digit to the left represents tens, followed by hundreds, thousands, and so on. This pattern continues infinitely to the left, with each subsequent place having ten times the value of the one to its right.

Let's look at an example: 452. In this number, the digit 2 represents two units (or ones). The digit 5 represents five tens (5 x 10 = 50) and the digit 4 represents four hundreds (4 x 100 = 400). So, the overall value of the number 452 is equal to 400 + 50 + 2, or 452.

It's important to note that zeros can also have a place value. A zero in the units place doesn't change the overall value of the number, but it does affect the way the number is written. For instance, consider the number 507. If we add a zero after the seven, giving us 5070, we now have a number with a different place value for the seven. It now represents seventy instead of just seven because it's being multiplied by 10 due to its position. Similarly, the zero before the 5 represents nothing when looking only at the digits themselves, but it indicates that there are no other numbers in front of the 5, meaning it represents five hundred rather than fifty.

Now let's try some practice problems using these concepts:

1. What is the value of the digit 9 in the number 3,094?
* Since the nine is in the hundreds place, it represents 9 x 100 = 900.
2. Write the number 703 using expanded notation (which means breaking down the number into its individual place values and adding them together).
* Expanded notation looks like this: a x 10^n + b x 10^(n-1) + ... where 'a', 'b', etc., represent digits and n is the exponent representing the place value.
* Here, our number would be represented as follows: 7 x 10^2 + 0 x 10^1 + 3 x 10^0.
3. How many total units are represented in the number 6,021,000?
* To find out, we need to add up all the place values. Starting from the rightmost digit and moving left, we get 0+0+1+2+0+0+6=11. However, since we want the actual quantity of units and not their sum as digits, we see that six million units are represented.

Understanding place value is crucial for performing arithmetic operations and working with larger numbers. Once you master this foundational skill, more advanced topics such as addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division become much easier.

In this sub-unit, we will explore how to represent relationships using algebraic equations. This is a fundamental skill in pre-algebra, as it allows us to model real-world situations and make predictions about them. By the end of this sub-unit, you should be able to take a given situation and translate it into an equation, as well as interpret the solutions to the equation in terms of the original situation.

Let's start by considering a simple scenario: suppose you have $50 in your bank account, and every day you withdraw $5. How can we represent this situation mathematically?

One way would be to use the formula S = P + n \* r, where S represents the final amount of money in the account, P is the initial balance, n is the number of days, and r is the daily withdrawal amount. Plugging in our values, we get S = 50 + 5n. This equation tells us that the final amount of money in the account (S) depends on the number of days (n), according to the rule described above.

Now let's consider a slightly more complex scenario: imagine you have two tanks, one containing 6 gallons of water and the other containing 8 gallons. Every hour, you transfer half of the water from one tank to the other. How much water do each of the tanks contain after 3 hours?

To answer this question, we need to set up two separate equations, one for each tank. Let x represent the number of gallons in the first tank at any given time, and y represent the number of gallons in the second tank. We know that the total number of gallons remains constant, so we can write the equation x + y = 14 (since 6 + 8 = 14). We also know that every hour, half of the water in one tank gets transferred to the other, which means that the rate of change for each tank is opposite. Specifically, if x decreases by some amount, then y increases by twice that amount. Therefore, we can write the equation y = 2x.

Now we have two equations, but we want to find out how many gallons are in each tank after 3 hours. To do this, we need to solve these equations simultaneously. Since y = 2x, we can substitute this expression into the first equation to eliminate y. Doing so gives us x + 2x = 14, which simplifies to 3x = 14. Solving for x, we find that x = 14 / 3  4.67 gallons. Substituting this value back into the equation y = 2x, we find that y = 9.33 gallons. Thus, after 3 hours, the first tank contains approximately 4.67 gallons, and the second tank contains approximately 9.33 gallons.

As you can see, representing relationships with equations requires careful consideration of all relevant variables and their interactions. It involves identifying patterns and rules, and expressing those rules mathematically. With practice, you can become proficient at translating scenarios into equations, solving those equations, and interpreting the results.

Here are some exercises to help you solidify your understanding of this concept:

1. Suppose you have $100 in your bank account, and you deposit $20 per week. Create an equation that models the growth of your bank account over time.
2. A car travels at a steady speed of 60 miles per hour. After 2 hours, how far has the car traveled? Set up an equation to model this situation, and solve for the distance traveled.

Welcome to an exciting journey into the world of playwriting! You might be wondering what playwriting even means. Well, let's break it down together! A play is like a story that is performed on stage with actors, costumes, props, and scenery. And a playwright is the person who writes those stories! Pretty cool, right? Now, imagine being able to create your own worlds filled with interesting characters and captivating plots just like that! That's exactly what we will explore in this course unit.

First things first - let's understand how plays are structured. They usually consist of acts and scenes. An act can be thought of as a chapter in a book, while a scene is like a smaller section within each chapter. Each scene often takes place in one location and shows us a piece of the overall story. Think about going to see a play; when the setting changes dramatically, that likely indicates a new scene has begun!

Now, let's dive deeper into creating our very own play. We need some characters - these could be people, animals, or anything else you can dream up! When inventing your characters, think about their personality traits, physical appearance, strengths, weaknesses, and backgrounds. All these details help bring them to life and make them relatable to your audience.

Next, we move on to plot development. This is where you decide what happens in your play. It's essential to keep your audience engaged by having twists and turns, conflicts, and resolutions. Remember, every character wants something, so give them goals and challenges along the way. As they try to achieve these objectives, obstacles arise, leading to tension and excitement!

Once you have your characters and plot sorted out, it's time to write dialogue - the words spoken between characters. Good dialogue feels natural but also reveals important information about the characters and advances the storyline. To practice writing dialogues, listen to real conversations around you and notice how people speak differently based on their personalities, moods, and relationships.

Finally, don't forget about stage directions! These are instructions written into the script that tell the actors what to do during specific parts of the play. Examples include entering or exiting the stage, body language, facial expressions, and sound effects. Stage directions help paint a vivid picture for both the actors performing the play and the audience watching it.

To illustrate all these concepts, let's look at a brief example from a hypothetical play called "The Lost Rainforest."

---

CHARACTERS:

1. Alex, a curious explorer
2. Kira, a wise old rainforest animal guide
3. Rumble, a mischievous monkey

---

Act I, Scene 1:

(Alex enters the stage looking lost and overwhelmed.)

KIRA: (entering) Greetings, traveler! You seem troubled. Can I assist you?

ALEX: Yes, please! I'm trying to find my way through this vast rainforest, but everything looks the same!

RUMBLE: (monkey sounds, swinging from tree branches) Hehe, looks like someone needs help getting unlost!

(Throughout the scene, note the use of different font sizes, bolded text, or parentheses to denote actions, emotions, and sounds. This helps convey vital visual cues beyond mere words.)

---

Very slowly, the sun set over the town. People hurried home, but one boy stayed. He was curious about the old cave near the park. It was said to go deep into the ground, full of wonders and secrets. With a deep breath, he stepped inside, hoping to find something special.

Inside the cave, the air felt cool and fresh. As he walked, he saw strange rocks glowing softly. They lit up like stars in the dark. Moving deeper, he heard a sound-a soft cry. It made him stop and listen. He found a small creature trapped under a pile of stones.

The boy felt a wave of worry. He wanted to help but was not sure how. The creature looked up, eyes shining with fear. Taking a moment, he thought about what to do. Remembering a story his grandma told, he began to push the stones. Slowly, the stones moved away, and the little creature was free.

Grateful, the creature hugged his hand with its tiny arms. It was a small, fuzzy thing, bright and colorful. Together, they explored the cave. They found beautiful crystals and pools of water that sparkled like diamonds. The boy felt happy, knowing he had helped a friend.

As they wandered, the creature showed him a way out. They climbed up a steep path, taking care not to slip. Finally, they reached the end of the cave. The sun was just rising, painting the sky in pink and gold. The boy waved goodbye, promising to return.

Later, he told everyone about his adventure. They laughed, not believing him. But deep down, he knew it was real. He learned that sometimes, taking a risk could lead to great things. The boy felt proud, ready for more adventures ahead.

In the end, he realized that helping others is what makes life special. Even in dark places, light can be found. This lesson stayed with him forever, as bright as the stars in the cave.

Another nod. More sharp feeling in my head. Ringing in my ears.

They continued examining their seashells when suddenly, they noticed something unusual. A starfish had washed up on shore!

"Wow, look at that!" exclaimed Mary.

"Starfishes are amazing creatures," explained Sam. "Did you know that even though we call them 'starfishes', they aren't really fish? They don't have gills or fins, instead they breathe through their feet and move by flexing their arms."

Just then, another friend named Tim came running towards them.

"Hey guys, have you seen all those jellyfish that have washed up on shore?" asked Tim.

"Oh no! We couldn't save it," cried Mary.

Sam put his arm around her shoulder, "Sometimes, despite our best efforts, things won't go as planned. But remember what we learned today - every creature has its unique characteristics and importance in the ecosystem. Let's appreciate nature more and try to protect it whenever we can."

And so, the three friends spent the rest of the day learning about various marine animals while also understanding the value of conservation.

Title: How to Perform a Back Bend Kick Over

Performing a back bend kick over is an impressive acrobatic move that requires strength, flexibility, and control. This tutorial will guide you through the process of mastering this skill safely and effectively. Before starting, make sure you have enough space around you and are wearing comfortable clothing that allows for full range of motion. Please consult with a healthcare professional before attempting any new physical activities.

Step 1: Warm Up

Warm up your body thoroughly to prevent injuries by doing some light cardio exercises such as jumping jacks or jogging in place for five minutes. Follow this with dynamic stretches targeting your major muscle groups, including arm circles, leg swings, hip openers, and torso twists. Dynamic stretching involves moving parts of your body through their full range of motion while increasing circulation and reducing muscular tension.

Step 2: Practice Bridge Pose (Setu Bandha Sarvangasana)

Bridge pose is essential for building the necessary strength and awareness required for a successful backbend kickover. To perform bridge pose:

1. Lie flat on your back with your legs bent, feet flat on the floor close to your buttocks, and arms resting at your sides.
2. Press into your feet and lift your hips off the ground until only your shoulders and head remain in contact with the floor.
3. Engage your core muscles and ensure that your knees stay directly above your ankles.
4. Hold for 5-10 breaths before lowering yourself gently back down to the starting position. Repeat 3-5 times.

Tips: Keep your gaze focused on your toes throughout the exercise to maintain proper spinal alignment. Also, engage your glutes and hamstrings to avoid putting too much pressure on your lower back.

Step 3: Master the Backbend (Urdhva Dhanurasana)

The next step is learning how to do a deep backbend using urdhva dhanurasana (wheel pose). Here's how:

1. Begin lying on your back with your hands placed shoulder-width apart near your ears, fingers pointing towards your feet.
2. Bend your knees and bring your heels close to your buttocks.
3. Exhale deeply and press firmly into your hands and feet to lift your body off the mat, creating an arch shape with your spine.
4. Lift your chest towards the ceiling, keeping your neck relaxed and aligned with your spine.
5. Gently release your head backward if it feels comfortable but never force it.
6. Stay in the posture for several breaths before slowly releasing your body back onto the mat.
7. Repeat 3-5 times, gradually increasing your hold time as you become more comfortable.

Key Tips: Focus on engaging your core, quadriceps, and gluteal muscles during this pose. Maintain steady breathing throughout the exercise to help distribute oxygen efficiently within your body.

Step 4: Learn the Rollback Technique

Before attempting the actual kickover, practice rolling back from your standing position to build trust in your ability to balance and control your movements.

1. Stand tall with your feet hip-distance apart and parallel.
2. Place your hands on your hips or extend them outwards for balance.
3. Slowly roll your upper body backwards, hinging at your waist, until your fingertips touch the ground behind you.
4. Use momentum to continue rolling back, lifting your legs off the ground as you transition into a tucked position.
5. Allow your body to swing forward again, returning to a standing position.
6. Practice this movement multiple times until you feel confident and coordinated.

Together, we traveled through forests made of paper and rivers of ink. Every step was full of magic. We met a brave girl who could talk to letters. She joined us, adding her strength. We battled wild creatures that tried to stop us, but my new friends were strong and clever.

Soon, we reached the Scribbler's castle, which looked like a giant, open book. It was dark and scary. I could feel my legs shaking, but I knew I had to be brave. Inside, the Scribbler sat at a big desk, scribbling furiously. "You cannot stop me!" he shouted, his voice echoing like thunder.

But I remembered the giant's words. "The power of stories is greater than you think!" I shouted back. I picked up a pen from the desk and wrote a story about friendship. The words glowed and filled the room with light. The Scribbler looked surprised, and for a moment, he stopped writing.

My friends joined in. The letters from our stories danced around us, creating a shield of light. Together, we pushed back against the Scribbler. His dark ink began to fade, and soon, he vanished, leaving only a faint whisper. We had saved the stories!

When I returned to the library, the book was closed, but I could still hear the whispers of my friends. I realized that stories hold power, and I had a part in that magic. With a smile, I promised to tell my own stories, to share the magic with the world.

Title: A Mysterious Invitation from Outer Space

Once upon a time, you received a strange invitation that seemed to come straight from outer space! It was a puzzle made up of different shapes and symbols, but there was one thing you recognized - a picture of Earth with another planet nearby. You knew that meant something related to space and planets. How exciting! But what could it mean? To solve the mystery, let's learn about Kepler's first two laws of planetary motion together. No need for fancy words or complicated math - just simple explanations and cool interactions so we can both understand.

Law #1: Planets Move in Ellipses (Not Circles!)
----------------------------------------------

You might think planets move around the Sun in perfect circles, right? Well, surprise! They actually follow oval-like paths called ellipses. Imagine tracing your finger along a squashed circle, moving closer to one side than the other. That wobbly path is similar to what planets do. Let's try it out:

[Interactive Element: Users drag their mouse or finger to draw an ellipse shape.]

Now imagine our home planet, Earth, following this weird route while orbiting the Sun. Seems odd, doesn't it? However, most of the time, Earth's path looks pretty circular since its ellipse is almost perfectly round. This helps us grasp why people used to believe in those neat little circles. Still, even if they seem close enough, remember: Most things in space aren't exactly what they appear to be!

Law #2: Speedy When Close, Slow When Far
----------------------------------------

Here comes law number two! As planets travel along their elliptical paths, guess what happens next... Their speed changes based on where they are in relation to the sun. What does this look like? Picture yourself rollerskating downhill versus skating across flat ground; which takes more effort? Rolling downhill, of course! Similarly, when planets get nearer the Sun, they pick up speed, kind of like rolling down a hill. And then slow down again once they reach the farthest point. Got it? Now, here's a game for practice:

[Interactive Element: Users control a miniature planet by clicking left and right buttons. Clicking "Go!" sends the planet along its orbital path. If users click too early or late, an error message pops up saying "Slow Down," "Speed Up," etc., depending on whether the planet should go faster or slower.]

Pretty nifty, huh? So now you know how some parts of the year feel warmer than others because Earth is racing through space at higher speeds during certain seasons. Isn't science amazing?

Solving Our Intergalactic Puzzle
-------------------------------

So, back to our mysterious invite - remember all these lessons about planets zipping around in squished circles and changing speeds? Those clues will help decode the meaning behind the symbols and shapes. By understanding Kepler's first two laws, maybe we can uncover who sent the riddle and find out what lies beyond our blue dot! Happy exploring!

Brittany
Brittany (French: Bretagne, Breton: Breizh) is a region in Northwest France. The adjective for Brittany is Breton.

Today the official administrative region has 4 departments:
Ctes-d'Armor
Finistre
Ille-et-Vilaine
Morbihan
Before 1941, a fifth dpartement was part of Brittany: Loire-Atlantique, which includes Nantes. The five departments form the cultural region of Brittany, also known as "historical Brittany".

Brittany is in the western France and its coastline points out into the Atlantic. Warmed by the Gulf Stream, Brittany has a mild and temperate climate with warm summers and wet winters.

Three languages are traditionally spoken in Brittany:
Breton language in the West part, a Celtic mix similar to Cornish;
Gallo (a Romance language) in the East part;
And everywhere, French.

The capital of Brittany is Rennes in the Ille-et-Vilaine department.

The name of Brittany is related to Great Britain (in French, Grand Bretagne). The region has also been called Lesser Britain or Little Britain in the past. After the Anglo-Saxons started arriving in Great Britain in the 5th century, many of the Ancient Britons (Celts) moved to this region. The region may have already had strong ties with the Ancient Britons even before that. These tribes gave Brittany its name, the Breton language, the local place names and many parts of its culture. Brittany was a separate country from the 9th century until it was united with France in 1532. It was a province of France until the French Revolution, when its land was divided in departments. Brittany regained a regional government in the 1980s.

Brittany is the home of the world's largest collection of standing stones in one place, the Carnac stones.

Brittany's main industry is agriculture, in particular: pork farming, chicken farming and the production of maize (for cattle feed). Brittany is also the name of a dog breed.

One sunny day, Sally and her robot friend, Tico, were playing with words. They loved making sentences and changing them around. Suddenly, their teacher, Mr. Brightspark, gave them a challenge!

Mr. Brightspark: Hey kids, today we're going to play a game called "Word Shrink." In this task, you need to remove all words of a given length in the sentence. Understand?

Sally: Yes, Mr. Brightspark! So, if you tell us to remove words with four letters, we find those words and take them out of the sentence, right?

Mr. Brightspark: Exactly, Sally! Let's try an example together. Here's a sentence: "the big red ball rolls so fast." What happens when we remove words with three letters?

Tico: Hmm, let me think... We would remove "red," "so," and "ball." That means our new sentence would be: "the big rolls fast."

But wait! When they looked closely again, Sally noticed something strange. She said, "Wait, Tico! Why does 'big' still remain even though it has only three letters?"

Mr. Brightspark smiled and explained, "Great observation, Sally! While 'big' has three letters, remember that sometimes words can join together and become one unit. This is called a contraction in grammar or a compound word in science. It helps make things shorter and easier to say!"

So, the final sentence was actually: "the bigrollsfast." Sometimes, shortening isn't always better; understanding how parts work together makes communication more efficient. Just like teamwork between friends and robots!

Autonomous communities of Spain
Spain is divided in 17 parts called autonomous communities. Autonomous means that each of these autonomous communities has its own executive, legislative judicial powers. These are similar to, but not the same as, states in the United States of America, for example.

Spain has fifty smaller parts called provinces. In 1978 these parts came together, making the autonomous communities.
Before then, some of these provinces were together but were broken. The groups that were together once before are called "historic communities": Catalonia, Basque Country, Galicia and Andalusia.

The Spanish language is the sole official language in every autonomous community but six, where Spanish is co-official with other languages, as follows:
Catalonia: Catalan and Occitan
Valencian Community: Catalan (also called Valencian there)
Balearic Islands: Catalan
Galicia: Galician
Basque Country: Basque
Navarre: Basque (only in the north and near the border with the Basque County)

List of the autonomous communities, with their Capital city (the place where the government has its offices):

Andalusia (its capital is Sevilla)
Aragon (its capital is Zaragoza)
Asturias (its capital is Oviedo)
Balearic Islands (its capital is Palma de Mallorca)
Basque Country (its capital is Vitoria)
Canary Islands (they have two capitals - Las Palmas de Gran Canaria and Santa Cruz de Tenerife)
Cantabria (its capital is Santander)
Castile-La Mancha (its capital is Toledo)
Castile and Len (its capital is Valladolid)
Catalonia (its capital is Barcelona)
Extremadura (its capital is Mrida)
Galicia (its capital is Santiago de Compostela)
La Rioja (its capital is Logroo)
Community of Madrid (its capital is Madrid)
Region of Murcia (its capital is Murcia)
Navarre (its capital is Pamplona)
Valencian Community (its capital is Valencia)

Spain also has two cities on the north coast of Africa: Ceuta and Melilla. They are called "autonomous cities" and have simultaneously the majority of the power of an autonomous community and also power of provinces and power of municipalities.

Lesson Title: Overcoming Fear and Anxiety through God's Grace

Objective: Students will understand how relying on God's grace can help us overcome fear and anxiety in our lives.

Introduction:
Have you ever felt scared or worried about something? Maybe it was a big test at school, a fight with a friend, or even just trying something new. When we feel this way, it can be hard to know what to do! That's where learning about God's grace comes in. By trusting in Him and remembering all the good things He has done for us, we can find the strength to overcome anything.

Section 1: What is Fear and Anxiety?
Fear is when we are afraid of something that might happen. We might worry about getting sick, failing a class, or losing someone we love. Anxiety is similar but happens more often and lasts longer than regular fear. Both fear and anxiety can make us feel nervous, have trouble sleeping, or struggle to focus. They can also cause physical symptoms like stomachaches, headaches, and fast heartbeats.

Section 2: Understanding God's Grace
Grace is a word used to describe the goodness and kindness of God towards us. Even though we don't deserve it, God loves us so much that He gives us gifts and blessings. This includes sending Jesus to die for our sins and giving us eternal life. Through God's grace, we can experience peace, joy, and hope - even during difficult times.

Section 3: How Does God's Grace Help Us Overcome Fear and Anxiety?
God's grace helps us remember that He is always with us and will never leave us alone. No matter what challenge we may face, God promises to give us the courage and wisdom we need to get through it (Joshua 1:9). Trusting in God's plan for our lives can bring comfort and reduce feelings of fear and anxiety (Proverbs 3:5-6). Prayer and reading the Bible can also remind us of God's faithfulness and power (Philippians 4:6-7).

Section 4: Stories of People Who Found Strength in God's Grace
Throughout history, there have been people who faced scary situations yet found strength in God's grace. One example is Corrie ten Boom, a Dutch woman who helped Jews escape persecution during World War II. After being sent to a concentration camp herself, she experienced forgiveness and healing through prayer and reliance on God's grace (The Hiding Place). Another example is the Apostle Paul, who continued sharing the Good News despite facing imprisonment and beatings (Acts 9).

Conclusion:
Living with fear and anxiety can be tough, but knowing that God offers His grace freely to everyone can provide comfort and encouragement. As believers in Jesus, we can rely on His promise to never abandon us and instead empower us to live boldly for Him. So let's choose to put our trust in God's grace and watch as He works wonders in our lives!

Activities:
1. Have students write down their fears and anxieties on slips of paper, then pray together as a group over each concern. Encourage students to think about ways they can apply God's grace to those specific issues.
2. Create posters showing different scenarios where people might feel anxious or afraid (e.g., taking a test, going to a doctor's appointment), along with verses reminding them of God's presence and grace. Display these around the classroom as a reminder throughout the week.

Sometimes, the wood can take on funny shapes as it dries. This is because of how much it gets smaller in the different ways. This picture tells us how a log changes when it is cut into boards. Some kinds of wood shrink more than others when they dry. This makes them harder to work with.
When wood shrinks, it can change in three ways. These changes can add up to anywhere from 9% to 15% for most types of wood.
The way the wood shrinks can tell us how stable it is. The best wood is as stable as possible. For example, Walnut wood is very stable.
Knowing how and why wood changes can help us use it better. Wood only changes size when it gets more or less wet. The temperature doesn't make a difference. Wood is like a sponge. It can soak up water from the air or let water out into the air. This depends on how wet or dry the air is. We can put finishes on the wood to slow this down, but the wood will always react to the water in the air. What does it mean when wood is 'kiln dried'? This is a term that means the wood is very dry, about as dry as it can get. Wood must be dry to use it for building. Big groups that know a lot about wood say that wood should be dry when it's used. This is because dry wood is best for building in most places. Some places are very dry, like a city in the desert, and some places are very wet, like a place in the south with lots of beaches. But in most places, wood is just right when it's a little bit dry. If the wood is too wet, it can change shape and break. Things that hold wood together and things that make wood look nice work best when the wood is a little bit dry. If the wood is too dry, it's hard to work with and it can mess up the things that hold it together and make it look nice.

When you bend wood, it can make it stressed. But when you bend wood, it only gets a little bit longer. Bending wood is like squishing the tiny parts of the wood together. This squishing is the most in the middle of the bend and less on the outside of the bend. If the bend is very sharp, the wood will squish a lot. The squishing also happens a little bit outside of the bend. When we dry wood, it changes shape because its tiny building blocks, the cells, get smaller. We change the shape of our wood-bending tool to help with this. After drying the wood, we make small changes so it's just the right shape before we send it away. Even after drying, the wood can still change shape. If it's very dry, like in winter when the heating is on, the wood might curve more. But in wet, humid summer, the curve might open up more.

Sometimes, the wood can have little splits, or checks, in it. This happens if the outside of the wood dries faster than the inside. If the inside is stronger, the outside might split. But if the outside is stronger, the inside might have empty spaces, like a honeycomb. The middle part of the wood, or the cathedral, can get these splits most often.


Symphony No. 7 (Shostakovich)
Symphony No. 7 in C major, Op. 60 is a symphony by Dmitri Shostakovich. It is also called the Leningrad symphony. It was composed in 1941. It is a very long work, lasting about 75 minutes. The symphony was first performed by the Bolshoi Theatre Orchestra on 5 March 1942. Shostakovich was awarded a Stalin Prize by the Soviet government for the symphony.

History of its composition

Shostakovich gave the symphony its title because it is about what was happening in Leningrad in 1941. It was during the World War II and the German army had invaded the Soviet Union and blocked communication between the city of Leningrad (now called St Petersburg) and the rest of the world. Conditions were terrible: the people hardly had any food to eat and they were very cold in the winter. About a million people died during the siege.

Shostakovich lived in fear most of his life because if Josef Stalin, the Soviet dictator, did not like his music he could have been sent to prison or put to death. Sometimes Shostakovich was made a hero by the government and sometimes he was told that his music was not good because it was not in the style that the government thought he should write it in. The symphony was very popular at first in countries that fought on the same side as Russia in World War II, as well as in Russia. It was performed many times in the United States and the United Kingdom. Many people in these countries liked the symphony because it seemed to show the Russians as heroes fighting to save their city from the Germans. Later, during the Cold War, many people in these same countries did not like the work very much, because the Russians were now their enemies and they thought that music written there was propaganda meant to show Russia and its leaders as better than other countries and their leaders. In more recent years, people have once more changed their minds about the meaning of the music. The music is now thought by some people who study music to show how cruel Stalin was as well as the terror of the Nazi invasion. Other people still think it was meant to support the Russian government and army as they fought the Germans, and to remember the people who died fighting.

One of the reasons it is so hard to know what the symphony means is that people disagree about when Shostakovich started writing it. If he started it before the war began, it is probably at least partly about the Soviet government, but if he started it during the war, it might be only about the war.

After the first performance on 5 March 1942 in Kuybshev (now called Samara), it was soon performed in Moscow, and then in Leningrad, which was still surrounded by the German army at the time. A copy of the music was smuggled out to the West on microfilm. It was performed by Sir Henry Wood in London at the BBC studios on 22 June and the next week at a Promenade Concert. On 19 July it was played in New York by the NBC Symphony Orchestra conducted by Arturo Toscanini in a studio concert played on the radio throughout the United States.

The Music
The work has four movements:
1 Allegretto
2 Moderato (poco allegretto)
3 Adagio
4 Allegro non troppo

When she finished, the poem felt perfect. Jean decided to deliver it in person. She put on her raincoat and stepped into the wet world. The rain fell on her face, and she smiled. It felt like a fresh start.

At Rita's house, Jean knocked on the door. When Rita saw her, her eyes widened. "I'm sorry," Jean said quickly, handing her the poem. As Rita read, her expression softened. "Thank you," she whispered. They hugged, and the rain continued to fall. Jean learned that art could mend hearts and bring friends back together.

Saturn
Some scientists think that the rings are material left after a moon broke apart. A new idea says that it was a very large moon, most of which crashed into the planet. This left a large amount of ice to form the rings and some of the moons. This includes Enceladus, which is thought to be made of ice.

History
The rings were first found by Galileo Galilei in 1610, using his telescope. They did not look like rings to Galileo. He called them "handles". He thought that Saturn was three different planets that were right next to each other. In 1612, when the rings were facing edge on with the Earth, the rings disappeared, then reappeared again in 1613, further confusing Galileo. In 1655, Christiaan Huygens was the first person to say that Saturn was surrounded by rings. Using a much more powerful telescope than Galilei's, he said that Saturn "is surrounded by a thin, flat, ring, nowhere touching...". In 1675, Giovanni Domenico Cassini found that the planet's rings were in fact made of smaller rings with gaps. The largest ring gap was later named the Cassini Division. In 1859, James Clerk Maxwell showed that the rings cannot be solid, but are made of small particles, each orbiting Saturn on their own. Otherwise, it would become unstable or break apart. James Keeler studied the rings using a spectroscope in 1895 which proved Maxwell's theory.

Physical features
The rings range from to above the planet's equator. While the equatorial circumference of Saturn is 378,675 km (235,298 miles). As proved by Maxwell, even though the rings appear to be solid and unbroken when viewed from above, the rings are made of small particles of rock and ice. They are only about thick; made of silica rock, iron oxide and ice particles. The smallest particles are only specks of dust while the largest are the size of a house. The C and D rings also seem to have a "wave" in them, like waves in water. These large waves are high, but only moving slowly at about each day. Some scientists believe that the wave is caused by Saturn's moons. Another idea is the waves were made by a comet hitting Saturn in 1983 or 1984.

The largest gaps in the rings are the Cassini Division and the Encke Division, both visible from the Earth. The Cassini Division is the largest, measuring wide. However, when the Voyager spacecrafts visited Saturn in 1980, they discovered that the rings are a complex structure, made out of thousands of thin gaps and ringlets. Scientists believe this is caused by the gravitational force of some of Saturn's moons. The tiny moon Pan orbits inside Saturn's rings, creating a gap within the rings. Other ringlets keep their structure due to the gravitational force of shepherd satellites, such as Prometheus and Pandora. Other gaps form due to the gravitational force of a large moon farther away. The moon Mimas is responsible for clearing away the Cassini gap.

Rochester, New York
Rochester is the third-largest city in the U.S. state of New York. It has a little over 200,000 people living in it and over a million people living in the metropolitan area. It is on the southern shore of Lake Ontario. It is between the cities of Buffalo and Syracuse.

Media

WHEC NBC

WROC CBS

WXXI PBS

WOKR American Broadcasting Company

WUHF Fox Broadcasting Company

WGBT UPN

Geography
Rochester is on the shore of Lake Ontario, one of the Great Lakes. Also, the Genesee River flows through it. In the area near Rochester, there are many streams, large hills called drumlins, and lakes, such as the Finger Lakes. The weather in Rochester is warm in the summer and cold in the winter, with a lot of snow falling in the winter and early spring.

Economy and education
Rochester is the headquarters of Eastman Kodak, a company that makes cameras and camera film. Rochester is also the home to universities such as the University of Rochester and the Rochester Institute of Technology.

Alice: Hi Bob! Have you ever heard about social work practice before? It's part of something called human services or social sciences.

Bob: No, I haven't. What is it exactly?

Alice: Well, imagine if someone needs help because they are having trouble at home or school, like fighting with their siblings or struggling with homework. A social worker might step in to offer guidance and support. They use what we call 'social work practice' to understand problems and come up with solutions.

Alice: Exactly! And sometimes social workers even create new ways to solve issues by studying different methods and ideas. This process is called 'theory and model development.' Imagine trying to build your own Lego set without any instructions - you look at lots of pictures and try various combinations until you find just the right fit. That's kind of like what social workers do too!

Bob: Cool! But where does the 'social science' part come in?

Alice: Great question! You know how scientists study nature and animals? Social scientists study people, society, and how we interact with each other. By learning more about those interactions, social workers can better assist individuals, families, and communities.

Bob: Got it! Now I feel smarter already. Thanks for explaining, Alice!

Alice: My pleasure, Bob! Remember, being curious and asking questions helps us learn and grow every day. Let's keep exploring together!

Chapter Title: Understanding Perfectionism: It's Okay to Make Mistakes!

Hey there, future champions! Have you ever felt like what you do just isn't good enough? Or maybe you get really upset when things don't go exactly according to your plan? You might be dealing with something called perfectionism - but don't worry, it happens to lots of people! Let's explore this idea together so you can learn how to handle these feelings and embrace being awesome just the way you are.

What does it mean to be a 'perfectionist'?
---------------------------------------------

Being a perfectionist means wanting everything to be perfect all the time. Sounds great at first, right? Who doesn't want to be the best they can be? But sometimes, our desire to be perfect can cause us stress and anxiety because we put too much pressure on ourselves. Imagine always feeling like you have to get an A+ on every test or never making mistakes while playing sports. That would be pretty tough! We're here to tell you that everyone makes mistakes; even adults mess up sometimes. And guess what? That's perfectly okay!

Why is perfectionism not so cool?
----------------------------------

When we strive for perfection, it sets us up for disappointment. Nobody is perfect, no matter how hard they try. When we expect nothing short of perfection, we focus more on our failures than our successes. This mindset can lead to negative emotions like frustration, sadness, anger, and low self-esteem. Over time, these feelings can impact other areas of life such as friendships, family relationships, and hobbies. So instead of trying to be perfect, let's work on doing our personal best and celebrating our achievements along the way!

How can I deal with my perfectionistic tendencies?
---------------------------------------------------

First, remember that nobody is perfect, including yourself. Embrace your unique qualities and understand that everyone has strengths AND weaknesses. Next, practice setting realistic goals for yourself. Instead of aiming for straight As, challenge yourself to improve in one particular subject each term. Finally, give yourself permission to make mistakes and use them as learning opportunities rather than seeing them as failures. By following these steps, you will find that managing perfectionism gets easier over time.

Fun Activity Time!
--------------------

Let's draw a superhero version of ourselves fighting off Mr. Perfect, the villain who wants to ruin our fun! Remember, your superhero character represents your authentic self - someone brave, strong, and capable of achieving anything they set their minds to (without needing to be perfect). Use colors and patterns that showcase your personality. Afterward, write down three positive traits about yourself in the speech bubble coming out of your hero's mouth. Hang this picture somewhere visible to remind yourself that you're amazing just the way you are!

In Conclusion...
---------------

We hope this chapter helped you better understand perfectionism and its effects on our lives. Just know that it's normal to feel pressured to be perfect sometimes, but striving for excellence and embracing imperfections leads to happiness, growth, and resilience. Keep working towards becoming the best version of YOU possible!

Lu Sheng-yen
Lu Sheng-Yen (, L Shngyn) (27 June 1945), is the founder and spiritual leader of the True Buddha School, which is a religious group with teachings taken from Taoism and Buddhism. He is called Master Lu by his followers. Within his sect, he is also known as Living Buddha Lian Sheng (, Liansheng Huf). He is worshipped by his followers as a Living Buddha.

His organization says that over five million students have taken Buddhist refuge under Lu. There are also more than three hundred local chapters of the True Buddha School, including thirty major temples, such as the Ling Shen Ching Tze Temple in Redmond, Washington, where he lives now. Many of his followers are from Taiwan, Singapore, and Malaysia.

Lu is married to Lian Hsiang, who is also a vajra master. She is referred as Grand Madam Lu. Lu and Lian Hsiang have two children.

Life
Lu was born in Chiayi County, Taiwan in 1945. He was raised a Christian and attended a Protestant school. His post-secondary education was at Chung Cheng Institute of Technology. He graduated with a degree in Survey Engineering. In his early twenties he was both a survey engineer and a Sunday school Bible teacher.

Lu has written that he had a mystical experience in 1969. This lead him to seek out a total of twenty-one human gurus in Taoism, Sutra, and Tantra. In 1982, Lu moved to the United States, and lived in the state of Washington.

To date, Lu has written over 200 books in Chinese on various topics, including feng shui and poetry.

According to his website, he went into hiding in Tahiti for six years starting late 2000 and lived in Taichung, Taiwan. Today he lives in the state of Washington.

Teachings
Lu teaches the Mahamudra way of attaining enlightenment. His teachings follow the traditional stages of the practice of the Four Preliminaries, followed by Guru Yoga, Deity Yoga, the Vajra Practices, and finally Highest Yoga Tantra. Lu has written that his spiritual gurus included the 16th Karmapa, Rangjung Rigpe Dorje and Tai Situ Rinpoche.

He describes the state of enlightenment using the allegory of Padmakumara, whom he identifies with Amitabha Buddha and his own enlightened self.

According to Noah Casey, Lu's teachings do not prohibit the consumption of meat and alcohol; however, "The consumption of alcohol is limited to quantities not resulting in intoxication, and the eating of meat is restricted to animals not butchered especially for the person consuming. Before consuming either of these, or any other nutritional substance, a special prayer is required. For meats, the spirit of the animal must be delivered." This is consistent with the Vajrayana traditions of Tibetan Buddhism.

Controversies
Lu made headlines during an investigation by the Washington State Public Disclosure Commission into his cash donations to Chinese American politician Gary Locke, who Lu had hoped would run for President of the United States. Locke was cleared of any wrongdoing by the commission in 1998. Anderson, Rick. Sex and the buddha in the Seattle Weekly, 5 September 2001.

He was also sued in civil court by a former disciple, who called herself SHC, a 41-year-old Malaysian immigrant, over claims of sexual misconduct, after the King County, Washington prosecutor declined to file charges for lack of evidence. The case was dismissed by King County Superior Court Judge Kathleen Learned citing constitutional issues. In the case S.H.C. v. Sheng-Yen Lu, the Superior Court of King County granted the Temple's motion for summary judgment, and the Court of Appeals later "affirm[ed] the trial court's grant of summary judgment dismissing all claims against the Temple."

World Wide Fund for Nature
The World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF) is an international environmental organization. It was founded as the World Wildlife Fund, which is still its official name in Canada and the United States.

Most of its offices are in Switzerland. Their mascot, or logo, is the Giant Panda. It is the world's largest independent wildlife management organization. It has over 5 million supporters worldwide, working in more than 90 countries. WWF supports 15,000 conservation and environmental projects around the world. It is a charity. About 90% of its fundraising money is from donations by private individuals and businesses.

The group says its mission is "to halt and reverse the destruction of our natural environment". Much of its work focuses on the conservation of three biomes that contain most of the world's biodiversity: forests, freshwater ecosystems, and oceans and coasts. Among other issues, it is also concerned with endangered species, pollution and climate change. The organization runs more than 1,200 field projects worldwide each year.

Studio
A studio is a place where an artist can work. Studios can be used for many things, such as photography, broadcasting, painting, making movies, television shows, cartoons, or music.

Movie studio
A movie studio is most often a company that makes movies. The place where movies are made may also be called a studio, or sometimes a "sound stage" because it also records the sound.

Television studio
A television studio is where video production takes place. It usually contains cameras, microphones, speakers, and spotlights. It is similar to a movie studio.

Recording studio
A recording studio is used for recording music, speech, or other kinds of sound. They are typically divided into three areas: an "isolation room" that has soundproofing for playing instruments and to prevent echo, a "live room" for general recording, and a "control room" to store the recording equipment that DJ's use.

**Unit Title: Expecting Change**

---

Once upon a time, there was a student named Alex who loved playing soccer. He spent hours each day practicing dribbling, shooting, and passing with his friends. When he started high school, Alex knew he wanted to join the school team. But then something unexpected happened - the coach announced that tryouts would conflict with band practice! Alex had also signed up for band because he enjoyed playing music too. Now, what should he do?

Interactive Element 1: Thought Experiment
Imagine you were Alex. What would YOU do if you found yourself facing this same challenge? Jot down three possible solutions below before moving forward.

---

Change can come from within us or around us. Sometimes we initiate changes ourselves due to new information or realizing our plans aren't aligned with our values and goals (internal factors). Other times, things happen beyond our control, like family moves, teachers leave, or global pandemics strike (external factors). Let's see how Alex navigates through this inner turmoil using some strategies for managing change.

Alex remembered that both activities brought him joy but required different skills and commitments. To manage this unexpected situation, he decided to consider these steps:

1. Identify the Problem: Understand the reason behind the need for change. For Alex, the problem was having conflicting schedules between soccer tryouts and band practice.
2. Brainstorm Solutions: Think creatively about various ways to address the issue. Maybe Alex could switch bands, negotiate with coaches, or seek advice from peers and mentors.
3. Evaluate Options: Weigh pros and cons of each solution carefully considering their impact on overall well-being and long-term objectives.
4. Choose & Implement Solution: Pick the best option, create a plan, and put it into action.
5. Reflect & Adjust: Assess whether the chosen path works out as expected. If not, don't hesitate to revisit earlier stages.

Interactive Element 2: Real Life Scenario
Now think about a recent change you experienced at school or home. Apply the five-step strategy above to tackle it effectively.

---

Remember, although change might feel overwhelming initially, learning to expect and adapt to it helps pave the way towards college success. With flexible thinking and proactive problem solving, young learners like Alex can turn challenges into opportunities and grow stronger along their academic journey.

Fire Island, New York
Fire Island is a barrier island, approximately 31 miles (49.5 km) long and varying between approximately 0.1 mile (0.16 km) to 0.5 mile (0.8 km) wide, in Suffolk County on the southern side of Long Island in the U.S. state of New York, running approximately WSW to ENE. The land area is 48 km2 (18.7 sq mi) and a permanent population of 310 persons was reported as of the 2000 census. (There are many thousands of seasonal residents.)

The Cherry Grove and Fire Island Pines hamlets of Fire Island have been known as a popular gay village.

Beneath a cloudy sky, a man sat alone on a park bench. He wore a dark, tattered coat that made him feel heavy inside. Once, he was a bright and cheerful superhero, flying high and helping others. But time had changed him. Now, he watched children play with bright, colorful kites, their laughter echoing in the air. He longed for the joy he had lost, yet bitterness filled his heart. Happiness felt far away, like a star in the sky.

In his mind, he thought of ways to bring joy back. "If I could just save one person," he said quietly. He remembered a time when he saved a small cat from a tree. The people cheered and called him a hero. But now, that moment felt small and far away. He thought, "Maybe being a hero is about making others happy, but what if they don't want to be saved?" This thought troubled him. Perhaps, he was not the hero he thought he was. Maybe he was just a shadow of his former self.

One day, he spotted a girl with bright, shining eyes. She was sad, sitting by herself. He wanted to help her, but fear gripped his heart. What if she didn't want help? What if she thought he was just a fool? He decided to sit near her, watching and waiting for the right moment. He saw her look at the other kids, wishing to join but feeling alone. It reminded him of his own pain.

Hours passed, and she still sat there. The sun began to set, casting a golden light. Finally, he spoke, "Why do you sit here alone?" She looked up, surprised. Her soft voice broke the silence, "I lost my kite. It flew away." The man's heart sank. A kite could not compare to the heroes he once was. "I can help you find it," he offered, his voice shaky. She smiled, and for the first time in years, he felt a spark of happiness.

As they searched together, they talked about dreams and wishes. He learned that she wanted to be a superhero, too. The girl's laughter brought warmth to his cold heart. They searched under bushes and behind trees, but the kite was nowhere to be found. His heart sank again, but he felt lighter. In helping her, he felt a bit of the hero he once was. Happiness was not just about saving the day; it was also about sharing moments with others.

Eventually, they sat down, tired but content. "You know," he said, "sometimes, the thing we look for is not what we really need." She tilted her head, confused. "What do you mean?" He smiled, "We found happiness in our search, didn't we?" The girl's eyes brightened. "Yes! I had fun with you!" He realized he didn't need a kite to feel whole. Helping her had filled a part of him he thought was lost forever.

When they parted, she waved and ran off, her laughter ringing in the air. He watched her go, feeling a warmth inside. Happiness was not in the big acts of heroism but in the little moments spent together. He understood that the pain he felt was part of the journey to find joy. The next day, he would wear a smile and search for more moments of happiness, no matter how small.

Title: How to Get a Long Spike on Animal Jam

Animal Jam is a popular online game that allows players to create their own animal characters, explore a virtual world, play games, and make friends. One way to customize your character's appearance is by obtaining different types of spikes. This tutorial will focus on getting a long spike for your Animal Jam character.

Step 1: Create an Account or Log into Your Existing Account
Before you can get a long spike, you need to have access to the Animal Jam platform. If you don't already have an account, visit the Animal Jam website (< and click on the "Sign Up" button. Follow the prompts to create your account. If you already have an account, simply enter your username and password to log in.

Step 2: Earn Gems
Gems are the primary currency in Animal Jam. You can earn gems by playing mini-games, completing adventures, trading with other players, or purchasing them with real money. To get a long spike, you'll need enough gems to buy it from the Diamond Shop. Aim to accumulate at least 500 gems, as this is the typical cost of most rare items in the Diamond Shop.

Key Tip: Focus on earning gems through activities rather than buying them. This encourages active engagement within the game and helps develop gaming skills.

Step 3: Visit the Diamond Shop
Once you have enough gems, navigate to the Diamond Shop. The Diamond Shop is where you can purchase rare items using your hard-earned gems. To find the Diamond Shop, look for the glowing diamond icon located near the top right corner of the screen while in Jamaa Township. Click on the icon to open the shop.

Guideline: Remember that stock in the Diamond Shop changes daily, so if you don't see the long spike available today, check back tomorrow!

Step 4: Browse Available Items
Upon entering the Diamond Shop, take some time to browse through the various categories of items displayed. These may include clothing, accessories, den decorations, and more. Look specifically under the "Hair & Tails" category for spikes. When you locate the long spike, click on its image to view additional details about the item.

Step 5: Purchase the Long Spike
After selecting the long spike, review its price to ensure you have sufficient gems. If you do, proceed to complete the purchase by clicking the green "Buy" button. Confirm the transaction when prompted. Once completed, the long spike should appear in your inventory.

Key Tip: Always double-check prices before making purchases to avoid wasting valuable gems.

Step 6: Equip the Long Spike
To equip the new long spike on your character, first open your inventory. You can do this by clicking on the backpack icon found near the bottom left corner of the screen. Inside your inventory, locate the long spike and click on it. Then select "Equip." This will add the long spike to your character's current outfit.

Step 7: Show Off Your New Style
Now that you've successfully obtained and equipped a long spike, feel free to show off your new style while exploring Jamaa Township, chatting with friends, or participating in mini-games. Enjoy expressing yourself through creative customization options available in Animal Jam!

Trail of Tears
The Cherokee travelled in groups of 1000 to 3000 people on three main routes. Different groups started in Chattanooga, Tennessee; Guntersville, Alabama; and Charleston, Tennessee. Most Cherokees had to walk; others, if they were wealthy men, could use wagons. The United States government also gave the Cherokee about 660 wagons.

The trip was about 1,200 miles long. During the trip, the Cherokees had to deal with winter weather, blizzards, and diseases. Not everybody agrees on how many people died on the trip. Some say 2,000 and others say 6,000, but most say about 4,000 people died. This was one out of every four people in the Cherokee population. They died from diseases like pneumonia, from freezing to death, from drinking bad water, and from other causes. About half of them died in camps, and the other half during the trip.

It is said that many Cherokees sang a Cherokee version of the song Amazing Grace, which became a kind of anthem for the Cherokee nation.

Finally the Cherokee who were still alive arrived in what is now Oklahoma.

Routes

There were different routes the Cherokees took. Some were by land and others by water. Some boats were destroyed, which was a danger on water routes. On the ground, people had to walk through mud and cold weather and it was harder walking on land.

Water route
This route was taken by three groups, in total 2,800 Cherokees. The first group left on June 6 and reached the territory after 13 days. All groups started at Ross's Landing at the Tennessee River. They used boats to travel to the Ohio River. They then took this river southward, which took them to the Mississippi River. From there they moved through the Arkansas River westwards. They arrived near Fort Coffee, Oklahoma. The second and third group had a lot of problems with diseases, so their trip took longer.

Land routes
All others took land routes. They traveled in groups with a size of 700-1,600 people, all led by conductors chosen by John Ross, except for those, who signed the Treaty of New Enchota. They were led by United States soldiers. They usually took the southern route, and John Ross' groups the northern route. Both sides used already existing "roads". Most Cherokees took the northern route. The route lead through central Tennessee, southwestern Kentucky, and southern Illinois. The groups crossed the Mississippi north of Cape Girardeau, Missouri, then traveled through southern Missouri and west of Arkansas. Many died because of diseases, lack of water and bad road conditions. All land routes usually ended near Westville, Oklahoma. There were many more different land routes only taken by few people. These routes cover more than 2,200 miles in 9 states.

Game Boy line
When Nintendo released the Nintendo DS handheld in 2004, they said it was a "third pillar" (the other two pillars were the Game Boy and the home console). It has two screens, one of which is a touch screen. DS games use cards in Slot 1. Slot 2 can accept Game Boy Advance games. A newer model, called the DS Lite, released in 2006, also plays GBA games. But like the GBA Micro, neither of them can play original Game Boy or Game Boy Color games. The DSi and DSi XL, released in 2008 and 2009, replaced the GBA slot with an SD Card. This makes it impossible to play GBA games. Some DS games also included extra features contained in "option paks", which were just like GBA games. So these features could not be used on those DS games if they were played on the DSi or DSi XL.

Nintendo 3DS

Like the DSi and DSi XL, the 3DS line lacks a GBA slot. However, GB and GBC games can be downloaded through the Virtual Console. Those who bought a 3DS prior to the 2011 price drop were lucky to download ten GBA games, along with ten NES games, through the Ambassador Program. While the NES games became available to the public, the GBA games remain exclusive to the Ambassadors.
