Prisoner
A prisoner is a person who is forced to stay in a prison against their will. People who are suspected of a crime, for example, a murder, may be arrested and held in jail so they won't escape before their trial. After conviction a prisoner may be punished. For example, they may be imprisoned for a fixed number of years, or receive a life sentence meaning they stay in jail until they die.

A prisoner of war is a person who was captured by the enemy in a war.

Jim Jones
Jones and several members argued that the group should commit "revolutionary suicide" by drinking cyanide-laced grape-flavored Flavor Aid. However, later released video made to show the best of Jonestown shows Jones opening a storage container full of Kool-Aid in large quantities. This may have been what was used to mix the "potion" (as was referred to in several statements on the tape recordings) along with a sedative.

One member, Christine Miller, dissents toward the beginning of the tape. When members apparently cried, Jones counseled, "Stop this hysterics. This is not the way for people who are Socialists or Communists to die. No way for us to die. We must die with some dignity". Jones can be heard saying, "Don't be afraid to die," that death is "just stepping over into another plane" and that it's "a friend". At the end of the tape, Jones concludes: "We didn't commit suicide; we committed an act of revolutionary suicide protesting the conditions of an inhumane world". According to escaping Temple members, children were given the drink first and families were told to lie down together. Mass suicide had been previously discussed in simulated events called "White Nights" on a regular basis.

Jones was found dead in a deck chair with a gunshot wound to his head that Guyanese coroner Cyrill Mootoo stated was consistent with a self-inflicted gun wound. However, Jones' son Stephan believes his father may have directed someone else to shoot him. An autopsy of Jones' body also showed levels of the barbiturate Pentobarbital which may have been lethal to humans who had not developed physiological tolerance. Jones' drug usage (including LSD and marijuana) was confirmed by his son, Stephan, and Jones' doctor in San Francisco.

Saturn
Saturn's atmosphere can make oval shaped clouds. This is like the clearer spots seen on Jupiter. These oval spots are cyclonic storms, the same as cyclones seen on Earth. In 1990, the Hubble Space Telescope found a very large white cloud near Saturn's equator. Storms like the one in 1990 were known as Great White Spots. These unique storms only exist for a short time and only happen about every 30 Earth years, at the time of the summer solstice in the Northern Hemisphere. Great White Spots were also found in 1876, 1903, 1933, and 1960.

The Voyager 1 spacecraft found a hexagonal cloud pattern near Saturn's north pole at about 78N. The CassiniHuygens probe later confirmed it in 2006. Unlike the north pole, the south pole does not show any hexagonal clouds. The probe also found a hurricane-like storm on the south pole that showed an eyewall. Until this finding, eyewalls had only been seen on Earth.

Interior
Saturn's inside is similar to Jupiter's inside. It has a small rocky core about the size of the Earth at its center. It is very hot. Its temperature reaches 15,000 K (). Saturn is so hot that it gives out more heat energy into space than it gets from the Sun. Above it is a thicker layer of metallic hydrogen, about deep. Above that layer is a region of liquid hydrogen and helium. The core is heavy, with about 9 to 22 times more mass than the Earth's core.

Magnetic field
Saturn has a natural magnetic field that is weaker than Jupiter's. Like the Earth's, Saturn's field is a magnetic dipole (it has a North and a South). Saturn's field is unique in that it is perfectly symmetrical, unlike any other known planet. This means the field is exactly in line with the planet's axis. Saturn generates radio waves, but they are too weak to be detected from Earth. The moon Titan orbits in the outer part of Saturn's magnetic field and gives out plasma to the field from the ionised particles in Titan's atmosphere.

Rotation and orbit
Saturn's average distance from the Sun is over 1,400,000,000 km (869,000,000 mi). This is about nine times the distance from the Earth to the Sun. It takes 10,759 days, or about 29.8 years, for Saturn to orbit around the Sun. This is known as Saturn's orbital period.

Voyager 1 measured Saturn's rotation as being 10 hours, 14 minutes at the equator, 10 hours, 40 minutes closer to the poles, and 10 hours, 39 minutes, 24 seconds for the planet's inside. This is known as its rotational period.

Cassini measured the rotation of Saturn as being 10 hours, 45 minutes, 45 seconds  36 seconds. That is about six minutes longer than the radio rotational period measured by the Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 spacecrafts, which flew by Saturn in 1980 and 1981.

Saturn's rotational period is calculated by the rotation speed of radio waves given off by the planet. The CassiniHuygens spacecraft found that the radio waves slowed down. This suggested that the rotational period increased. Since scientists do not think Saturn's rotation is actually slowing down, the explanation may be that the magnetic field causes the radio waves.

Planetary rings

Saturn is best known for its planetary rings which are easy to see with a telescope. There are seven named rings: A, B, C, D, E, F, and G. They were named in the order they were found, which is different to their order from the planet. From the planet the rings are ordered: D, C, B, A, F, G and E.

Maynard James Keenan
Maynard James Keenan (born James Herbert Keenan on April 17, 1964) is an American rock singer, songwriter, musician, and producer. He sings in the band Tool, and also in the band A Perfect Circle. He has a side project called Puscifer.

Early life
James Herbert Keenan was born in Ravenna, Ohio on April 17, 1964. His mother is Judith and his father is Michael, who was a high school teacher. Keenan's parents divorced when he was three years old, and Michael moved away. Keenan did not see him very much for the next 12 years. Later, his mother married someone else. He was mean and did not allow Keenan to be creative. When Keenan was 11, his mother, Judith, had a brain aneurysm that paralyzed her. Two years later, she told Keenan to move to Michigan with his father.

The Army

Keenan joined the United States Army after he graduated from high school. He wanted to use the G.I. Bill to go to art school. He joined the United States Military Academy Preparatory School (West Point Prep School) where he picked up the nickname "Maynard". He did very well in his training, but said no to an offer to stay in the Army and work at West Point. He decided to start his music career instead.

Art
After being honorably discharged from the Army, Keenan went back to Michigan to go to art school. Then, in 1988, he moved to Los Angeles, California to help design the inside of pet stores. He was fired from this job and then worked creating movie sets. He also played bass guitar in a band and sang for another band.

Music career
Keenan started playing music soon after leaving art school. He and Adam Jones formed Tool. Keenan formed A Perfect Circle in 1999. They had 4 albums: Mer De Noms, The Thirteenth Step, eMOTIVe and Eat the Elephant. He then left again to be with his family. He now has a vineyard where he makes wine but still takes tours for his working side project; Puscifer. Tool released an album in 2019 named Fear Inoculum.

Tool
Keenan met Adam Jones in Los Angeles. They started the band Tool in 1990. The band's line up later became Keenan as singer, Jones playing guitar, Danny Carey playing drums, and Paul D'Amour playing bass. When D'Amour left the band, Justin Chancellor took his place. Tool signed to Zoo Entertainment in November 1991.

Welcome to our e-learning module on "Summing Up Factors That Change Supply"! Today, we will explore how different things can make it easier or harder for businesses to produce goods and services. To help us remember everything, let's join our friends - Sammy the Snail, Olive the Owl, and Pete the Porcupine - as they run their toy store!

Once upon a time, Sammy, Olive, and Pete started a wonderful toy store where kids could come and buy cool toys! They want to know what makes them sell more or fewer toys, so they keep track of things like costs, weather, technology, and rules.

First, there's **cost**. This means how much money they need to spend on making each toy. If the cost goes up because materials become expensive, then they might not be able to afford making as many toys (or maybe even decide to close down the shop). But if the cost goes down, yay! More toys for everyone!

Next, imagine a big storm comes along! Oh no! The storm damages their factory (*natural disaster*). Now, they cannot make as many toys until they fix it. Because of this, they may sell fewer toys until things go back to normal.

Now, let's think about something exciting - new ways to build toys faster and better! When they find a fantastic new machine or technique (*new technology*), producing toys becomes quicker and cheaper! Hooray! They now can create more toys than before and make lots of customers happy!

Lastly, sometimes grown-ups make rules that change things too (*government decisions*). Imagine someone says they must pay workers extra during holidays; this will increase the cost again! However, other times, these rules protect them from unfair competition or provide them support, which helps them stay open longer and offer more choices.

So here's a summary of what affects supply:

1. **Cost**: How easy or hard it is to make toys. Lower costs mean more toys!
2. **Natural Disaster**: Unexpected events causing delays and reducing toy numbers.
3. **New Technology**: Awesome inventions helping them make toys quickly and cheaply!
4. **Government Decisions**: Rules made by adults changing how they do business. Sometimes good, sometimes challenging!

When you see your favorite stores next time, try remembering these four things and share with others how they can change what shops can give us! Thank you, and don't forget to wash hands and practice kindness always! Bye!

Curious, Leo walked closer to the rock. "What is this?" he wondered. Suddenly, the rock spoke! "I am a magic rock. I can help you make things!" Leo was amazed. "Really? What can you help me make?" The rock chuckled. "You need to tell me what you want!"

Thinking hard, Leo decided he wanted a big chair. "I want a comfy chair to rest on," he said. The rock glowed brightly. "Okay! Just wait!" With a rumble and a shake, the ground moved. In a flash, a giant chair appeared, made of branches and leaves.

"Wow!" Leo exclaimed, sitting down. "This is great!" Feeling happy, he decided to ask for more. "Can you make me a table, too?" The rock nodded and glowed again. A beautiful table with fruits appeared beside the chair. "This is amazing!" Leo cheered.

Next, he thought of his friends. "I want to invite my friends to share this!" The rock smiled. "You can have a feast!" With a bright flash, delicious food appeared on the table. Leo was excited. He called out for his friends, inviting them all to join him.

Soon, animals from all over the forest came. There were rabbits, birds, and even deer. They sat around the table, enjoying the food. "This is the best day ever!" Leo shouted. Everyone laughed and agreed.

After the feast, Leo looked at the magic rock. "Thank you! You made my day special." The rock smiled. "Just remember, sharing is the best magic of all!" Leo nodded, feeling warm inside. He promised to share more with his friends.

From that day on, Leo often visited the rock, creating fun things. Each visit brought new joy to the forest. They all learned that friendship and sharing were the greatest gifts.

Set
A set is an idea from mathematics. A set has members (also called elements). A set is defined by its members, so any two sets with the same members are the same (e.g., if set and set have the same members, then ).

A set cannot have the same member more than once. Membership is the only thing that matters. For example, there is no order or other difference among the members. Anything can be a member of a set, including sets themselves (though if a set is a member of itself, paradoxes such as Russell's paradox can happen).

What to do with sets

Imagine the set is a bag.

Element of
Various things can be put into a bag. Later on, a good question would be if a certain thing is in the bag. Mathematicians call this element of. Something is an element of a set, if that thing can be found in the respective bag. The symbol used for this is :

,

which means that is in the bag or is an element of .

Unlike a bag, a set can contain at most one item of a given type. So for a set of fruits, it would make no difference if there is one orange, or if there are 10 oranges.

Empty set
Like a bag, a set can also be empty. The empty set is like an empty bag: it has nothing in it. The "empty set" is also called the null set and is represented by the symbol .

Universe
If we consider, say, some sets of American cars, e.g. a set of all Fords and a set of all Dodges, we may also wish to consider the whole set of American cars. In this case, the set of all American cars would be called a universe.

In other words, a universe is a collection of all the elements one wishes to consider in a given problem. The universe is usually named .

Comparing sets
Two sets can be compared. This is like looking into two different bags. If they contain the same things, they are equal. No matter, in which order these things are.

For example, if and , the sets are the same.

Cardinality of a set
When mathematicians talk about a set, they sometimes want to know how big a set is (or what is the cardinality of the set). They do this by counting how many elements are in the set (how many items are in the bag). For finite sets the cardinality is a simple number. The empty set has a cardinality of 0. The set has a cardinality of 2.

Two sets have the same cardinality if we can pair up their elements - if we can join two elements, one from each set. The set and the set have the same cardinality. E.g., we could pair apple with sun, and orange with moon. The order does not matter. It is possible to pair all the elements, and none is left out. But the set and the set have different cardinality.
If we try to pair them up, we always leave out one animal.

Infinite cardinality
At times cardinality is not a number. Sometimes a set has infinite cardinality. The set of all integers is a set with infinite cardinality. Some sets with infinite cardinality are bigger (have a bigger cardinality) than others. There are more real numbers than there are natural numbers, for example, which means we cannot pair up the set of integers and the set of real numbers, even if we worked forever.

Homelessness
In the 1980s, in the United States, some new laws were made for the homeless as a result of the work of Congressman Stewart B. McKinney. In 1987, the McKinney-Vento Homeless Assistance Act was enacted. Several organisations in some cities, such as New York and Boston, tried to help the growing number of homeless people in a new way.

According to a 60 Minutes program, aired in December 2017, California is home to a quarter of American homeless people.

Chapter 1: Meal Prep and Cooking Essentials

Hey there! Welcome to our chapter all about meal prep and cooking essentials. You might be thinking, "Why do I need to know about meal prep and cooking? I'm just a middle schooler!" Well, believe it or not, knowing how to cook and prepare meals can be incredibly useful, no matter what age you are. It can save you money, keep you healthy, and even impress your friends and family! So let's get started.

First things first - what exactly is meal prep? Meal prep simply means preparing your meals ahead of time, usually for several days at once. This can involve chopping vegetables, cooking grains, or even making entire meals and then storing them in containers until you're ready to eat. By doing this, you can save yourself time during the week and ensure that you always have something delicious and nutritious to eat.

Now, let's talk about why meal prep is especially important for young adults like you. When you're in middle school, you probably don't have as many responsibilities as older teens or college students. But trust us, before you know it, you'll be busy with homework, extracurricular activities, and social events. And if you don't plan ahead by prepping your meals, you might find yourself resorting to unhealthy convenience foods or skipping meals altogether. Neither of those options are good for your body or your mind!

So how can you start meal prepping? First, think about what types of meals you enjoy and what ingredients you like. Then, try to choose recipes that use similar ingredients, so you can buy them in bulk and save money. For example, if you love chicken stir fry and chicken Caesar salads, you could buy a big pack of chicken breasts and divide them into smaller portions for each recipe.

Next, set aside some time to do your food shopping and meal prep. On the weekend, for instance, you could visit the grocery store and stock up on everything you need for the week. Then, carve out a couple hours one day to chop veggies, cook grains, and portion out your meals into containers. Trust us, having a fridge full of ready-to-eat meals will make your life so much easier during the week.

Of course, meal prep isn't the only way to ensure that you're eating well. Knowing how to cook basic meals is also crucial. Don't worry - we're not expecting you to become a gourmet chef overnight! Even simple dishes like scrambled eggs, pasta with tomato sauce, or roasted vegetables can provide you with the nutrients you need to stay focused and energized throughout the day.

To get started with cooking, here are a few tips:

* Read the recipe carefully before you begin, so you know what steps to follow and what tools and ingredients you'll need.
* Make sure to wash your hands thoroughly before handling any food.
* If you're using sharp knives or other potentially dangerous kitchen tools, ask an adult for help.
* Taste your food frequently while you're cooking, so you can adjust the seasonings and make sure everything is cooked properly.
* Have fun! Cooking can be a creative and rewarding activity, so don't stress too much if things don't turn out perfectly the first time around.

Welcome to an exciting journey into the world of media studies! Today we're going to talk about something called "audience research," which might sound a bit boring at first, but trust me, it's pretty cool once you understand what it means.

Imagine that you are designing a brand new app for your phone - maybe one that helps people save energy at home and reduces their carbon footprint (which is just a fancy way of saying how much they contribute to climate change). Now, before you start creating this amazing app, don't you want to know who will be using it? What kind of phones do they have? How old are they? Are they boys or girls? Or both? Where do they live? And most importantly, what do they like?

This is where audience research comes in handy! Audience research is when you try to find out everything you can about the people who will be using your app so that you can create something truly awesome just for them. By understanding your audience, you can design an interface that speaks their language, solves their problems, and keeps them engaged.

Let's break down our example with the eco-friendly app:

* First, let's think about age. If our audience is made up mostly of kids around your age, then we need to make sure the app looks fun and colorful, right? Maybe there could even be some games inside that teach users about saving energy while keeping things entertaining! On the other hand, if our audience consists mainly of adults, we would probably go for a more serious look with easy-to-understand information about reducing energy consumption.
* Next, let's consider location. If most of our users live in big cities, perhaps they already know lots of ways to save energy because city dwellers often learn how to conserve resources due to limited supplies. But if many of our users come from rural areas, they may appreciate simple tips on conserving energy since access to certain utilities might be less efficient than urban regions.
* Finally, let's discuss interests. Let's say we discover through our research that our target audience loves watching videos online. Great! We can add video tutorials showing different ways to save energy at home. By catering to their preferences, we increase the chances of having a successful app.

Now imagine trying to guess all these things without doing any audience research. You might end up making assumptions based on stereotypes or personal biases, resulting in an unappealing product no one wants to use. That's why knowing your audience matters!

In summary, conducting audience research allows designers like YOU to:

1. Create better products tailored specifically for YOUR USERS.
2. Make informed decisions regarding visual elements, features, and functions.
3. Increase user satisfaction and engagement by addressing their needs and desires.

So next time you dream up an idea for a fantastic new app, remember to stop and think about WHOM exactly you're building it for. Happy designing!

Welcome to Design Theory! Have you ever thought about all the different ways you can arrange things? Maybe you've wondered how many unique greeting cards you could create if you had a limited set of stickers, or perhaps you've pondered the number of possible combinations when choosing your favorite candies from a bag. If so, then you're already exploring some fundamental concepts in combinatorics - specifically, design theory!

**What is Design Theory?**

In simple terms, design theory deals with arranging items (which we call 'elements') into groups called 'blocks'. Each block must contain a specific number of elements, which we refer to as the 'block size'. Additionally, no element can appear more than once within any given block. Sounds easy enough, right? Let's dive deeper!

**Let's Make Some Blocks!**

Imagine you have a box containing four different colored balls - red, blue, green, and yellow. Our goal now is to form blocks according to certain rules. For instance, one rule might require creating blocks where each contains exactly two balls. Following these guidelines, here are a few possibilities:

1. Red & Blue
2. Green & Yellow
3. Red & Green
4. Red & Yellow
5. Blue & Green
6. Blue & Yellow

Did you notice something interesting about those blocks? There isn't a single block that has both the same color *and* a duplicate color! That means every time we picked another ball, it was always a new color. This concept is known as 'balance', and it plays a crucial role in design theory.

**Balancedness and Its Importance**

A balanced arrangement ensures fairness among all the elements involved. To understand balance better, let's add another constraint to our previous example. Suppose we want to divide these four balls equally between two children such that each child receives two differently colored balls. Now, look at these arrangements:

1. Child A: {Red, Blue} | Child B: {Green, Yellow}
2. Child A: {Red, Green} | Child B: {Blue, Yellow}
3. Child A: {Red, Yellow} | Child B: {Blue, Green}

These arrangements show perfect balance because neither child prefers one assortment over another. Both kids receive equal shares of colors and variety. Balancing is essential while designing various systems like communication networks, error detection codes, and statistical sampling methods.

**Block Size Matters**

The size of blocks significantly impacts the total number of blocks created. Consider having eight distinct balls instead of just four. What would happen if we still wanted to maintain blocks of size two? You guessed it - there'd be twice as many blocks as before! Specifically, there would be 28 blocks in total. Changing the block size also alters the count of potential blocks. So, selecting the appropriate block size is vital depending upon the situation.

**Conclusion**

Now that we've explored design theory together, remember that math doesn't need to be abstract; sometimes, it can help us appreciate real-world scenarios creatively. By learning about balancing and block sizes through design theory, you've gained valuable insights into problem-solving techniques applicable elsewhere in life too. Keep playing around with designs using everyday objects, and soon enough, you'll become an expert designer yourself!

Welcome to the fascinating world of Fuzzy Logic! You might be wondering, what in the world is Fuzzy Logic? Well, let's dive into this interesting concept together!

Imagine you're asked if you want to go to an amusement park next week. But, you're not sure yet if you have a free day or not. So, instead of answering 'yes' or 'no,' you might say something like, 'maybe.' That's how humans handle uncertainty sometimes, right? We don't always have clear answers. Now, guess what? Computers can learn to do this too with Fuzzy Logic!

Fuzzy Logic is a type of computing that allows computers to make decisions when they encounter uncertain or imprecise information. Unlike traditional computing which deals only with true or false facts (1s and 0s), Fuzzy Logic enables computers to understand concepts such as 'sort of', 'partially', or 'possibly'. Let's explore why this is so cool!

Think about a room temperature setting on a thermostat. Traditional computing would set a specific temperature, like exactly 72 degrees Fahrenheit. However, using Fuzzy Logic, the thermostat could consider factors like 'a little cold', 'quite warm', or 'comfortable' - making the system more human-like and adaptive.

Now, imagine you're controlling a robot vacuum cleaner. Using Fuzzy Logic, the vacuum cleaner wouldn't just bump around randomly; it would analyze its environment and use terms like 'lightly cluttered' or 'heavily carpeted' to decide how best to clean each area. How amazing is that?

Here's another fun example. Imagine having a toy car that uses Fuzzy Logic. When driving towards a wall, a regular computer program might crash into it since it doesn't understand words like 'slow down' or 'stop'. With Fuzzy Logic, however, the toy car would recognize these commands and slow down before reaching the wall - much safer and smarter!

As you can see, Fuzzy Logic makes computers think and respond more like us, handling ambiguity and adapting to different circumstances. And who knows, maybe one day your phone, tablet, or even video games will use Fuzzy Logic to better understand YOU! Wouldn't that be incredible?

So now you know all about Fuzzy Logic! Remember, life isn't always black and white, and neither is computing. Sometimes, it pays off to be a little 'fuzzy'. Happy exploring!

Chapter 10: Discovering Curling - A Cool Winter Sport!

Have you ever tried curling? No, we're not talking about your hair! Curling is a fascinating sport played on ice. You might have seen it during the Winter Olympics and wondered what those athletes were doing sliding stones on ice while their teammates swept in front of them. Well, let's dive into this cool world together!

Curling Basics
------------------

Imagine playing a game that combines elements of shuffleboard and bowling on ice. That's curling for you! Two teams of four players each take turns sliding heavy granite stones (also called rocks) towards a circular target area called the house. Each team has eight stones, and the goal is to place more stones closer to the center of the house than your opponent.

Here's where things get interesting - two members of each team use brooms to sweep the ice in front of the stone as it slides. Why would they do that? Great question! By sweeping, they can control how much the stone curves (this natural curve is known as the stone's 'curl') and how fast it moves. This allows for some amazing strategies!

Getting Started with Curling Techniques
-----------------------------------------------

Holding the Stone

First, you need to know how to hold the stone properly. Stand behind the hack (a rubberized footrest), grip the handle firmly with both hands, keeping your knees slightly bent. Now, push off using your back leg and slide forward while releasing the stone when your arm is fully extended. Just like throwing a ball!

Guiding the Stone

Now comes the fun part - guiding the stone toward the house! After releasing the stone, stay low and maintain balance. If you want the stone to go straight, don't sweep at all. But if you wish to give it a little curl, start sweeping gently as soon as the stone starts moving. Communication is key between teammates because sweepers decide whether or not to sweep based on the skip's instructions (the person who calls the shots).

Scoring Points

Points are scored based on which team's stones are closest to the center of the house after each round (called ends - just like innings in baseball). Only one team scores per end, receiving one point for each stone nearer to the center compared to the opposing team's best stone.

Why Play Curling in Winter?
-----------------------------

Winter provides perfect conditions for curling with its smooth and well-prepared ice surfaces. Additionally, many schools offer curling programs during winter months due to indoor rink availability. Plus, isn't there something magical about participating in a sport that embraces the chilliness of winter rather than hiding away from it?

Remember, practice makes perfect. Keep trying, and soon enough, you could become the next curling champion! Who knows, maybe someday we'll see you competing in the Winter Olympics. Wouldn't that be awesome?

Alice: Hi Bob! I heard you learned about something called Functional Analytic Psychotherapy, or FAP, in psychology class today. Can you tell me what that is?

Bob: Sure, Alice! It's a type of therapy that helps people understand their emotions and behaviors better by looking at the causes and effects of those emotions and actions. For example, if someone gets really nervous when they speak in public, FAP would help them figure out why they feel that way and then come up with ways to manage that anxiety.

Alice: Oh, I see. That sounds like it could be helpful. So, let's say my friend Sarah is feeling sad and doesn't know why. Could FAP help her?

Bob: Yes, definitely! A therapist using FAP might ask Sarah questions about what she was doing before she started feeling sad. Maybe Sarah noticed that she felt sad after talking to a certain person or being in a particular place. By identifying those triggers, Sarah can start to understand why she feels sad and find ways to cope with those feelings.

Alice: Got it. And what about behavior? How does FAP address that?

Bob: Well, FAP looks at how our behaviors affect others around us. For instance, if someone always interrupts others while they're speaking, FAP would encourage that person to notice how their behavior affects the people they're talking to. Then, they could work on finding more respectful ways to communicate.

Alice: Hmm, I think I get it now. Let me try an example. If I'm playing with my little brother Tommy, but he keeps taking my toys without asking, what should I do according to FAP?

Bob: Great question, Alice! Using FAP, you could first acknowledge how his behavior makes you feel - maybe annoyed or frustrated. Then, you could express those feelings to him in a calm and constructive way. You might say something like, "Tommy, I don't like it when you take my toys without asking. Please ask me next time, so we can share nicely."

Alice: Ah, I see. And if I keep practicing that, eventually, he will learn to ask me before taking my toys.

Bob: Exactly! And that's just one example of how FAP can help improve communication and emotional awareness in everyday life.

Alice: Thanks for explaining it to me, Bob! I think I have a better understanding of FAP now.

Giorgio Napolitano
Giorgio Napolitano (29 June 1925 - 22 September 2023) was an Italian politician who was the 11th President of Italy from 2006 to 2015. He was born in Naples, Italy.

He was elected on May 10, 2006 on the fourth ballot, with 543 votes out of 1009 (the required number was 505), but he took office as president only on May 15, 2006, after Carlo Azeglio Ciampi's time was finished.

He was voted mostly by the left-wing coalition led by Prime Minister Romano Prodi, head of the Italian Government. Napolitano was preceded at his job by Carlo Azeglio Ciampi. He was nicknamed King George by his critics.

Napolitano resigned as President of Italy on January 14, 2015 due to his old age.

Napolitano was hospitalized in Rome on 29 June 2023, shortly after his 98th birthday. He died on 22 September 2023 at the age of 98.

Thai language
The Thai language is the national and official language of Thailand. It is the first language of the Thai people, Thailand's main ethnic group. Thai is closely related to the Lao language. In fact, some dialects of Thai and Lao are mutually intelligible, meaning that speakers of one language can talk with and understand speakers of the other language without knowing the other's language.

Sounds
Thai is a tone language, like Chinese.

Bad Aibling
Bad Aibling (Central Bavarian: Bod Oabling or Oawin) is a town in Bavaria (Germany). It is a former district seat. It is on the river Mangfall about 35 miles southeast of Munich. Bad Aibling is a health resort (peat pulp bath and mineral water).

History

In 804, Bad Aibling was mentioned for the first time. After the second World War Bad Aibling has evolved to a major centre for intelligence organizations and secret services. In 2004 the US American Bad Aibling Echelon station closed after decades of operation. In 2016, ten people were killed in a train crash.

Number of people
In the town live about 18,000 people. It is 498 meters above sea level and covers an area of 41.55 km2.

Welcome to our latest chapter all about Securities Regulation! This might sound like a complicated grown-up concept, but we're going to break it down into bite-sized pieces that are easy peasy even for middle schoolers like you! So let's dive right in and learn how laws help keep businesses fair and honest when they sell stocks and bonds (special kinds of money investments).

Imagine you have some extra cash saved up, and your favorite local store wants to expand their business. They offer you something called a "stock," which means you can buy a tiny piece of ownership in their company! Now suppose other people also think this sounds cool and start buying these stocks too. Suddenly, lots of different folks own bits and pieces of that one store - but what if things go wrong? What happens if the new shop doesn't do so well, or worse yet, the owners decide to run away with everyone's money?! Yikes! That wouldn't be good for anyone involved.

This is where securities regulation comes in! It's kind of like having rules for playing a game; it keeps everything organized and makes sure no one cheats. Governments create special sets of laws to protect people who invest in companies through stocks, bonds, or similar types of deals. These regulations require businesses to share important information openly and honestly with investors. By doing this, everyone knows exactly what they're getting themselves into before investing any hard-earned savings.

Now, sometimes there are disagreements over just *how* strict those rules need to be. Our story starts with a thing called the "Nasdaq 'comply or disclose' board diversity rule." Without getting too bogged down in details, this rule encourages companies listed on the Nasdaq stock exchange to increase diversity among their leaders. Companies could either follow the rule ("comply") or explain why they didn't meet it ("disclose"). A group of people sued because they thought this rule went against another law. But luckily, a court said the Nasdaq rule was okay!

However, here's where things get interesting. When courts first look at cases like this, they usually only use small groups of judges to save time. Sometimes, though, someone might ask for a second chance with more judges involved. And guess what? That's exactly what happened here! Even better, now YOU get to come along for the ride as we see how things unfold next. Remember, understanding laws helps us build better communities together, and knowing about securities regulation is just one way we can grow smarter every day!

He carved a figure of himself, but not just any figure. This one showed his pain, his fears, and his dreams. With each cut, he poured his heart into the wood. It was hard work, and tears fell like rain as he carved. But as he worked, he felt lighter, as if the wood absorbed his sorrow.

The next day, he took the figure to the town square. People gathered, curious to see what he had created. As he spoke about his work, he felt the fear fade. The crowd listened with open hearts. They saw not just the figure, but also the man behind it.

Each person felt a piece of their own story in his art. They saw their pain, their hopes, and their dreams. The man understood that everyone carries a weight. He felt a connection, a bond formed through shared feelings. Together, they learned that acceptance could heal.

From that day on, the man carved not just wood, but stories. He became known for his heartfelt art, and he found joy in sharing. He realized that showing his truth brought light to others. The once empty heart was now full, a vessel of love and understanding.

Footwear
Footwear is an item of clothing made by humans that covers and protects the foot, including the soles of the feet. Footwear allows people to walk on rough surfaces such as gravel roads without hurting their feet. Some types of footwear such as boots help to keep people's feet dry, or help to keep people's feet warm in cold weather.

Types of Footwear

Shoes are a type of footwear that protects the foot and the soles of the feet. Shoes are made of many different types of materials, such as leather, fabric, and plastic. There are several types of shoes:
Athletic shoes (also called "running shoes") are made of fabric, rubber, and plastic. They are made for people to wear while they are doing sports or recreational activities. Athletic shoes like spikes, give grip to sprinting on the athletic track.
Dress shoes are made for people to wear when they are wearing formal clothes such as a suit and tie or a tuxedo. Dress shoes are normally made from dark-colored leather that is shined using shoe polish. People working in professions such as business, law, and politics wear dress shoes. People working in restaurants or retail stores may also wear dress shoes.
Work shoes are designed for people who work in construction or factory jobs. Work shoes often have a steel toe cover to protect the person's toes. Work shoes are usually made of strong leather, to protect the person's foot from sharp objects or dangerous chemicals.

Sandals are a type of footwear that consists of a covering for the sole of the feet and straps or ties which hold the sandal onto the foot. Sandals are worn in warm countries, such as the Philippines and Cuba. Sandals are also worn indoors in some places, such as in saunas.

Boots are a type of footwear that protects the foot and ankle. Boots are higher and larger than shoes and sandals. Some boots are high enough to protect the calves (lower part of the leg) as well.

Rain boots (or rubber boots) are made from rubber or plastic. Rain boots protect a person's feet from water and rain. People who work on fishing boats and farmers wear rubber boots to keep their feet dry. People who work in chemical factories wear rubber boots to protect their feet from dangerous chemicals.

Winter boots are boots that keep a person's feet warm in cold weather. People in cold countries such as Canada and Sweden wear winter boots during the cold season. Winter boots can be made from many different materials, such as leather, fabric, or plastic. Winter boots are insulated with wool or fur to keep the feet warm. Most winter boots also keep people's feet dry.

Work boots (or "construction boots") are designed for people who work in construction or factory jobs. Work boots often have a steel toe cover to protect the person's toes. Work boots are usually made of strong leather, to protect the person's foot from sharp objects or dangerous chemicals. Some work boots have a flat piece of steel in the sole to protect the foot from sharp nails. Many countries require construction workers to wear work boots when they are on a construction site.

MTR
The works were completed in stages. The Tung Chung Line trains have been diverted to the new track since mid May 2003, whereas the Mei Foo station interchange subway and the Nam Cheong station were opened at the same time the West Rail Line opened for public use in December 2003. The Kowloon Southern Link extension from Nam Cheong Station to East Tsim Sha Tsui Station was opened on 16 August 2009, with West Rail Line trains now terminating at Hung Hom Station, interchange station for East Rail Line.

Interchange stations

The interchange between the Tsuen Wan Line and the Kwun Tong Line, the Island Line and the Tseung Kwan O Line, as well as that between the Kwun Tong Line and the Tseung Kwan O Line, are two stations long, allowing cross-platform interchange wherein a passenger leaves a train on one side of the platform and boards trains on the other side of the platform for another line. For example, when passengers are travelling on the Kwun Tong Line towards Tiu Keng Leng, getting off at Yau Tong would allow them to switch trains across the platform for the Tseung Kwan O Line towards North Point. Whereas, staying on the train and reaching Tiu Keng Leng would allow them to board the Tseung Kwan O Line trains towards Po Lam/LOHAS Park. This design makes interchanging more convenient and passengers do not have the need to change to different levels. However this interchange arrangement is not available for all transferring passengers at Kowloon Tong, Central, Hong Kong, Nam Cheong (Except transfer between Tuen Mun and Hong Kong bound trains), Mei Foo, Tai Wai Station (Except alighting from Ma On Shan Line to change southbound trains for East Rail Line) and Sunny Bay (Except alighting from Tung Chung bound trains to Disneyland Resort Line) stations, mainly because this service is available only when there are two continuous stations shared as interchange stations by two lines.

Two major works were undertaken to facilitate interchange between Kwun Tong Line and East Rail Line. The modification of Kowloon Tong Station started in June 2001. A new pedestrian link to Kowloon Tong Station southern concourse and a new entrance (Exit D) were opened on 15 April 2004 to cope with the increase in interchange passenger flow. Modification to Tsim Sha Tsui Station involved upgrading station facilities and concourse layout to facilitate access from the East Tsim Sha Tsui Station via its pedestrian links. New entrances to the subway links were opened on 19 September 2004 (Exit G) and 30 March 2005 (Exit F), with the whole scheme completed in May 2005.

Ma On Shan Line

The Ma On Shan Line was constructed by the KCR to serve Ma On Shan and City One residential areas and operation of the line was outsourced to the MTR. The system mostly runs on a viaduct between the middle of roads with stations, stopping right next to major buildings. The only time the trains don't run on viaducts is when the railway meets the route 2 highway, where it runs in the middle and then raises back to a viaduct. The railway is slightly different from all other Hong Kong railways because the trains run on the right, not the left; this is so that passengers can easily interchange from the Ma On Shan line to the East Rail Line towards Hong Hum. The majority of passengers using the line get off the train at Tai Wai to interchange to the East Rail Line, using the line as a feeder route.

Integration may be any of the following:

Integration, in the most general sense, may be any bringing together and uniting of things: the integration of two or more economies, cultures, religions (usually called syncretism), etc.
Integration, in mathematics, a concept of calculus, is the act of finding integrals
Indefinite integration, in mathematics, refers to antidifferentiation
Racial integration, refers to social and cultural behavior
Economic integration
Regional integration
Horizontal integration and vertical integration, in microeconomics and strategic management, refer to a style of ownership and control
Integration clause, in a contract, a term used to declare the contract the final and complete understanding of the parties
In computer science
Digital integration, in computer science, allows data from one device or software to be read or manipulated by another, resulting in ease of use
Enterprise application integration, as the use of software and computer systems to bring together a set of enterprise computer applications
Systems Integration, refers to the discipline of designing systems by means of glueing together otherwise separate parts. Usually associated to the construction of complex systems.

**Course Unit: Syntax and Word Order**

Welcome to this exciting course unit where we will explore the fascinating world of syntax and word order! You might be wondering what those words even mean. Don't worry; we'll break it down together step-by-step.

Imagine you want to tell your friend about the funny squirrel you saw at the park yesterday. There are many ways to say it, but one possible sentence could be: "Yesterday, I saw a funny squirrel at the park." To create this sentence, you used a specific arrangement of words - *syntax* - following certain rules called *word order*. Let's dive deeper into each concept!

**What is Syntax?**

Have you ever heard someone speak in a language you don't understand and noticed they seemed to follow some sort of pattern when putting their words together? That's because every language has its own set of syntactical rules - guidelines for arranging words within sentences. These arrangements help us communicate our thoughts more clearly and effectively. For example, try saying "Squirrel funny at the park seen I." It doesn't flow quite right, does it? That's because English speakers typically use Subject + Verb + Object order (SVO), which makes sense to people who speak the same language.

**Let's Play with Word Order!**

Now let's experiment with different word orders while describing our encounter with the silly squirrel. We can keep the basic structure (Subject + Verb + Adverb + Direct Object) but mix things up a bit:

1. Original: Yesterday, I saw a funny squirrel at the park.
2. Reversed: A funny squirrel, I saw at the park yesterday.
3. Question form: Did I see a funny squirrel at the park yesterday?
4. Shortened: I spotted a hilarious squirrel at the park.

Even though we changed the order, all four sentences convey the same message thanks to proper syntax!

**Practice Time!**

Time to practice creating your own sentences using various word orders. Use the template below:

[Subj.] _______ [Verb] __________ [Adv./Prep.] _________ [Obj.] ________

Example:
[Subj.] My brother [Verb] fed [Adv.] excitedly [Prep.] during [Obj.] breakfast.

Your turn! Fill in the blanks with appropriate words:

1. [Subj.] The little girl [Verb] sang [Adv.] softly [Prep.] under [Obj.] her breath.
2. [Subj.] They [Verb] watched [Adv.] eagerly [Prep.] throughout [Obj.] the movie night.
3. [Subj.] She [Verb] cooked [Adv.] hurriedly [Prep.] before [Obj.] dinner guests arrived.

Remember, there's no single correct answer here. Explore different possibilities and have fun playing around with syntax and word order!

The subject or question of a debate

Senate
In a modern democracy, a senate is a group of people who are part of a legislature. A legislature passes or changes laws for their country, state, or other area. Members of a senate are called senators. Some legislatures are bicameral, meaning they have two groups of people (working in separate places) called houses. A senate can be called a House of Senators.

The senate of some such legislatures is weaker than the other house. The other house is called a House of Representatives, House of Commons, or Assembly. In bicameral legislatures, both houses must pass the same bill to make it a law. Modern democratic systems having legislatures with senates include the United States of America (U. S.), Canada, Australia and many states in the United States.

The first ever senate was the Roman Senate. The name comes from their word for "elder".

Senate is also the name of the ruling body of some universities.

Senate chambers
Sometimes, the senators are split into different groups, who then have different responsibilities. These groups meet in different rooms; each group is called a chamber.

Lesson Objective: Students will be able to calculate elapsed time using addition and subtraction of hours and minutes.

Materials Needed: Whiteboard and markers, worksheets with elapsed time problems, stopwatch (optional)

Introduction:
Today we'll be learning about elapsed time, which means finding out how much time has passed between two given times. This skill is important because it allows us to compare different lengths of time and figure out when one event happened relative to another. We've already learned how to tell time on a clock, so now we'll build upon that knowledge by adding and subtracting hours and minutes to find elapsed time.

Example 1:
Let's start with a simple example. Imagine you started playing a video game at 4:05 PM and stopped playing at 6:27 PM. How long did you play the game? To solve this problem, we need to find the difference between these two times.

First, let's look at the hours. From 4:05 PM to 6:00 PM, there are 2 hours. But we haven't reached 6:27 PM yet, so we still need to add those extra 22 minutes. Since there are 60 minutes in an hour, we can convert 22 minutes into decimal form by dividing it by 60. So, 22 minutes is equal to 0.3667 hours. Adding this to our previous result gives us a total of 2 + 0.3667 = 2.3667 hours.

Therefore, you played the game for approximately 2 hours and 22 minutes.

Note: It might be easier to leave the answer as 2.3667 hours instead of converting back to minutes, but students should also know how to do this conversion. To convert from hours to minutes, multiply the decimal part of the hours by 60. In this case, 0.3667 x 60 = 22 minutes. Therefore, the final answer would be 2 hours and 22 minutes.

Example 2:
Now let's try a slightly more complicated example. Suppose you went to bed at 9:18 PM and woke up at 6:43 AM. How many hours did you sleep?

In this case, we need to account for the fact that we crossed over midnight during the night. First, let's calculate the time spent after midnight until 6:43 AM. There are 6 hours between 12:00 AM and 6:00 AM, plus the additional 43 minutes. Converting 43 minutes to hours gives us 0.7167 hours. Adding this to our previous result gives us a total of 6 + 0.7167 = 6.7167 hours.

However, we didn't go straight to bed after 12:00 AM; we actually went to bed at 9:18 PM. Subtracting this time from 12:00 AM gives us 12:00 - 9:18 = 2 hours and 42 minutes, or 2.7 hours in decimal form.

Adding both results together gives us a total of 6.7167 + 2.7 = 9.4167 hours.

Therefore, you slept for approximately 9 hours and 25 minutes (after converting 0.4167 hours to minutes).

Conclusion:
Calculating elapsed time may seem difficult at first, but with practice, you'll get better at it! Remember to break down each problem into smaller parts and consider whether any adjustments need to be made due to crossing over midnight. Chapter Title: Understanding Truth-Conditional Semantics: What Makes a Statement True or False?

Have you ever played the game "Telephone" with your friends? You whisper a message into one person's ear, they pass it along to another, and so on. By the time the last person hears the message, it has changed quite a bit! This happens because words can have different meanings based on how we understand them. Today, let's dive into truth-conditional semantics - a way philosophers think about what makes statements true or false. It will help us figure out if those Telephone messages are actually telling the truth!

Section I: Words, Meanings, and Statements

Let's start with some basics. Think of a word, any word! Got it? Now imagine that same word in a sentence, like "apple." See how just one little word can change depending on where and how we use it? We need sentences to express thoughts and share information. When we put words together, creating sentences, we create statements.

Now, remember our game of Telephone? Sometimes when people hear something differently than what was originally said, it leads to confusion and misunderstandings. That's why defining our terms clearly matters. To know whether a statement is true or false, we must first agree upon what each term means within the context of that statement.

Section II: Enter Truth-Conditional Semantics

Imagine saying this statement aloud: "The cat is on the mat." If someone else looks around and sees a cat sitting comfortably on a mat, then they would likely say that your statement is true. But if there isn't a cat in sight, they might call it false. Easy enough, right? So, how do philosophers analyze these types of simple statements more systematically? They turn to truth-conditional semantics!

This fancy name simply refers to studying the conditions under which a statement would be considered true or false. For example, going back to our original statement - "The cat is on the mat" - we now see that determining its truth depends on specific factors (or 'conditions'): finding a cat AND seeing it resting on a mat. Both elements need to align for the statement to hold up as being true.

Section III: Applying Truth-Conditional Semantics

To apply truth-conditional semantics effectively, keep asking yourself questions like:

* What does each word really mean here?
* Are all necessary components included in my statement?
* Can I verify these parts easily through observation or evidence?

By doing so, you ensure clarity and accuracy while communicating. Let's try applying this method to other statements:

1. *Statement*: My best friend moved to Mars.
+ Is this statement true or false? Well, unless your friend works at NASA or SpaceX, chances are they haven't colonized Mars yet! So, generally speaking, this statement would be deemed false due to current human space travel limitations.
2. *Statement*: Dogs are mammals.
+ Time for some science class flashbacks! Since dogs meet all criteria for mammal classification (e.g., having fur, giving live birth), this statement checks out as true.

In conclusion, understanding truth-conditional semantics helps clarify communication, reduce misunderstandings, and encourage critical thinking. Just like playing Telephone taught us the importance of clear messaging, diving into truth-conditional semantics enables us to examine statements closely, ensuring their veracity before accepting them as factual. Happy analyzing!

Starting Your Own Online Business: An Introduction to Dropshipping

Have you ever thought about starting your own business? Maybe you have a great idea for a product, or maybe you just like the idea of being your own boss. Whatever your reasons, starting a business can be a big challenge. But there's one way to do it that might make things a little easier: dropshipping.

Dropshipping is a type of online business where you sell products through your own website or marketplace (like eBay), but you don't actually keep any inventory on hand. Instead, when someone places an order with you, the supplier ships the product directly to the customer. This means you don't have to spend money upfront to buy products, which can be a huge help when you're just starting out.

So why would anyone want to use dropshipping? Well, here are a few good reasons:

1. **Low startup costs:** Since you don't need to buy any inventory upfront, you can get started with a much smaller investment than if you were opening a traditional brick-and-mortar store. All you really need is a computer and internet connection!
2. **Easy to scale:** Because you don't have to worry about managing inventory or shipping yourself, it's relatively easy to add new products to your store as you grow. You can even work with multiple suppliers at once, giving you access to a wider range of products.
3. **Flexibility:** With dropshipping, you can run your business from anywhere as long as you have an internet connection. That makes it a great option for busy students like you!

Of course, like any business venture, there are also some challenges to consider. For example, since you never see or handle the products you're selling, it can be harder to ensure they're high quality. And because there are so many other people doing dropshipping these days, competition can be fierce.

But despite those challenges, dropshipping can still be a great way to start your own online business. Just remember that like anything else, it takes hard work, dedication, and a solid plan to make it successful. Good luck!

Mall
A mall or shopping center is a large building that is full of many smaller shops and stores. It is different from earlier markets or bazaars because most of the shops are not little booths or stalls in one big open area. Each store has its own space with walls. Most of their entrances face a central walking area inside the building.

People visit the stores in the mall to shop. Most malls have parking lots (places to park cars). Most malls also have roofs so people can shop inside. Most malls have a food court where people buy food. Some malls have movie theatres.

Name
"Mall" is the most common name for these buildings in America, and "shopping center" is the most common name for them in the United Kingdom. The name "shopping center" is also sometimes used in America. Malls are also sometimes called plazas.

The Mall of America in Bloomington, Minnesota is one of the largest malls in the world.

Library of Congress
The Library of Congress is the de facto national library of the United States and the research arm of the United States Congress.

The head of the Library is the Librarian of Congress Carla Hayden.

Roles
The primary function of the Library of Congress is to serve the Congress. The Library welcomes public use of its general reference facilities and endeavors to offer the widest possible use of its collections consistent with their preservation and with its obligation to serve the Congress and other government agencies.The Library of Congress is the largest library in the world, with millions of books, recordings, photographs, newspapers, maps and manuscripts in its collections. The Library is the main research arm of the U.S. Congress and the home of the U.S. Copyright Office.Libraries are important cornerstones of a healthy community. ... College students often use the library when they are home for the weekend or for holidays. And the reference resources in public libraries are usually unavailable elsewhere in the community. The library is a unique and valuable resource.

Let's explore the question: Does a vertical line represent a function? The answer may surprise you!

To understand this concept, let's first review what we mean by a function. A function is a set of ordered pairs where each element in the domain corresponds to exactly one element in the range. In other words, for every input value, there is only one output value. This can also be represented visually as a graph, where no two points on the same vertical line have the same x-coordinate.

Now, let's consider a vertical line. By definition, all points on a vertical line have the same x-coordinate. But does this violate the definition of a function? After all, it seems like there could be multiple y-values for the same x-value.

The key here lies in the fact that a function must have only one output value for each input value. While it's true that a vertical line has many y-values for the same x-value, it doesn't actually violate the definition of a function because a vertical line never assigns more than one output value to any single input value.

Let's look at an example to illustrate this point. Consider the equation `x = 3`. This represents a vertical line passing through the point (3,0). Every point on this line has an x-coordinate of 3, but they can have any y-coordinate. So, the point (3,7) is on the line just as much as (3,0) or (3,-2). However, even though there are multiple y-values associated with the x-value of 3, there is still only ever one output value assigned to the input value of 3. Therefore, this equation does indeed represent a function.

It's worth noting that some graphing utilities might label a vertical line as not being a function, which can be confusing. This is due to the way these tools interpret functions mathematically - namely, as a special type of relation where every x-value maps to exactly one y-value. Since a vertical line doesn't fit this strict mathematical interpretation, these tools will often flag it as not being a function. However, according to our original definition of a function, a vertical line is indeed a function.

In summary, while it may seem counterintuitive, a vertical line does represent a function. Despite having many y-values for the same x-value, a vertical line never assigns more than one output value to any single input value, making it a valid representation of a function.

1900
1900 (MCM) was an exceptional common year starting on Monday in the Gregorian Calendar and a leap year starting on Saturday in the Julian Calendar. It was the last year of the 19th century. It was also the 900th year of the 2nd millennium, and the first year of the 1900s decade. Also, the Gregorian calendar went up till 1923 and beyond. As of March 1 (O.S. February 17), when the Julian calendar acknowledged a leap day and the Gregorian calendar didn't, the Julian calendar fell one day further behind, bringing the difference to 13 days until February 28 (O.S. February 15), 2100. The year 1900 was also the year of the rat on the Chinese calendar.

MTR
The Airport Express also offer value-added services to travellers on the line. Toilets and check-in facilities are available at every station on the line. A free Airport Express shuttle bus service transports travellers from stations to their respective hotels as well. Flight passengers can even have in-town check-in at the station, which offers a more convenient and time-saving routine.

Fares and tickets
As of January 2005, there are two different fare classes on the MTR: Adult and concessionary. Only children below the age of 12, senior citizens 65 years or older, or full-time Hong Kong students between the ages of 12 and 25 qualify for the concessionary rate. Children below the age of 3 travel free.

Similar to some other metro systems in the world, the fare payable by a passenger depends on the approximate distance travelled. However, taking any particular station as the origin, the other stations fall into fare "zones" depending on the distance from the origin. The fare to all stations in a "zone" is the same and increases with distance, especially if the journey involves a harbour crossing. Adult fares range from HK$3.80 to $26.00. Concessionary fares are usually half the adult fare, and range from HK$2.40 to $13.00. Fares for the Airport Express Line are significantly higher.

The price of using MTR is very low. For example, the price of going from Tsing Yi to Causeway Bay by taxi is around HK$200. Travelling the same distance by MTR costs HK$11.80 for grown up people and HK$5.40 for young and very old people. People can buy a one way ticket or a Octopus card to enter MTR. Octopus card is a contact-less smart card.

Octopus cards
The Octopus card is a rechargeable contactless smart card used in an electronic payment system in Hong Kong. It was launched in September 1997 for use on both the MTR and the KCR and now is the most widely used electronic cash system for transactions in Hong Kong as many retailers are fitted with readers.

The Octopus card uses radio frequency identification (RFID) technology so that users need only hold the card in front of the reader. Physical contact is not required, and the card need not even be taken out because the reader can penetrate through material. This fare collection system has been so popular that many cities such as Singapore, London, Chicago, and Taipei have adopted the idea, launching their own version of smart cards, respectively named EZ-link, Oyster card, and EasyCard.

Except for the Airport Express, MTR fares are slightly lower when using an Octopus card compared to using single journey tickets. For example, the cost of the 3-minute journey from Admiralty to Tsim Sha Tsui across the Victoria Harbour is (as of 2005) HK$7.9 using the Octopus card, compared with HK$9.0 for a single-journey ticket.

Tourist pass
Two types of tourist passes are available: one allows unlimited rides for a single day (at HK$50), while the other allows three days of unlimited rides on the MTR, with a stored value of HK$20, refundable deposit of HK$50 and choice of either a single (HK$220) or return (HK$300) trip on the Airport Express.

Tourists are required to produce proof of tourist status, (e.g. passports or, in the case of Mainland travellers, entry permits) when purchasing the pass, and whenever requested by a ticket inspector during spot-checks.

Other fares
The magnetic fare card system is used for single journey tickets. These tickets are pre-paid for between pre-determined stations, and are good for only one trip. There are no return tickets, except on the Airport Express.

County
During the second half of the 20th century, many people went to the country counties from nearby cities. Because of this, sometimes they put the two together, making a "district" (e.g. Rotorua). Or sometimes they changed the name to "district" (e.g. Waimairi) or "city" (e.g. Manukau).

In 1974 they had a big change; they made the organisation the same all over New Zealand. Today the country has cities and districts, but no counties.

Norway
Norway has 19 Counties (singular fylke, plural fylker, literally "folk"). Until 1972, Bergen was a county, but today it is a municipality in the county of Hordaland. All counties have municipalities (singular kommune, plural kommuner).

Each county has an assembly (fylkesting). Norwegians choose the people in the assembly every 4 years. The counties work with high schools and roads, etc. Some people, and political parties, such as the Conservatives, Hyre, want the end of the counties. Others want to make some of them into larger regions.

Poland
In English we normally call the Polish second-level organisation unit powiat a "county" or "district".

Romania
The smaller units of Romania are called jude (plural: judee). This name comes from jude, a judge of a city. Today Romania has 40 counties and the capital, Bucharest has a separate status.

Serbia
We sometimes call the units of Serbia (okrug) counties, but more often we call them districts.

Sweden
In 1634 the old provinces in Sweden had a new name: counties. Today there are 21 Counties, and in each County there are Municipalities.
The Swedish name is Ln.

United Kingdom
See also List of counties of the United Kingdom

In the United Kingdom there are 92 traditional counties (also known as shires), 86 in Great Britain and 6 in Northern Ireland. The British counties are different ages.

In England, in Anglo-Saxon times, Shires were units for getting taxes. They usually had a town at their centre. People called these towns the shire town. The shires had the same name as their shire town (for example Bedfordshire). Later people called these towns the county town. The name "county" came from the Normans, from a Norman word for an area under a Count (lord).

In 1539 Wales got thirteen counties. The counties in Scotland are this age or older.

The county boundaries (borders) of England are different today. In medieval times, some important cities got the status of counties, for example London, Bristol and Coventry. Some small places, e.g. Islandshire, were also counties. In 1844, a lot of these small places returned to their old counties.

United States

The name "county" is also used in 48 of the 50 states of the United States, for the next government unit smaller than the state. Louisiana uses the name parishes and Alaska uses boroughs. The U.S. Census Bureau lists 3,141 counties or organisation units of this sort. The power of the county government is very different in every state.

In New England, counties are mostly for law. In Connecticut, Massachusetts and Rhode Island, they have no governmental use; they are only geographic names. Most power is in the New England town.

In other places than New England, counties are for the police, water, gas and electricity, libraries, statistics and birth certificates. County sheriffs are the head of the police in some states, for areas outside of cities and towns. Other places have "County Police" and county sheriffs are for law. Each county has a county seat, usually the biggest town, where the county offices are.

Province of Alicante
Alacant () province is the fifth largest Spanish province by population with 1,750,000, and the second largest in the Valencian Community. It is on the south-east Mediterranean coast and the capital is the city of Alicante, a sea- port with a university. It is a commercial city with monuments like Sainte Barbra Castle. Other important cities are Elche, 215,000 with palms trees and its important shoe industry; Torrevieja, 100,000, tourist centre with the world-famous Habaneras contest; Orihuela, 75,000, agricultural important center; Benidorm, 67,000, the Mediterranean Manhattan; Alcoi, 60,000; textile center, and Elda, 55,000, shoes industry.

The most important river is the Segura, in the south, which provides the water to Alicante, Elche, Torrevieja, Orihuela and other cities. There are others like Vinalopo, Serpis, Amadorio, Ravine of the Sheeps and Monnegre.

The biggest mountain is Aitana, and other mountains are Mariola, Puig Bell, Maigmo and Gold Head, near Alicante. In the coast there are islands, the most important is Tabarca, and other is the Benidorm island. An important coast success is the Penon of Ifach, in Calpe.

The activities in Alicante province are tourism, industry (shoes, carpets, plays, dolls, textiles) and modern agriculture of regadium (oranges, lemons, tomatoes, almonds, wine). There are two universities: University of Alicante and University of Michael Hernandez.

...Now that we've learned how to plot inequalities on a number line and identify their solutions, it's time to apply this knowledge to real-world situations through word problems! Inequality word problems can seem intimidating at first, but by breaking them down step-by-step, you'll find they're just as approachable as any other math problem. Let's dive into some exciting scenarios together!

**Example 1:**
Sophia wants to buy a sketchbook that costs $8. She has saved up allowance and birthday money, which totals more than enough for the sketchbook. If we represent Sophia's savings as the variable S, would you write an inequality to describe her situation? What would be the solution set for this inequality?

*To solve this problem, let's break it down:*

1. We need to determine an inequality based on the information given. Since Sophia has saved more than enough money for the sketchbook, our inequality should show that S (her savings) is greater than the cost ($8). Therefore, our inequality will look like this: S > 8.
2. To graph this inequality, draw a number line from 0 to 10 (a reasonable range considering Sophia's purchase), place a solid dot over 8 since S is strictly greater than 8, and shade the area to its right:
![Graph showing shaded region representing Sophie's savings being greater than 8 dollars](data:image/png;base64,iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAAYAAAAECAYAAACNByblAAAAFElEQVQIW2P8z8AARIQB42+1AD9YvCMrDyAg6JjFpkiWFoTvCnkqOd++vZ2fnxmAAAAASUVORK5CYII=)
3. The solution set for this inequality includes all numbers greater than 8. In interval notation, the solution set would be written as (8,).

**Example 2:**
Lena loves baking cookies during the holiday season. This year, she plans to bake at least 25 dozen cookies for family gatherings and gifts. Each bag of flour contains about 5 cups, and Lena needs at least twice as much flour as there are cookies. Assuming each cookie requires 14 cup of flour, would you write an inequality to determine how many bags of flour Lena must buy? Use x as the number of dozens of cookies.

*Let's analyze the problem and formulate an inequality:*

1. First, convert the number of cookies to cups needed. Since each cookie takes 14 cup of flour, 1 dozen cookies require 12 \* 14 = 3 cups of flour. With x dozens of cookies, Lena needs 3x cups of flour.
2. Next, consider that Lena needs at least twice as much flour as there are cookies. That means she needs at least 2 \* (3x) = 6x cups of flour.
3. Now, recall that each bag of flour holds around 5 cups. Thus, divide the amount of flour required (6x cups) by the capacity of a single bag (5 cups): 6x / 5 = y (the number of bags).
4. Finally, translate these findings into an inequality: y >= 6x / 5. Here, x represents the number of dozens of cookies Lena makes, and y stands for the minimum number of bags of flour she must buy.

When faced with inequality word problems, always remember to dissect the given scenario carefully and translate it accurately into mathematical terms. By doing so, you'll unlock the power of algebra to make sense of intriguing challenges and develop valuable critical thinking skills along the way!

Manhattan
The Sons of Liberty, a Boston based group, were part of a long-term battle with British authorities over liberty poles that were sometimes raised by the Sons of Liberty and cut down by the British. The disputes ended when the revolutionary New York Provincial Congress took power in 1775.

Manhattan was the center of a series of large battles in the early American Revolutionary War. These battles were called the New York Campaign, where British forces and colonists fought for control of New York City and the state of New Jersey. The rebel Continental Army, led by George Washington, had to leave Manhattan after losing the Battle of Fort Washington on 16 November 1776. Shortly after, Manhattan was greatly damaged by the Great Fire of New York in 1776.

Victory gave the British control of the area. They used the city as the center for political and military activities for the rest of the war. Loyalists from elsewhere came to the city as refugees from the Rebels and to join the war.

Years later, Washington came back to Manhattan with his army. On Evacuation Day, the last British occupation forces left the city on 25 November 1783. On 30 April, 1789, Washington was inaugurated (officially became) the first president of the United States and took his oath of office at Federal Hall on Wall Street.

Immigration influx and Gilded Age

In the early 19th century, Manhattan grew in population and economically. Another great fire in 1835 destroyed much of the city but it was soon rebuilt. Because of the Great Irish Famine, a lot of Irish people emigrated (left their country) to live in New York; they made up for 25% of Manhattan's population at the time. Many of the Irish people lived in a part of the Lower East Side known as the Bowery or in another section called Five Points.

After the Civil War, many immigrants of Italian, Polish and Jewish backgrounds came to Manhattan and lived in tenements in a part of the city called the Lower East Side. Over a million people lived in the area at one point.

An Irish political machine called Tammany Hall was very important to New York City during the Gilded Age. With the support of mostly Irish immigrants, it grew as a political machine. The support helped win the election for the first Tammany mayor, Fernando Wood, in 1854. Central Park, which opened to the public in 1858, became the first landscaped park in any American city and the country's first public park.

The rate of immigration from Europe shot up after the Civil War, and New York became the most popular state for immigrants in the United States. Because of this, the French built and gave New York the Statue of Liberty on October 28, 1886. Soon after, the boroughs of Manhattan and Brooklyn were combined into one city.

Economic downfall and rise

In the beginning of the 20th century, many new things were built in the city, like skyscrapers and the New York City Subway. The first subway transit center, the Interborough Rapid Transit or IRT, opened to the public in 1904. The installation of the Subway helped tie the new city together, as did new bridges to Brooklyn. In the 1920s, many African-Americans came to live in Manhattan during the Great Migration from the American South, and the Harlem Renaissance. New York City became the most populous city (city with the most people) in the world in 1925, overtaking London, which had held the title for a century.
