When we bend the wood, it doesn't just get shorter but also thinner. The more we bend it, the more it gets compressed. For example, a piece of walnut wood bent more than halfway compressed from quite thick to pretty thin at the bending point. The wood at the bend becomes very dense. This isn't a bad thing, but we need to remember this when we plan to bend wood pieces. Making a piece of wood thicker for bending can only go so far. At some point, the wood can't be squished anymore and it may crack under the pressure. If too much pressure is in one place, the wood can fold like a paper. This isn't good, and we try to remove any folded pieces before we send them out. Any kind of wood can fold when we bend it, and it can happen for many reasons. If the wood is steamed too much or too little, it can fold more easily. Softer woods, weaker woods, or woods that are lighter can fold more often. If a tree grows really fast, the wood is weaker and can fold or break more easily.

Feathering is what we call it when the lines in the wood start to come apart a little bit.

Tiny knots in the wood are like fossils of a tree branch that never grew all the way. All kinds of trees have these knots, but cherry trees have them a lot. Walnut and soft maple trees also have them. There are too many of these knots to remove from every piece of wood, but they can cause problems when we try to bend the wood. If a knot breaks when we bend the wood, it can leave a diamond-shaped hole and we have to throw away that piece of wood.

There is a limit to how much we can bend a piece of wood with our machines. Our bending machines are strong and tough, just like a superhero. They can bend wood into different shapes. The machines can make the wood bend so much that it can even form a circle!

Let's talk about wood and water. Just like we need water to live, wood also needs water. But too much water is not good for the wood. Imagine the wood as a pile of straws. The water can go inside these straws and also stick to them.

When a tree is first cut, it can have lots of water in it, just like a soaked sponge. But when we leave the wood alone, the water starts to go away. If there is still a lot of water in the wood, it's like the straws are filled with water. When the wood loses this water, it doesn't change much. But when it loses more water, the straws start to dry out. That's when the wood starts to shrink. When a piece of wood dries, it gets smaller. This happens until the wood has the same amount of water as the air around it. This is like when a sponge gets smaller as it dries. But, wood is different because it doesn't get smaller the same way all around.

There are three ways that the wood can get smaller. First, it can get shorter. But this doesn't happen a lot, so we don't really notice it. Second, it can get thinner from the outside to the inside. This happens a little bit more. Third, it can get thinner along the lines that you see in the wood. This happens the most.

I told him, You're a silly boy. You don't know anything. Uncle Gabriel is gone, he's become a ghost. If you chase after a ghost, it'll catch you and take your soul. Then you won't be able to go home. Then where would I find you? You're so silly, you little guy! Talking to you is useless, you don't understand anything! Hurry up and come with me.

Frowning, he followed me. The path was winding up out of the valley. I looked back and saw that Uncle Gabriel was gone, nowhere to be seen, leaving a few dry yellow leaves on the path.

I said, Second Boy, don't be upset, hurry up and come with me. Do you remember what Uncle Gabriel just said?

Second Boy said, Yes, I remember. Uncle Gabriel said to tell Dad that he should bury him at FM field. Brother, why do you think Uncle Gabriel wants to be buried there?

I said, Samuel, don't talk about it; let's go. I don't understand why either.

Dry brown leaves covered the ground. There was no wind, there were no clouds, there was no noise or shadow. Where did Uncle Gabriel come from? Was he really gone or not?

I said, Let's go, Samuel.

Samuel nodded and said, Let's go.

I asked, Samuel, are you scared?

Samuel said, No. I just want to see Uncle Gabriel. Samuel asked, Brother, are you scared?

I said, No.

Samuel asked, Brother, Uncle Gabriel is gone but he can still talk. If we went away tomorrow and turned into breezes and could go wherever we want and talk in the wind too, would the people in our town be scared?

I said, Samuel, don't say such silly things. If you do, Uncle Gabriel might come back.

With a determined heart, Jose set off to find the giant. He walked for a long time until he reached a high hill. At the top, a giant sat on a rock, staring at the water. "What do you want, little boy?" the giant asked, its voice booming. Jose explained about the fish and his wish.

The giant frowned. "Wishes can be dangerous. What do you want to wish for?" Jose thought about it. He wanted to be the best in everything-school, sports, and more. "I want to be great!" he said. The giant shook its head. "True greatness comes from hard work, not wishes."

Feeling a bit sad, Jose looked at the river. "But I want to help my family," he replied. The giant smiled gently. "That is a wish worth considering. Work hard, and you can make a difference." Inspired, Jose decided he would rather earn his greatness.

"Thank you," he said to the giant. With a wave, the giant returned to its thoughts. Jose went back to the river and let the fish go. "I don't need a wish," he told it. "I will find my own way." The fish smiled and swam away, leaving Jose with a sense of peace.

As he walked home, Jose felt proud. He realized that being great did not come from magic but from effort. With every step, he felt stronger, ready to take on the world.

**Course Unit: Reflective Writing Strategies - Exploring Fascinating Careers**

Welcome to this exciting course unit where we will explore fascinating careers while learning reflective writing strategies! We all have dreams and aspirations about what we want to become when we grow up. Some of us may want to be actors, writers, scientists, or even astronauts. By studying different career paths and reflecting on our thoughts and feelings, we can gain insights into ourselves and discover more about our passions and goals. This process involves critical thinking and self-awareness, which you can practice through reflective writing. So let's get started!

**What is Reflective Writing?**

Reflective writing is a way of expressing your thoughts, feelings, and observations about a particular experience or situation. It allows you to think deeply about yourself and the world around you. When you engage in reflective writing, you ask questions like: What did I learn? How did this make me feel? What would I do differently next time? These questions help you understand your experiences better and develop essential skills such as problem-solving, decision making, and empathy.

**Exploring Fascinating Careers: Actor Edition**

In this course unit, we will focus on the acting profession. Actors bring stories to life on stage, television, and film. They study scripts, rehearse lines, and perform in front of audiences. Being an actor requires creativity, dedication, and hard work. To illustrate these points, let's look at some famous actors and their journeys.

* Example 1: Robert Carlyle

Robert Carlyle is a Scottish actor known for his roles in Trainspotting, The Full Monty, and Once Upon a Time. He grew up in a working-class family and discovered his passion for acting during high school. After attending college, he joined a local theater group and began performing in plays. His big break came when he landed a role in the movie Trainspotting. Since then, he has built an impressive career spanning over three decades.

* Activity: Imagine you are Robert Carlyle. Write a reflection about how you felt when you got the call that you were cast in Trainspotting. What went through your mind? How did you celebrate?

* Example 2: Emma Watson

Emma Watson is a British actress who became famous for her role as Hermione Granger in the Harry Potter series. At just nine years old, she auditioned for the part and beat out thousands of other girls for the role. Over the next ten years, she worked tirelessly on the films while also pursuing her education. Today, she continues to act in movies and advocates for gender equality.

* Activity: Put yourself in Emma Watson's shoes. Describe your emotions when you found out you got the part of Hermione Granger. Did you ever imagine that the Harry Potter series would become so popular? Why or why not?

By examining the lives of real-life professionals like Robert Carlyle and Emma Watson, you can begin to see the patterns and practices that lead to success in any field. You can apply these lessons to your own life and use them to guide your decisions and actions.

**Putting it All Together: Reflection Prompts**

Now that you know more about reflective writing and the acting profession, it's time to put your newfound skills into action. Use the following prompts to write reflections about your interests, goals, and experiences. Remember to consider your thoughts, feelings, and observations as you respond. Happy writing!

1. If you could be any type of actor (stage, TV, or film), which one would you choose and why? Describe your ideal role and the steps you would take to achieve it.

Geography
Geography (from Greek: , geographia, literally "earth description") is the study of earth and its people. Its features are things like continents, seas, rivers and mountains. Its inhabitants are all the people and animals that live on it. Its phenomena are the things that happen like tides, winds, and earthquakes.

A person who is an expert in geography is a geographer. A geographer tries to understand the world and the things that are in it, how they started and how they have changed.

Geography is divided into two main parts called physical geography and human geography. Physical geography studies the natural environment and human geography studies the human environment. The human environmental studies would include things such as the population in a country, how a country's economy is doing, and more. There is also environmental geography.

Maps are a main tool of geography, so geographers spend much time making and studying them. Making maps is called cartography, and people who specialize in making maps are cartographers.

Branches

Physical geography

Physical geography (or physiography) focuses on geography as an Earth science. It aims to understand the physical problems and the issues of lithosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, pedosphere, and global flora and fauna patterns (biosphere).

Physical geography can be divided into many broad categories, including:

Human geography

Human geography is the social science that covers the study of people and their communities, cultures, economies and their interaction with the environment. Geographers studying the human environment may look at:
Population
Countries of the world
Land use
Agriculture
City
Industry
Energy

History
The oldest known world map dates back to ancient Babylon from the 9th century BC. The best known Babylonian world map is the Imago Mundi of 600 BC. Star charts (maps of the sky) are of similar age.

During the Middle Ages, people in Europe made fewer maps. People in the eastern countries made more. Ab Zayd al-Balkh created the "Balkh school" of mapping in Baghdad.

Western Europe became known as the leader of geographic thought during the European Renaissance and The Age of Exploration (1400-1600). The printing press made maps and information about the world available to everyone.

This caused more interest in how the world worked.

In the 1700s and 1800s scientists started to study the relationship between the environment and its people

A gentle breeze whispered through the meadow as a girl lay on the soft grass. She dreamed of a place where flowers could talk. One day, she closed her eyes and wished to visit that magical land. When she opened her eyes, she was surrounded by flowers that danced in the wind.

To her surprise, the flowers began to speak. They shared stories of the sun and rain. The girl listened closely, fascinated by their tales of joy and sadness. Each flower told her its dreams, and she realized how much each one longed to grow tall and bright.

The girl felt a deep connection to the flowers. She promised to take care of them when she returned home. As she left the magical land, she understood that nature is full of voices and dreams. She became their friend, ready to help them bloom.

"Let's try it on the door!" They ran to the door and put the key in the lock. They turned it and heard a click. They were very happy. They opened the door and saw a big surprise. There was a big dog outside. It was not a friendly dog. It was a mean dog. It barked and growled and showed its teeth. It wanted to bite them. Sam and Ben were very scared. She realized that the key was not a magic key. It was the key to the neighbor's house. The neighbor had a bad dog that hated kids. She had told them to never go near her house. She scolded Sam and Ben for being naughty and careless. She took away their toys and sent them to bed. They had no dinner and no dessert. They were miserable. They wished they had never found the key.

Bright lights flashed all around as Alex wandered through the busy market. There were stalls with strange machines and glowing fruits. He felt drawn to a corner where an old robot sat. Its metal skin was scratched and dirty, but its eyes sparkled with stories. Curious, Alex approached it, hoping to learn something new.

The old robot began to speak in a slow, wise voice. "Long ago, I was the guardian of the city," it said. "I kept the peace with my magic wires. But one day, a young boy betrayed me. He wanted my powers for himself." Alex's heart sank. He wanted to know more about this betrayal. Why would someone hurt a friend?

"His name was Leo," the robot continued. "He was once my helper, a kind soul. Together, we made the city bright. But greed took over him. He stole my magic and left me broken." Alex listened closely, feeling a knot in his stomach. He could not imagine betraying a friend like that.

"Now, I wait for someone pure of heart," the robot said. "Someone who can help me regain my magic." Alex felt a spark of hope. Could he be that person? He looked around, seeing the bustling crowd. He knew he had to act fast, before someone else discovered the robot's secret.

As he reached into his pocket, he found a small crystal. It glowed softly, just like the old robot's eyes. Alex had found this crystal in his backyard, thinking it was just a pretty stone. But now, it felt important. He took a deep breath and placed it in the robot's hands.

The robot's eyes widened. "This is the key!" it shouted. In a swirl of colors, the magic returned to the old robot. It stood tall, its form shining like the sun. "Thank you, young one," it said, voice stronger now. "You have broken the chains of betrayal."

Suddenly, Leo appeared from the shadows. "What have you done?" he yelled. "I wanted that power!" Alex felt fear but stood his ground. "You can't take what you don't own," he said boldly. The old robot turned to Leo, its eyes glowing fiercely. "You will not harm him, not again."

With a wave of its hand, the old robot sent Leo away, leaving only light in his place. Alex smiled, feeling free. He had chosen trust over betrayal, and the city was safe once more.

Lily and Tom are friends. They like to play in the park. One day, they see a big dog. The dog is brown and fluffy. It has a long tail and a wet nose. "Can we touch the dog?" Lily asks Tom. "I don't know. Maybe we should ask the owner first," Tom says. They look around and see a man sitting on a bench. He is reading a book. He has a leash in his hand. The leash is attached to the dog. "Excuse me, sir. Can we touch your dog?" Lily says. The man looks up and smiles. He sees Lily and Tom. They are cute and polite. "Sure, you can touch my dog. His name is Rover. He is very friendly and loves children," the man says. Lily and Tom walk towards the dog. They reach out their hands and touch his fur. It is soft and warm. The dog wags his tail and licks their faces. Lily and Tom giggle. "Hello, Rover. You are a nice dog," Lily says. "You are a good boy," Tom says. They pet the dog and play with him. They throw a ball and he fetches it. They rub his belly and he rolls over. They have fun. But then, they smell something smelly. It is coming from the dog. They pinch their noses and make a face. "Yuck! What is that smell?" Lily says. "I think he rolled in something bad," Tom says. They look at the dog and see some dirt and grass on his fur. They also see some poop. "Ew! He rolled in poop!" Lily says. "That's gross!" Tom says. They run away from the dog and back to the man. They tell him what happened. "Oh, no! Rover, you naughty dog! You need a bath!" the man says. He apologizes to Lily and Tom. He says he will take the dog home and clean him. He thanks them for playing with him. Lily and Tom say goodbye to the man and the dog. They are still friends. They are not mad at the dog. They know he did not mean to be smelly. They hope to see him again. But next time, they hope he will be clean.

1835
Events
January 1 - Ole Pedersen Hoiland breaks into the Bank of Norway and steals 64.000 dalers (Swedish dollars)
January 30 - Unsuccessful assassination attempt against President Andrew Jackson in the United States Capitol - first assassination attempt against a President of the United States.
February 20 - Concepcin, Chile is destroyed by an earthquake
March 2 - Ferdinand becomes Emperor of Austria.
April 18 - Lord Melbourne becomes the new British Prime Minister.
May 5 - In Belgium a railroad opens from Brussels to Mechelen. It is the first railway in continental Europe.
May 6 - James Gordon Bennett, Sr. makes the first issue of the New York Herald.
July 4 - The Baltimore and Ohio Railroad finishes the Thomas Viaduct, at the time the longest bridge in the United States, and the second longest in the world. (London Bridge was the longest in the world at the time)
September 7 - Charles Darwin gets to the Galapagos Islands aboard HMS Beagle.
October 2 - Texas Revolution begins: Battle of Gonzales - Mexican soldiers try to get the people of Gonzales, Texas to give up their weapons, but the Texans fight back
December 9 - The Army of the Republic of Texas captures San Antonio.
December 16 - Fire in New York City destroys 530 buildings
December 19 - Toledo Blade newspaper begins publishing.
December 28 - Seminole fighter Osceola and his warriors attack U.S. government agent Thompson outside Fort King in Central Florida, starting the Second Seminole War.
The State of Ohio and the Michigan Territory fight the Toledo War over the city of Toledo and the Toledo Strip.
De Revolutionibus Orbium Coelestum, Copernicus' book on the motion of the Earth, is removed from the Index of Prohibited Books.
Samuel Colt patents the first revolver
Civil war erupts in Uruguay between supporters of Blanco and Colorado parties
The first Bulgarian-language school opens in the Ottoman Empire.
The French word for their language changes to franais, from franois
The Australian city of Melbourne is founded by John Batman and John Pascoe Fawkner.

Art, music, theatre, and literature
May 8 - Hans Christian Andersen publishes his first four fairy tales
June 2 - P.T. Barnum and his circus begin their first tour of the United States
September 26 - Donizetti's opera Lucia di Lammermoor is performed for the first time

Births
March 15 - Eduard Strauss, Austrian composer (d. 1916)
April 9 - King Lopold II of Belgium (d. 1909)
June 2 - Pope Pius X (d. 1914)
October 23 - Adlai E. Stevenson, Vice President of the United States (d. 1914)
November 25 - Andrew Carnegie, American industrialist and philanthropist (d. 1919)
November 30 - Mark Twain, American writer and humorist (d. 1910)

Deaths
March 2 - Emperor Francis I of Austria (b. 1768)
April 21 - Samuel Slater, American industrialist (b. 1768)
May 13 - John Nash, English architect (b. 1752)
June 18 - William Cobbett, English journalist and writer (b. 1763)
July 28 - douard Adolphe Casimir Joseph Mortier, French marshal (b. 1768)
September 23 - Vincenzo Bellini, Italian composer (b. 1801)

Bright stars lit the night sky over the city. A young girl named Mia looked out her window. She loved to dream about heroes. One evening, she heard a loud crash. Curious, she rushed outside. There, she found a strange creature. It was green and furry, with big eyes.

"Help me!" the creature cried. Mia felt sorry for it. She asked, "What is wrong?" The creature pointed to a tall building. "Bad guy inside!" it said. Mia was scared but wanted to be brave. She decided to help. "Let's go!" she said, and they ran toward the building.

Inside, they found a man in a black suit. He was stealing shiny things! Mia and the green creature hid behind a big desk. The creature whispered, "We need a plan." Mia thought hard. "What if I distract him?" she suggested. The creature nodded.

Mia took a deep breath and shouted, "Hey, you! Why are you stealing?" The man turned, surprised. As he did, the creature quietly grabbed a shiny gem. But just then, a loud alarm went off! The man looked back and ran away, leaving the shiny things behind.

Mia was confused. "Was he really a bad guy?" she asked. The creature replied, "Not the real danger!" Mia realized the man was a red herring, just a thief. The real danger was the alarm. They needed to escape fast.

They ran out of the building just in time. The police arrived and caught the man. Mia felt proud. She learned that things are not always what they seem. Sometimes, a hero comes from the most unexpected places.

Before the dawn, a boy found a feather on the ground. It was soft and white, shining with morning light. He picked it up, feeling a sense of wonder. He wondered who it belonged to and what it meant. The feather felt like a sign, a message from the sky.

That day, the boy saw a bird in a tree. It was bright and beautiful, flying high above. The boy felt a wish in his heart. He wanted to fly like the bird, to feel the wind beneath him. The feather in his hand reminded him of that dream.

With each passing day, he practiced climbing trees. He learned to balance and jump. He imagined soaring through the air. The feather became his lucky charm, always with him as he tried new things. Each attempt brought him closer to his goal.

One sunny afternoon, he climbed the tallest tree. The boy took a deep breath and leaped. For a moment, he felt free, like the bird. He landed safely but laughed in joy. He realized that flying was not just about the air; it was about courage and belief.

From then on, he shared the feather with friends. He told them about dreams and taking risks. The feather became a symbol of their friendship and courage. They all knew that they could reach for the sky, no matter how high.

IV. Conclusion and Assessment (25 min)

Great job, little scholars! You've learned so much about the New York Blackout of 1977! Now it's time for a fun activity where you can show off your knowledge and imagination.

Let's imagine that we're all back in 1977 during the big citywide blackout. Each one of you gets to choose a special character to be in our story. Who do you want to be? A brave firefighter helping people in the dark? Or maybe a clever police officer keeping everyone safe? How about being a curious news reporter sharing stories with the world? It's up to you!

Once you've picked your character, let's think about how they might feel when the lights go out unexpectedly. Are they scared because it's dark outside? Or excited about trying something new and different? What adventures could they have in the city without power?

Now, grab your pencils and paper. I want each of you to write a sentence or two telling us what happened to your character during the New York Blackout of 1977. Remember to use simple words and phrases so everyone can understand.

Here are some ideas to help get you started:

* If you chose to be a firefighter: "Even though it was dark, I helped people by using my flashlight to guide them home safely."
* If you chose to be a police officer: "During the blackout, I made sure no one took advantage of the darkness to steal things from stores."
* If you chose to be a news reporter: "I saw people singing songs together under the stars since there were no streetlights shining!"

Take a few minutes to write down your sentences. When you're done, share your story with a friend or family member. They'll be proud of everything you've learned in this e-module!

Well done, young explorers! By creating these fun stories, you've shown me just how much you know about life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness during challenging times like the New York Blackout of 1977. Keep up the great work!

Through the bright flowers, Lily walked slowly, searching for her friend Leo. She loved visiting the garden, where colors danced in the sunlight. When she spotted Leo sitting on the swing, she ran over. "Hey, let's play!" she said with a big smile. Leo jumped up, excited to spend the afternoon together.

They played tag among the flowers, laughing and shouting. Leo was fast, but Lily was clever. "I will catch you!" she yelled, chasing him. They ran until they were out of breath, flopping down on the grass. "That was fun!" said Lily, grinning from ear to ear. Leo agreed, his heart full of joy.

After resting, they noticed a butterfly fluttering by. "Look at that!" said Leo, pointing. They watched as the butterfly danced from flower to flower. "It is so free," said Lily. Leo thought for a moment. "Like us," he said. They both realized that their friendship felt like flying, full of joy and laughter.

As the sun began to set, the garden was painted in shades of gold. Lily turned to Leo. "We should always meet here," she said. "This place is special." Leo nodded, knowing they would come back to share more adventures. "Next time, we can bring paint and make the flowers even more colorful!" he suggested.

With that idea, they agreed to return the next day. They hugged goodbye, knowing that their friendship was like the garden, growing more beautiful every day. They walked home with smiles, dreaming of all the fun they would have together.

Long ago, in a small village, a kind boy lived. He often helped his neighbors. One day, he found a strange box in the woods. Curious, he opened it. To his surprise, a fairy appeared! She was stunning, with sparkling wings.

The fairy said, "You have freed me! I will grant you one wish!" The boy thought hard. He wanted to be brave and strong. With a flick of her wand, she turned him into a lion! "Roar!" he shouted, feeling powerful. But deep down, he missed being a boy.

As a lion, he met a lovely girl. She was picking flowers near a stream. He approached her and felt a connection. The girl was not afraid; she smiled at him. She sat near the water, and he listened to her dreams about adventure and love.

When rounding a number to the nearest thousand, we want to find the closest multiple of 1,000. To do this, we look at the digit in the hundreds place (the third digit from the right). If this digit is less than 5, we leave the digits in the thousands, hundreds, and tens places as they are and replace all of the remaining digits with zeros. If the digit in the hundreds place is greater than or equal to 5, we increase the digit in the thousands place by one and then replace all of the remaining digits with zeros.

For example, let's say we want to round the number 38,792 to the nearest thousand. The digit in the hundreds place is 9, which is greater than 5. This means we need to increase the digit in the thousands place by one (from 3 to 4) and replace all of the remaining digits with zeros. So, the rounded number is 40,000.

Here are some more examples:

* Round the number 12,456 to the nearest thousand: The digit in the hundreds place is 4, which is less than 5. This means we can leave the digits in the thousands, hundreds, and tens places as they are and replace all of the remaining digits with zeros. So, the rounded number is 12,000.
* Round the number 56,873 to the nearest thousand: The digit in the hundreds place is 8, which is greater than 5. This means we need to increase the digit in the thousands place by one (from 5 to 6) and replace all of the remaining digits with zeros. So, the rounded number is 57,000.
* Round the number 999,999 to the nearest thousand: Even though there is no actual digit in the hundreds place, we still consider it to be 9 (because 9 comes after 0). Since 9 is greater than 5, we need to increase the digit in the thousands place by one (to 1,000,000) and replace all of the remaining digits with zeros. So, the rounded number is 1,000,000.

There may be times when the number you are working with has extra digits beyond the ones place (i.e., the ninth digit from the right). In these cases, you should ignore those additional digits when determining whether to round up or down. Here are some examples:

* Round the number 3,879,245 to the nearest thousand: The digit in the hundreds place is 9, so we need to increase the digit in the thousands place by one (from 3 to 4) and replace all of the remaining digits with zeros. It does not matter what the other digits are; they should be ignored. So, the rounded number is 4,000,000.
* Round the number 123,456,789 to the nearest thousand: The digit in the hundreds place is 5, so we need to leave the digits in the thousands, hundreds, and tens places as they are and replace all of the remaining digits with zeros. Again, it does not matter what the other digits are; they should be ignored. So, the rounded number is 123,000,000.

It is important to note that rounding always introduces some amount of error because we are approximating the original number rather than giving its exact value. However, rounding can make large numbers easier to work with and understand. Just be sure to keep track of how much rounding you are doing and be aware of any potential consequences of introducing error into your calculations.

San Francisco Bay Area
The San Francisco Bay Area, also known as the Bay Area, is a metropolitan area that goes around the San Francisco Bay in Northern California. It includes the cities of San Francisco, San Jos, and Oakland, and their many suburbs. It also includes the smaller urban and rural areas of the North Bay. Over seven million people live in the San Francisco Bay Area. The San Francisco Bay Area is the 43rd largest metropolitan area in the world in population.

The Bay Area includes cities, towns, military bases, airports, and related regional, state, and national parks.

San Jos is the largest city in the Bay Area since 1990 and the tenth largest city in America. But for most of its history, San Francisco was the city with the most people. San Francisco is still the city people pay the most attention to, and it is the major cultural center in the region.

Bay Area Rapid Transit connects the different parts of the Bay Area.

Subregions

North Bay

The region north of the Golden Gate Bridge is known locally as the North Bay. This area includes Marin County and continues north into Sonoma and Napa counties and east to Solano County. With some exceptions, this region is quite rich: Marin County is listed as the richest in the nation.

San Francisco

The City and County of San Francisco is generally placed in a category by itself in terms of geography and culture. It is separated by water from the north, west and east, and by a county line from its neighbors to the South. San Francisco has been the cultural, financial and urban center of the region for a long time. For most of the Bay Area's history, it has also been the main population center. But because the size of the county is limited, the growth of the city was limited as well. The resulting urban sprawl has given other cities and counties more population growth.

Peninsula

The area between the South Bay and the City and County of San Francisco is the San Francisco Peninsula, known locally as The Peninsula. This area includes many small cities and suburban communities in San Mateo County and the northwestern part of Santa Clara County, as well as several towns along the Pacific coast, such as Pacifica and Half Moon Bay.

East Bay

The eastern side of the bay, consisting of Alameda and Contra Costa counties, is known locally as the East Bay. The East Bay is split into two regions, the inner East Bay, which is on the coast of the Bay, and the outer East Bay, including the inland valleys separated from the inner East Bay by hills and mountains.

South Bay
The communities along the southern edge of the Bay are known as the South Bay, Santa Clara Valley, and Silicon Valley.
This region is home to a large number of major technology companies. Some tech companies in the South Bay are Intel, AMD, Cisco Systems, Hewlett-Packard, Apple, Google, and Yahoo!, Microsoft and much much more.

The San Francisco Bay Area is one of the richest regions in the United States.

Visigoths
The Visigoths (Western Goths) were one of two main branches of the Goths, an East Germanic tribe (the Ostrogoths were the other). Both were among the loosely-defined Germanic tribes that fought the Roman Empire during the Migration Period.

Most famously, a Visigothic force, led by King Alaric I, succeeded in storming Rome in 410 AD. Later Visigothic kings ruled southern Gaul, and Hispania after they had taken it from the Alans and the Vandals.

After the collapse of the Western Roman Empire, the Visigoths played a major role in southwestern Europe for another 250 years and adopted Roman culture and clothing.

Welcome to Unit 14: Converting Units of Time! In this unit, we will explore how to convert different units of time, such as seconds, minutes, hours, days, weeks, months, and years. By the end of this unit, you should feel confident converting between these units with ease.

Let's start by reviewing some basic facts about time:

* There are 60 seconds in a minute.
* There are 60 minutes in an hour.
* There are 24 hours in a day.
* There are 7 days in a week.
* There are approximately 30.44 days in a month (this varies depending on whether it is a leap year).
* There are approximately 365.25 days in a year (again, this varies slightly due to leap years).

Now, let's dive into our first conversion problem. Suppose you want to convert 3 hours to minutes. Since there are 60 minutes in an hour, you can multiply the number of hours by 60 to find the equivalent amount of time in minutes:

3 hours  60 minutes per hour = 180 minutes

So, 3 hours is equal to 180 minutes.

Next, let's try converting 120 minutes to hours. To do this, divide the number of minutes by 60 (since there are 60 minutes in an hour):

120 minutes  60 minutes per hour = 2 hours

Therefore, 120 minutes is equal to 2 hours.

Let's try one more example involving larger units of time. Suppose you want to convert 5 days to weeks. Since there are 7 days in a week, you can divide the number of days by 7 to find the equivalent amount of time in weeks:

5 days  7 days per week = 0.71 weeks

So, 5 days is equivalent to roughly 0.71 weeks.

As you practice converting units of time, keep in mind that it might be helpful to set up ratios comparing the two units involved in the conversion. This can help ensure that you're setting up the correct multiplication or division problem.

For example, suppose you want to convert 180 minutes to hours. You could set up the following ratio:

1 hour : 60 minutes

This means that 1 hour is equivalent to 60 minutes. From here, you can see that you need to divide the number of minutes (180) by the number of minutes per hour (60) to find the equivalent amount of time in hours:

180 minutes  60 minutes per hour = 3 hours

Setting up ratios like this can be especially helpful when working with more complex conversions involving multiple steps.

In summary, converting units of time involves understanding the relationships between various units (such as seconds, minutes, and hours), as well as being able to perform calculations using those relationships. With practice, you should become increasingly comfortable performing these types of conversions. Good luck!

George Washington Bridge
The George Washington Bridge is a suspension bridge over the Hudson River. It connects part of New York City, New York to Fort Lee, New Jersey. It is long. It was designed by Othmar H. Ammann. Building began on October 21, 1927. The bridge was opened on October 25, 1931. It cost $59 million. A second level was added below the main level and opened to traffic on August 29, 1962. There are also walkways for pedestrians and bicyclists on the north and south sides of the bridge.

The main span of the bridge is long. It is wide. It is suspended by four cables. Each cable weighs 28,450 tons and is made from 26,474 individual wires. The total length of all the wire in the four cables is .

Ammann chose the location for the bridge because the river was narrower at this point. The banks on either side were high. That meant the bridge could be tall enough for ships to pass underneath, without having to build long rising bridge approaches.

**Unit 6: Body Sculpture Photography**

Have you ever seen a photograph that made you stop and stare? Maybe it was a picture of a beautiful landscape, a stunning portrait, or even something unusual like a sculpture. But have you ever thought about taking pictures of people's bodies as if they were sculptures? That's what body sculpture photography is all about!

Imagine being able to capture the curves and lines of someone's body in a way that makes them look like a work of art. It might sound difficult, but with practice and patience, anyone can do it. And don't worry - we won't be asking you to take nude photographs! Instead, we will focus on how to use light, shadow, and poses to create interesting and artistic images of the human form.

First, let's talk about lighting. Light can make or break a photo, especially when it comes to body sculpture photography. By using different types of lights and angles, you can emphasize certain parts of the body while hiding others. For example, side lighting can create long shadows and highlight the shape of muscles, while backlighting can give the image a soft, dreamy quality.

Next, let's discuss poses. When taking photos of people, it's important to make sure they are comfortable and confident. Encourage your model to try different positions and movements until you find one that looks great. Remember, there are no right or wrong ways to pose - it's all about finding what works best for each individual person.

Now, let's put everything together. Imagine you want to take a photo of someone standing up. You could position them so that their weight is shifted onto one leg, creating a more dynamic pose. Then, you could use a soft front light to illuminate their face and upper body, while also casting subtle shadows on their lower half. This would draw attention to the curve of their waist and hip, making them look strong and graceful at the same time.

Of course, body sculpture photography isn't just about technique - it's also about creativity and self-expression. So don't be afraid to experiment with different styles and approaches. Who knows - you might discover a new passion for capturing the beauty of the human form!

Remember, when taking any type of photograph, always respect your subjects and ask for their permission before shooting. Be kind, patient, and understanding, and most importantly, have fun exploring this fascinating world of art and photography!

Ulster
Ulster is one of the four historical provinces which make up the island of Ireland. The others are Leinster, Munster and Connacht.

There are nine counties in Ulster. Three of them are in the Republic of Ireland:
County Cavan
County Donegal
County Monaghan

The other six counties make up all of Northern Ireland, which is part of the United Kingdom:
County Antrim
County Armagh
County Down
County Fermanagh
County Londonderry
County Tyrone

Because most of Ulster is in Northern Ireland, the name "Ulster" is also sometimes used to mean Northern Ireland, even though Northern Ireland is only part of Ulster. This is called totum pro parte in Latin which means "the whole for a part".

Weserstadion
The Weserstadion is a stadium in Bremen, Germany. It lies to the right side of the Weser, in the Pauliner Marsch, a flooding area in the quarter of Peterswerder. It is the homeground of the Werder Bremen football club.

History
The Weser stadium was built in 1909 by Bremen's Allgemeiner Bremer Turn- und Sportverein as a sports field. After its first change in the year 1926, it was given the name ATSB Kampfbahn. Today's name, which goes back to the direct situation at the Weser river, exists since the year 1930. Since this time there also the sports association Werder Bremen makes its plays. At the beginning of the first season of the soccer Bundesliga in the year 1963 the stadium received its first roofed grandstand. In the following decades also the other grandstands were built and modernized gradually. 1992 for the first time in a stadium a VIP Loge was inserted.

Course Unit: Understanding Our New Life in Christ

Welcome to this course unit where we will learn about our new life as followers of Jesus! Have you ever felt like it's hard to do the right thing or make good choices? Does it seem challenging to always be kind, patient, or honest? Well, there's great news! When we decide to follow Jesus, He gives us a fresh start and helps us live better lives through His Holy Spirit. This is called sanctification - the process of becoming more holy, just like Jesus. Let's dive into understanding what happens when we become Christians and how God empowers us to grow spiritually.

Section 1: A Fresh Start - Union With Jesus
When someone accepts Jesus as their Lord and Savior, they enter into a special relationship with Him. We call this having 'union with Christ.' Imagine being connected to Jesus like branches are attached to a vine (John 15:5). As part of this connection, we receive forgiveness for all our past sins and mistakes. That means we can leave behind old habits and patterns that didn't please God. Now, we get to enjoy a clean slate, filled with endless possibilities to love others and serve God!

Section 2: Walking in Newness of Life
Now that we have this amazing gift of salvation, God invites us to live differently. Instead of letting negative feelings control our actions, we can now choose kindness, patience, and self-control. Think of this as putting on a brand-new pair of shoes. At first, walking might feel strange, but soon enough, those shoes fit perfectly and help us move forward positively. Similarly, living according to God's ways may take practice, yet eventually, it becomes second nature.

Section 3: Fruitfulness Through Resurrection Life
As Christians, we also share in Jesus' victory over sin and death. Just as He rose again, so will we one day. For now, though, let's focus on bringing forth fruits of the Spirit daily (Galatians 5:22-23). These qualities reflect who Jesus is and show people around us that following Him makes a difference. To remember them easily, think of the word 'FRIEND': Faith, Righteousness, Integrity, Empathy, Nurturing Love, and Dependability. Isn't it awesome knowing that God transforms us inside out and equips us to shine brightly for Him?

Section 4: Experiencing the Power of the Holy Spirit
God doesn't expect us to change on our own strength. Thankfully, He sends His Helper, the Holy Spirit, to guide, encourage, and empower us along the way. By spending time getting to know God through prayer, reading the Bible, worshipping Him, and joining other Christians in community, we open ourselves up to experience the Spirit's work in our lives.

Imagine having your very own superhero sidekick helping you navigate every situation! The Holy Spirit does exactly that for us. So whenever you need wisdom, courage, or encouragement, don't forget to ask God for assistance. Remember, He loves you deeply and desires nothing more than seeing you flourish in your faith journey.

In conclusion, our new life in Christ offers boundless opportunities for growth and transformation. Embrace each step of this incredible adventure, trusting that God will never leave your side. And before long, you too will marvel at the beautiful person He shapes you to be!

Spider-Man (2002 movie)
Spider-Man is an American 2002 superhero movie. It was made from the story of the Marvel Comics superhero, Spider-Man. It was the first in the Spider-Man movie series. It was written by David Koepp and directed by Sam Raimi. Tobey Maguire starred as Peter Parker / Spider-Man. Kirsten Dunst played the girl Peter loves, Mary-Jane Watson, and Willem Dafoe played the bad guy, Norman Osborn.

Plot
At the start of the movie, Peter Parker is a very smart teenager, who lives with his Aunt May and Uncle Ben. He is friends with Harry Osborn and Mary Jane Watson. Peter has loved Mary Jane since he was young. Peter is bullied at school by the other teenagers. On a school trip Peter is accidentally bitten by a spider that had been mutated (or changed) in a science study. This allows him to climb up walls, make spider webs come from his wrists, jump high, move fast and become very strong. Peter uses his powers to fight the bully Flash Thompson and beats him up. When Ben finds out, he teaches Peter that "with great power comes great responsibility." Peter ignores Ben and uses his powers to win a wrestling competition, to win prize money to impress Mary Jane. However, the cashier does not pay Peter what he said he would. A criminal steals a lot of money from the cashier and runs off. Peter does not try to catch the criminal, as revenge for not getting paid as much as he wanted. The criminal then steals Ben's car and shoots Ben. Peter returns to find Ben shot, and Ben dies in his arms. Peter angrily sets off to capture the killer. When he does, he is horrified to find that the man is the same criminal he refused to stop. From then on, Peter becomes Spider-Man and vows to fight crime, using Ben's words to their fullest. Peter takes a job as a photographer at the Daily Bugle selling photos to J. Jonah Jameson, who seems to be jealous of Spider-Man and makes Spider-Man look bad in the paper.

Meanwhile, Harry's father Norman Osborn is in trouble. Norman is the CEO (or head) of his own company name Oscorp. Oscorp does science studies and is working on a device that will allow someone to fly, as well as a new formula that will make a person stronger. Norman is ready to test the formula on humans, but his fellow scientists say the formula is still too dangerous. Norman decides to test the formula on himself. The formula does allow Norman to move fast and makes him very strong, but also drives him insane. Later the executive board of Oscorp kicks Norman off the board, angering him. Norman steals the flying device and becomes the Green Goblin. The Green Goblin attacks and kills the board members at a parade, causing a fight with Spider-Man. Later Green Goblin captures Spider-Man and offers to work together. During a fire at a building, the Green Goblin uses his voice and pretends to be someone trapped. When Spider-Man goes to rescue the person, he finds the Green Goblin. Spider-Man refuses Green Goblin's offer to work together, causing another fight. During the fight, Spider-Man's arm is cut. Later Peter, Norman, Harry, Mary Jane and Aunt May meet at Peter's apartment for Thanksgiving. Norman notices Peter's cut on his arm and realizes that Peter Parker is Spider-Man.

Isaac Asimov
Isaac Asimov ( - April 6, 1992) was a writer of science fiction. He was also a biochemist with a PhD from Columbia University.

Life
Asimov was born in Petrovichi, Smolensk Oblast, Russian SFSR to a Jewish family, on an unknown date between October 4, 1919 and January 2, 1920. Asimov celebrated his birthday on January 2. He was taken to the United States when he was three, and learned English and Yiddish as his native languages. He wrote many books. People know about Isaac Asimov because of his science fiction books and his science books for non-scientists.

Writing
Asimov's most famous books were the Foundation series. He also wrote the Galactic Empire, the Robot Series, mystery, fantasy, and non-fiction books. He wrote the Norby series with his wife, Janet Asimov. He wrote or edited over 500 books and about 90,000 letters. Other subjects he wrote about were history, the Bible, literature, and sexuality.

Many of Asimov's early writings were short stories published in cheap science fiction and fantasy magazines. Years later, most of them were collected and republished as collections. Well-known collections include I, Robot, The Rest of the Robots, Earth is Room Enough and The Early Asimov.

Asimov's reading list
Asimov made a list of 15 of his science fiction books, which he advised should be read in this order:
I, Robot (1950). Alternatively, The Complete Robot (1982).
Caves of Steel (1954).
The Naked Sun (1957).
The Robots of Dawn (1983).
Robots and Empire (1985).
The Currents of Space (1952).
The Stars, Like Dust (1951).
Pebble in the Sky (1950).
Prelude to Foundation (1988).
Forward the Foundation (1993).
Foundation (1951).
Foundation and Empire (1952).
Second Foundation (1953).
Foundation's Edge (1982).
Foundation and Earth (1986).

Numbers 1-5 are 'Robot' books; 6-8 are 'Galacticos Empire' books; 9-15 are Foundation series books.

Asimov's novels have influenced science fiction on television and movie. Especially his 'Three Laws of Robotics' is a lasting contribution to our thinking.

A robot may not injure a human being or, through inaction, allow a human being to come to harm.
A robot must obey any orders given to it by human beings, except where such orders would conflict with the First Law.
A robot must protect its own existence as long as such protection does not conflict with the First or Second Law.

Beliefs
Although ethnically a Jew, Asimov was an atheist:
"I am an atheist, out and out. It took me quite a long time to say it. I've been an atheist for years and years, but somehow ... it was better to say one was a humanist or an agnostic".

Death
When he had heart surgery in 1983, he received blood infected with HIV. He developed AIDS, and died of the effects of the medical condition in 1992. His widow did not speak of this until years later.

Welcome to our new chapter all about Active Learning! Have you ever heard that phrase before? It might sound like something simple - after all, we're always learning when we're active, right? But there's actually a lot more to it than meets the eye.

Imagine you're sitting in class, listening to your teacher talk about a new math concept. You could sit quietly, taking notes and trying to pay attention. Or, you could work together with your classmates to solve problems using that new concept. Which way do you think would help you learn better? If you chose the second option, then congratulations! You already understand one important aspect of active learning.

Active learning means doing things that help us truly understand what we're learning, rather than just hearing or reading about it. When we use active learning strategies, we're much more likely to remember what we learned, because we've had a chance to practice and apply it ourselves. This is especially true for subjects that some people find challenging, like science and math. By actively working through those concepts, instead of just passively listening to someone else explain them, we give ourselves a much better shot at really understanding them.

So what does active learning look like in action? There are tons of different ways to incorporate active learning into any classroom, but here are a few examples:

1. **Collaborative problem solving:** Instead of just having each student try to figure out a problem on their own, why not let them work together in small groups? They can bounce ideas off each other, share different perspectives, and even teach each other along the way. Plus, research shows that when we work collaboratively, we tend to feel more engaged and motivated to learn.
2. **Hands-on activities:** Sometimes the best way to learn is by getting hands-on experience! Whether it's building a model, conducting an experiment, or creating art, these types of activities allow us to explore concepts in a fun, interactive way. We also get to see how they connect to real life, which can make them seem less abstract and confusing.
3. **Gamification:** Who says learning has to be boring? Turning lessons into games can make them much more enjoyable and memorable. For example, maybe you create a scavenger hunt where students search for clues related to a particular topic, or design a quiz game that challenges teams to answer questions correctly within a certain time limit. These kinds of activities tap into our natural competitive instincts while still helping us learn valuable skills and information.
4. **Inquiry-based learning:** Rather than simply giving students answers, encourage them to ask their own questions and seek out solutions. This helps build critical thinking skills and encourages curiosity and exploration. Maybe you provide a prompt, such as "What makes a good leader?" Then, challenge students to come up with their own criteria and examples, supporting their arguments with evidence.

Now that you know a little bit more about active learning, I hope you'll start looking for ways to bring its principles into your own studies. Remember, learning shouldn't just be passive; it should be an active process that engages your mind and body. With the right tools and techniques, anyone can become a confident, curious learner!

EFL Cup
The EFL Cup, known for most of its history as the Football League Cup and also known in the past by several sponsored names, is a national association football competition in England, with a few clubs in Wales also playing. It is like the FA Cup, but has fewer teams, and starts and ends earlier in the season.

Unlike the FA Cup, which is open to hundreds of clubs belonging to The Football Association, which runs football in England, the EFL Cup is open only to the 92 teams in the top four divisions of English football - those playing in the top-level Premier League and the English Football League, which includes the next three lower divisions.

Chapter Title: Author Interview: William S. Burroughs

Imagine you could sit down with your favorite author and ask them anything you wanted! That's what we get to do today - sort of. We can't physically meet William S. Burroughs, but through his words and stories, we can learn more about him and his life experiences that shaped his work. So grab a notebook and pen because this will be like having a conversation with one of America's most fascinating authors!

First off, let's talk about names. Have you ever met someone who shares the same name as another family member? Well, our friend Bill did just that! To keep things clear between him and his famous grandfather, also named William S., he added the 'S.' before his last name. This stood for nothing special; it was simply there so people wouldn't confuse them. It might seem strange, but think about how confusing it would be if everyone thought your grandpa's latest book was actually written by YOU!

Now, picture this: A young boy growing up in a family full of interesting characters. On his mom's side, her dad was a Methodist preacher, while over on his dad's side, his pa ran an antique store filled with treasures waiting to tell their own tales. Imagine all those curious objects whispering secrets from days gone by - sounds pretty cool, right? Being surrounded by such diverse backgrounds must have given Bill lots of inspiration for his future writings.

As a teenager, Bill went to schools that offered unique learning environments. One of them, called the Los Alamos Ranch School in New Mexico, even inspired a popular movie series set in space camp (*wink wink* Hint hint: Star Wars fans!) While attending these schools, Bill explored different parts of himself, including discovering his feelings of being attracted to other boys. Although he understood his sexual orientation early on, he chose to hide it from others during his adult years. Can you imagine having something important about yourself that you feel scared to share with others? How do you think that affected his relationships and daily life?

After leaving Los Alamos due to some trouble involving pills, Bill wrapped up his high school education back home in St. Louis. Then came college time! Off he went to study at Harvard University starting in 1932. There, he dove deep into subjects like general semantics and medicine under a wise teacher named Alfred Korzybski. These topics taught him ways to look at language and information differently than most people. Pretty neat stuff!

And now, here we are, getting to know Bill better through reading about his life and imagining ourselves sitting beside him, asking questions. Even though he isn't around anymore, his works continue to inspire us and open doors to new worlds. Maybe someday soon, you too can create stories that touch others' lives just as deeply as Bill has done with his readers. Happy exploring!

Beneath the glowing stars, a young girl sat alone in her backyard. She looked up, dreaming of flying among the stars. "What if I could touch them?" she thought. She imagined a magic spaceship that could take her away. Her heart raced at the thought of exploring new worlds, where anything could happen.

One night, while she gazed at the sky, a small light appeared. It twinkled like a star but moved slowly. "Is that a spaceship?" she wondered, her eyes wide. Suddenly, the light landed in her yard, and a tiny door opened. A small creature stepped out, with big eyes and shiny wings. It smiled at her, as if it knew her dreams.

"Come with me!" the creature said in a soft voice. Together, they flew into the sky, leaving Earth behind. They danced around stars, explored colorful planets, and shared stories of their homes. As they traveled, the girl felt joy and peace. "I never want this to end," she thought, as they soared through the vast, magical universe.

Lesson 5.2: Understanding Linux and Package Managers
--------------------------------------------------

Today, we're going to learn about something really cool called *Linux* and its helpful friends known as *package managers*. Now don't get scared off by those big words just yet - I promise they aren't as complicated as they sound. By the end of our lesson, you'll have a good understanding of what these things are and why people use them. So let's dive right in!

What is Linux?

Imagine having your very own computer playground where you can build anything you want while being guided by clear rules that keep everything running smoothly. That's kind of like Linux! Developers created Linux back in the '90s because they wanted a reliable and flexible operating system. Think of an operating system like the boss of your computer who makes sure all the programs work together nicely. Some popular operating systems you might already know are Windows and macOS.

So what sets Linux apart? Well, one neat thing is that anyone can access and modify its code, making it open source. This means lots of creative minds contribute their skills to improve it constantly. Plus, since it was designed to be used across various devices, from tiny computers to huge mainframes, you can trust Linux to run efficiently and handle tons of tasks at once.

Why Use a Package Manager?

Now imagine building your dream house but realizing halfway through that you forgot some crucial tools. You could spend hours searching online for each tool individually, or you could go to a home improvement store and find someone who knows exactly what you need. Package managers are like that friendly expert! They save us time and energy when installing new software on our Linux systems.

There are several package managers out there, such as `apt`, `yum`, and `zypper`. Each one helps manage packages (software) differently depending on the specific distribution (type) of Linux being used. For example, say you'd like to add a fun drawing program to your Linux computer. Instead of downloading files, finding dependencies (supporting pieces), and hoping nothing breaks along the way, you simply ask your package manager to fetch the drawing application and any additional bits required. Just like magic, your wish appears within seconds!

Hands-On Activity: Using a Package Manager

Let's try using a package manager ourselves! Since most schools won't allow us to install actual software on their computers, I made a pretend version instead. Follow these steps:

1. Imagine we've logged into our super cool Linux machine. To start working with our package manager, we first need to launch it. Type "fancy_pm" in the terminal and press Enter. Our imaginary package manager comes alive!
2. Let's look around before adding new applications. We can list currently installed packages by typing "list\_installed" and pressing Enter. Oh wow, look at all those amazing programs!
3. Time to install a brand new game! Simply type "install\_package space\_shooter" and hit Enter. After a few moments, our shiny new spaceship shooting game will appear in the list of installed packages.
4. Sometimes, we change our minds about certain programs. No worries - uninstalling is just as easy. Just type "remove\_package space\_shooter" and watch as it disappears from the installed list.

That wasn't too hard, right? With practice, you'll become more confident navigating real-world package managers and customizing your Linux experience. Happy exploring!

Welcome to our lesson about design and animated gifs! Have you ever heard of clip art? Clip art are pictures that artists create and then share online so that people like us can use them in projects. They're kind of like digital stickers! Today we'll learn all about how to find and use clip art, as well as how to turn those still images into fun animations called animated gifs.

Let's start by talking about where to find clip art. There are many websites out there that offer free clip art images for anyone to use. Some popular ones are Freepik, PNG Tree, and Openclipart. When looking for clip art, try searching for specific things you might want to add to your project, such as "cell phone" or "holiday." These sites will show you lots of different options to choose from. Just remember to always check if the site requires credit to the artist before using their work.

Now that you know where to look for clip art, let's talk about how to actually use it. Most websites will allow you to download the image right onto your computer. Once you have the picture saved, you can open up a program like Microsoft Word or PowerPoint and insert the clip art into your document. From there, you can resize it, move it around, and even change its color to fit your needs.

But why stop at just still images? Let's take it one step further and create an animated gif! Animated gifs are moving images made up of multiple frames played quickly in sequence. To create an animated gif, first find several clip art images that tell a story or show movement when put together. For example, you could use a series of images showing someone drawing a picture, starting with a blank page and ending with a finished piece of artwork.

Once you have your images ready, you'll need to use a special tool to combine them into one file. There are many tools available online, some free and others paid. A few popular choices are Ezgif, Giphy, and Adobe Photoshop (this last one does require payment). Simply follow the instructions provided by whichever tool you choose, and soon you'll have your own custom animated gif!

So now you know how to find and use clip art, as well as turn those images into awesome animated gifs. Get creative and see what cool projects you can come up with! Remember to always give proper credit to any artists whose work you use, and most importantly - have fun exploring the world of design!

Beside the river, a boy watched the water flow. The leaves were turning gold and brown, whispering secrets to the wind. It was autumn, a time for change and harvest. The boy loved this season. His family had a special tradition: a festival by the river to celebrate the year's work.

Every year, they made lanterns from pumpkins. The boy's father would carve faces into the orange skin. The boy helped, his small hands feeling the smooth flesh inside. Each lantern became a smile that would light up the night. The boy could hardly wait for the festival to begin.

As the sun set, the family gathered by the river. They placed the lanterns in the water, watching them float. The river sparkled like stars, and the boy felt magic in the air. Each lantern was a wish, a hope for the future. The boy thought about what he would wish for.

With friends and family around him, the boy felt happiness in his heart. They sang songs and told stories of the past. Each story was like a thread, weaving their lives together. The river became a mirror of their lives, flowing and changing, but always moving forward.

As night fell, the lanterns glowed brighter. They danced on the water, casting shadows on the trees. The boy laughed, feeling the joy of being together. The festival was not just about lanterns; it was a time to remember and celebrate life. The river flowed on, just like their stories.

As autumn faded, the boy felt a hint of sadness. But he also felt hope for what was to come. The lanterns would return next year, just like the seasons. The boy understood that every change brought new beauty. The festival was a promise that life would continue to flow.

With the last lantern flickering in the distance, the boy felt a warmth inside. He knew that traditions would always keep them together. They were like the river, strong and true. Each year, they would gather, sharing laughter and love. And the lanterns would light the way home.

Self-esteem is like your own personal cheerleader! It's how much you value and appreciate yourself. During adolescence, self-esteem can really affect how you feel about growing up, making friends, and doing well in school. A strong sense of self-esteem helps you believe in yourself and try new things. So let's learn more about it and discover ways to boost our confidence!

Imagine you just finished a fantastic drawing that you're super proud of. When someone compliments you on it, you think, "Wow, I did a great job!" That feeling inside is what we call high self-esteem. But sometimes, when people criticize our work, even if it's constructive criticism, we might focus only on the negative parts instead of celebrating our achievements. Building self-esteem means learning to see ourselves in a positive light and appreciating all the amazing qualities we possess.

Now, why does developing self-esteem matter? Well, imagine standing in front of a crowd giving a presentation. If you have high self-esteem, you would likely feel excited and confident, ready to share your thoughts. On the flip side, if your self-esteem isn't so robust, you might feel anxious or scared, which could prevent you from performing your best. By working on our self-esteem, we become braver, happier, and more resilient - ready to face any challenge that comes our way!

Here are some simple strategies to help build self-esteem:

1. **Positive Affirmations:** These are kind words or phrases that you repeat to yourself. For example, saying "I am creative," "I am smart," or "I am worthy" every day will help reinforce those beliefs in your mind. You can write them down and post sticky notes around your room, or say them aloud whenever you need a little boost.
2. **Set Small Goals:** Accomplishing small goals gives us feelings of pride and achievement. Try setting daily or weekly objectives, like reading a chapter in a book, practicing a musical instrument, or helping out around the house. Once you meet these goals, celebrate your success!
3. **Practice Kindness:** Being nice to others makes us feel good about ourselves too! Compliment a friend, assist a classmate who needs help, or volunteer in your community. Helping others strengthens connections and contributes to higher self-esteem.
4. **Embrace Mistakes:** Nobody's perfect! We all mess up sometimes, but mistakes are opportunities to learn and grow. Instead of getting upset when something goes wrong, take a deep breath and ask yourself, "What can I do differently next time?" This attitude will help develop resiliency and increase self-confidence.

As teenagers, having healthy self-esteem sets the foundation for becoming happy, successful adults. With practice, patience, and positivity, you can unlock your true potential and enjoy this incredible journey called life!

Esperanto
Esperanto's grammar (rules of language) is meant to be simple. The rules in Esperanto never change and can always be applied in the same way

Alphabet

The Esperanto alphabet is based on the Latin script. It has six letters with diacritics: , , , ,  (with circumflex), and  (with breve). The alphabet does not have the letters q, w, x, or y.

The 28-letter alphabet is:

A is like a in father
B is like b in boy
C is like zz in pizza
 is like ch in chair
D is like d in dog
E is like e in egg
F is like f in flower
G is like g in go
 is like j in jam
H is like h in honey
 is like ch in Scottish loch
I is like i in it
J is like y in yes
 is like s in measure
K is like k in king
L is like l in look
M is like m in man
N is like n in no
O is like o in open
P is like p in pie
R is like r in road but is rolled (trilled, as in Spanish, Italian, Arabic, Russian)
S is like s in simple
 is like sh in sheep
T is like t in tree
U is like u in bull
 is like w in well
V is like v in cave
Z is like s in his.

Writing diacritics
Even though the world uses Unicode, the letters with diacritics (found in the "Latin-Extended A" section of the Unicode Standard) can cause problems with printing and computing, because they are not found on the keyboards we use.

There are two remedies of this problem, both of which use digraphs for the letters with diacritics. Zamenhof, the inventor of Esperanto, devised an "h-system", which replaces , , , , , and  with ch, gh, hh, jh, sh, and u, respectively. A more recent "x-system" has also been used, which replaces , , , , , and  with cx, gx, hx, jx, sx, and ux, respectively.

There are computer keyboards that support the Esperanto alphabet, for example, for Microsoft Windows, Mac OS X, and Linux, for Windows Phone, and Gboard & AnySoftKeyboard for Android.

Thessaloniki
Thessaloniki is the second-largest city in Greece after Athens. There were 325,182 people at the census of 2011. Including the suburbs, there were 1,110,312 people. It is in the region of Macedonia in northern Greece. It is the capital of the Thessaloniki prefecture and it is the capital of the periphery of central Macedonia. It is the largest city in the geographical region of Macedonia. It has a humid subtropical climate (Cfa in the Kppen climate classification). The average rainfall is relatively low, due to the rain shadow from the Pindos mountains. Unlike in Athens, there are frequent frosts and snow every winter.

History

Thessaloniki was established by King Cassander of Macedon, friend of Alexander the Great in the fourth century B.C. He named the city after the sister of Alexander the Great, princess Thessalonike, which in Greek means victory over Thessaly.

From late antiquity to the late Middle Ages (330AD-1430AD) it was the second most important city of Byzantine Empire. Then Thessaloniki faced many invasions from enemies such as the Avaroi, Bulgars and others. In the year 1204, the crusaders conquered Thessaloniki and created the Kingdom of Thessalonica. Later it was liberated by Byzantines and then sold to the Republic of Venice but the year 1430, it was conquered by the Ottoman Empire.

Thessaloniki was a part of Ottoman Empire for approximately 500 years and in 1912 it became part of Greece when Greece acquired Macedonia following the Balkan Wars. Many famous people have lived or were born here, such as the Roman statesman and philosopher Cicero, many saints like Cyril and Methodius, who invented the Cyrillic alphabet, and Saint Demetrius, who is the patron saint of the city, and many politicians, such as the founder of modern-day Turkey, Mustafa Kemal Atatrk. Most of the city was completely destroyed in a large fire in 1917 and was rebuilt in the 1920s. Thessaloniki was place to both the Salonica and Macedonian fronts during World War 1, this fronts were made of French, Serbian, English, Italian, and a Russian division. This fronts were key in 1918 to the Entente victory over both Bulgaria and Austria. It was later occupied by Nazi Germany during the Second World War, during the Greek Invasion.

Sights of Thessaloniki

Thessaloniki has many sights. The most famous sight in Thessaloniki is the white tower. The White tower was a part of Thessaloniki's ancient walls that were built many times through the ages. Thessaloniki was the second-most well-fortified city in the Byzantine Empire, after Constantinople (Istanbul). The walls can still be seen above the city today and despite the many earthquakes, they are still standing. The city was home to a Roman imperial palace and mausoleum. The palace ruins can be seen today but the mausoleum together with a Roman arch can be still seen standing today. Very important sights of Thessaloniki are the medieval churches such as Agios Dimitrios, Agios Georgios and Agia Sofia. Agios Dimitrios it the largest and oldest Basilica in Greece. Thessaloniki's Christian monuments are part of the UNESCO World Heritage initiative. The city also has many Ottoman monuments, such as the Bey Hammam and the old district of the city near the walls, with its distinctly Turkish architecture. Many museums are in the city and some of them are: Archaeological Museum of Thessaloniki, Museum of the Macedonian Struggle, Jewish Museum, Ethnological Museum of Macedonia and others.


MTR
The future

MTR Corporation Limited has suggested several future projects to the Hong Kong Government, with some already being built. The network is also set to grow quite much when MTR Corporation Limited joins with the government-owned Kowloon-Canton Railway Corporation (KCRC), with the non-binding "Memorandum of Understanding" agreement signed on 11 April 2006 to give MTR Corporation control of the KCR network for 50 years. The new Sha Tin to Central Link that was first given to KCRC would now also be run by MTR Corporation Limited, which will run from Tai Wai Station in Tai Wai to Central.

It has also been suggested to improve parts of MTR that are running now. Airport Station on the Airport Express will have a new platform to serve passengers flying out of Hong Kong International Airport's Skyplaza. New subway links to the stations are also being made, and it has been proposed to lengthen the Tseung Kwan O Line with a branch line to Tseung Kwan O South, and the Kwun Tong Line as far as Whampoa Garden, also linking with the Sha Tin to Central Link expansion.

The West Island Line and South Island Line, first suggested to the government by MTR on 21 January 2003, was finally accepted on 30 June 2005. It was made up of the West Island Line that took the Island Line to Kennedy Town, and the South Island Line (East section) from Admiralty to Ap Lei Chau and South Island Line (West section) that connects the other two lines. This is being talked about now and the whole longer line should be finished and running by 2012.

Welcome to our journey through ancient Greek thought! Today we're going to meet two interesting characters from one of the most famous philosophical texts ever written - Plato's "The Republic". Their names are Socrates and Thrasymachus.

Imagine you're sitting in a circle with your friends, listening to Socrates talk about justice. He thinks it's always better to be fair and just because it leads to happiness in the long run. Suddenly, someone barges into the group, angry and loud. This is Thrasymachus!

Thrasymachus doesn't believe that being just is important at all. Instead, he says, "Might makes right!" To him, whoever has power gets to decide what's true or false, right or wrong. If they want something, they take it, regardless of whether it hurts others or not. He even claims that laws are just tools used by those in charge to keep their grip on power and control over everyone else.

Now imagine if this happened during recess at school. What would happen if the biggest bully decided that they could break any rule they wanted because they were stronger? That wouldn't be fair, would it? It turns out that adults back then didn't think it was fair either!

Socrates steps up to challenge Thrasymachus. Over time, he convinces Thrasymachus that there are flaws in his thinking. Being unfair may give temporary benefits, but eventually, people get caught, lose friends, and feel bad inside. Justice, according to Socrates, brings harmony between individuals and within society. Laws protect us and ensure things remain balanced.

But here's where it gets really fascinating... A philosopher named Leo Strauss believed that Thrasymachus wasn't completely wrong. Even though Socrates won the argument, Strauss felt that Thrasymachus still had valuable insights. Sometimes, powerful people can misuse their influence and bend rules. So, we need to stay critical and question authority when necessary.

In conclusion, meeting Socrates and Thrasymachus gives us a glimpse into some big questions about power, fairness, and morality. Remember, these debates started thousands of years ago, yet they continue to shape our discussions today. By understanding them, we become smarter and more responsible citizens - ready to build a better tomorrow!

European Court of Human Rights
The European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) hears and decides particular type of complaints. These complaints relate to abuse of human rights. ECoHR's other popular name is "Strasbourg Court". Member countries of the Council of Europe created ECoHR to arrange all such complaints, listen to the complaints, and to give decisions. European Convention on Human Rights tells about many human rights. ECoHR sees that people should enjoy all these human rights.

ECoHR' has a number of judges. The number of judges is seven normally but at the case of dealing a great issue, the number will be 21 and the judges are equally from member countries of the Council of Europe. At present, there are forty seven member countries of the Council of Europe. Each country may have one judge in the ECoHR. But, judges work independently for the ECoHR, and not for their country.
