Copyright
Copyright is a law that gives the owner of a work (for example, a book, movie, picture, song or website) the right to say how other people can use it. Copyright laws make it easier for authors to make money by selling their works. It is one part of a group of laws about intellectual property (the others being trademark and patent law). It helps protect authors from other people copying their works without permission and/or for commercial purposes.

With copyright, a work can only be copied if the owner gives permission. If someone copies a work without permission, the owner can say they infringed their copyright. When this happens, the owner may sue for the amount that should have been paid. Most cases are handled by civil law. In more serious cases, a person who copies a work that is protected under copyright could be arrested, fined or even go to prison. Commonly, the copyright law will protect the authors and their heirs for 50 to 100 years since the author's death, or the first day of multiple authors' deaths.

Many countries have modified their copyright law to meet international standards. However, there are still differences in national laws. In some countries, someone violating copyright law will be sued only to the civil law courts but other countries they can also be charged by criminal courts.

History of
Copyright was originally made in the 18th century for books. Before printing presses were made, books could only be copied by hand, which would take time. But when printing presses were made, books could be copied faster and easier. Because of this, some books were copied by people who did not own the book themselves. So lawmakers gave only owners the right to copy. National laws were somewhat standardized by international treaties.

Because technology got better over time, copyright began to cover other types of media such as pictures, sound, and film. Commonly, copyright violation warning would be shown at the beginning of the media to warn audiences against violating copyright law.

Who owns copyright?

In most countries, authors automatically own the copyright to any work they make or create, as long as they do not give the copyright to someone else.

In most countries, there is no need to register the copyright, and some countries do not even have procedures to register copyrights. But, where registration is available, many authors register anyway, especially for works that are sold for money. That is because registration helps to prove that the copyright of a work belongs to a certain author.

If an author gets paid to make a work for someone else, the person who pays for making the work (for example, the author's employer) will often get to own the copyright instead of the author themselves. For example, if a person working for a company, Microsoft creates a new computer software program at work, the Microsoft company would own the copyright. It is very common that the company will instead register the copyright to avoid their employees from claiming their works.

Length of copyright protection

Now that we have introduced the concept of slope and how it relates to lines on the coordinate plane, let's learn how to graph a line when given a point and its slope. This skill will allow us to take the concepts we learned in the previous chapters and apply them in new ways.

First, let's review what slope means. The slope of a line is a measure of how steep it is and can be calculated as the change in y over the change in x (denoted as y/x). A positive slope indicates that the line rises from left to right, while a negative slope indicates that the line falls from left to right. When graphing a line given a point and its slope, we can use this information to determine where the line should go.

Let's start with an example. Suppose we want to graph the line that passes through the point (-3,5) and has a slope of 2. To do this, we first plot the point (-3,5) on the coordinate plane. Next, we need to find another point on the line. Since we know the slope, we can use it to find a second point by moving along the line in the direction indicated by the slope. In this case, since the slope is positive, we move up one unit and to the right two units (since the slope is 2), which places us at the point (1,7). We then connect these two points with a straight line, giving us the graph of our line.

But how did we know to move up one unit and to the right two units? Let's consider the definition of slope again: y/x. If we start at the point (-3,5) and move to the point (1,7), our change in x (x) is equal to 4 (1-(-3)), and our change in y (y) is equal to 2 (7-5). Therefore, our slope is 2/4 = 0.5. However, recall that the slope tells us how much the line rises or falls for every unit it moves horizontally. So instead of using the actual values of x and y, we can simplify the calculation by choosing any convenient value for x (or y) and solving for the other variable. In this case, we chose x=4 because it makes the calculation easier (we could also choose y=2 and solve for x). But no matter what value we choose for x (or y), the resulting slope will always be the same.

Now let's try a slightly more complicated example. Suppose we want to graph the line that passes through the point (2,-6) and has a slope of -1/3. First, we plot the point (2,-6) on the coordinate plane. Then, to find a second point on the line, we move down one unit (because the slope is negative) and to the right three units (the reciprocal of 1/3) from the initial point. This gives us the point (5,-7). We then connect these two points with a straight line, giving us the graph of our line.

Manhattan
Between World War I and World War II, reformist Fiorello La Guardia was elected as the new mayor in 1933 and took office in 1934, marking the fall of Tammany Hall after 80 years of dominating politics in New York City. Once the city's demographics were steadier, labor unionization provided protection and affluence to the working class. Despite the Great Depression, some of the world's tallest skyscrapers of the time were built in Manhattan during the 1930s, including many Art Deco masterpieces that are still part of the city's skyline today. The most well-known structures are Empire State Building, the Chrysler Building, and the GE Building.

Following the end of World War II, a lot of veterans came home to the United States. This led to the development of private communities that were intended to be sold or rented out to returning soldiers, resulting in an economic boom. An example of one of the communities built to attract veterans looking for homes is Stuyvesant Town - Peter Cooper Village, which opened in 1947. In 1951, the United Nations relocated from its first headquarters in Queens, to the East Side of Manhattan.

Population and industry began to decline in the 1960s. The Stonewall riots were a series of violent demonstrations by members of the gay community. By the 1970s, the city had gained a reputation as a graffiti-covered, crime-ridden relic of history. In 1975, the city government went bankrupt (ran out of money), and its pleas for financial help were rejected at first. On 30 October 1975, the New York Daily News reported the event with the headline as "Ford to City: Drop Dead". The city received a federal loan and debt restructuring. After the economic downfall and recovery, New York State kept a close watch on New York City's economy.

In the 1980s, Wall Street was revived from its slump, and the city reclaimed its role at the center of the worldwide financial industry. During this time, Manhattan was also at the heart of the AIDS crisis, with Greenwich Village being a major center of the epidemic. Gay Men's Health Crisis (GMHC) and AIDS Coalition to Unleash Power (ACT UP) were organizations that were started because of the crisis Their purpose was to advocate on behalf of those AIDs victims.

Crime rates began to drop greatly in the 1990s. Murder rates were 537 in 2008 compared to 2,245 in 1990. The crack epidemic and its associated drug-related violence had died down, and was under great control by the city. Many people who had moved out of the city came back because the city once again became the destination of immigrants from around the world, joining with low interest rates and Wall Street bonuses to fuel the growth of the real estate market.

Welcome to our newest chapter all about Active Recall! You might be wondering, what exactly is active recall? Well, imagine you're trying to remember the capital cities of different countries. Instead of simply reading them over and over again, you challenge yourself by writing down each answer without looking. When you test your own memory like this, that's called active recall!

Now, why is active recall so important when studying? Think about it - if you want to build muscles, you need to exercise regularly, right? Your brain works similarly! By practicing active recall consistently, you help strengthen your memory and retain information better.

Let me share a fun example to illustrate this concept further. Imagine you have a big test on famous artists and their paintings. Rather than passively rereading your notes, try using active recall techniques instead:

1. Create flashcards: Write the name of an artist on one side and the titles of some of their significant artworks on the other. Test yourself by only looking at the artist's name and seeing if you can remember their paintings.
2. Quiz games: Gather friends who are also studying the same topic. Take turns asking questions like "Who painted the Mona Lisa?" or "What's Vincent van Gogh known for?" This will not only reinforce your knowledge but also turn studying into an enjoyable activity!
3. Teach someone else: One of the best ways to ensure you understand something fully is by teaching it to someone else. Explain the key points about various artists and their work to a family member or friend. If they ask thoughtful questions, even better! Their curiosity will push you to dig deeper into the subject matter.

By incorporating these strategies into your study routine, you'll find that actively recalling information becomes second nature. And don't worry if you get things wrong initially; everyone makes mistakes while learning! Remember, every time you practice active recall, you're giving your brain a good workout and building those mental muscles. Happy studying!

Program
The term Program can be used in many ways.

A program or programme can be a plan of how to do something. It tells the steps that we think we need to do to make something happen. For example, a government might make a program to improve the health of the people in part of a country by giving the people better food, by helping to kill insects that carry diseases, and by bringing more doctors.

an event program is a thing that lists the what will happen during an event such as an opera or auction.

Legalism
Legalism was one of the four main philosophies in Chinese history during the Warring States Period. It is a political philosophy which says that people are bad by nature and need to be controlled by the government. It was introduced by Qin Shi Huang.

One of the most important contributors to Legalism was Han Fei (). He said that a ruler must use following tools to govern a state:
Fa (; literally "law or principle"): The law must be known by everyone. Everybody under the ruler is equal before the law. If you do what law wants you will be rewarded. If you break the law or try to break it, you will be punished.
Shu (; literally "method, tactic or art"): These are methods the ruler has to use so that nobody is able to abolish the system.
Shi (; literally "legitimacy, power or charisma"): The position of the ruler is important, not the ruler himself.

Chapter 6: Code Breaking and Espionage

Have you ever wanted to send a secret message to your best friend that only they could read? Or maybe you've wondered how spies communicate with each other without getting caught. Welcome to the fascinating world of code breaking!

In simple terms, code breaking is figuring out hidden messages or secrets. People have been sending coded messages since ancient times. During wars, armies would use codes to keep their plans confidential. Today, we still use codes to protect sensitive information, especially in espionage (spy work).

Imagine being a spy during World War II. You need to get important information about enemy plans back to your country, but you can't let anyone else see it. So, you create a secret message using a special code. To decode the message, someone needs to figure out what letters or numbers represent which words or ideas. That's where code breakers come in!

Let's try making our own simple code:

1. Write down the alphabet A-Z in two rows.
2. Underneath each letter, write its opposite - Z-A. For example, A goes under Z, B goes under Y, C goes under X, etc.
3. Now, choose a word or phrase you want to encode. Let's pick "CODEBREAKING."
4. Replace every letter in your chosen word or phrase with the corresponding letter underneath it from step 2. Using our chart, CODEBREAKING becomes SVOXWDULHOD.
5. Share your encoded message with a friend and challenge them to crack the code!

Now imagine having to decipher something much more complicated than SVOXWDULHOD! Real spies often used complex systems involving multiple layers of encoding. Sometimes, they even changed these systems daily to make sure their secrets stayed safe.

But what happens when those secrets aren't so secure anymore? What if another country starts reading your top-secret messages? This leads us to one of history's most famous codebreakers: Alan Turing.

During World War II, Britain faced Germany's unbreakable Enigma code machine. Thousands of lives depended on finding a way to crack it. Enter Alan Turing, a brilliant mathematician who built a machine called the Bombe. It helped him solve the Enigma code, giving Allied forces crucial advantages in battles across Europe. Without his contributions, the outcome of WWII might have been very different.

Of course, sometimes countries admit to hacking others' computers instead of relying solely on codebreaking. Hacking means accessing someone else's electronic data without permission. Governments may do this for various reasons - including catching spies or stealing military secrets. However, hacking can lead to international incidents, causing tension between nations.

So next time you think sending secret messages is all fun and games, remember that real spies around the globe risk their lives doing just that! Whether through old-fashioned code books or cutting-edge technology, the art of code breaking continues to play a vital role in protecting national security.

Penalty
A penalty is most often a punishment, and may also mean:
in law:
Sentence (law), for example the death penalty
Sanctions (law), a punishment for violating rules of procedure, or for abusing the judicial process.
in sports:
getting a Penalty (American football) gets a punishment for your team's rule infraction
getting a Penalty kick (football)/(soccer) gets a "reward" for the other team's rule infraction, or refers to the tiebreak procedure where there has been no rule infraction, and there is neither a punishment nor a reward. See also Penalty area.
in Contract Bridge and other card games a penalty can be both an "intra-game" scoring bonus which is not associated with any rule infraction, or an "extra-game" punishment for a rule infraction such as a "revoke".
Penalty (ice hockey). See also Penalty box.
Penalty (rugby)
Penalty (Brazilian sports manufacturer)
in other sports or games, penalties may be referred to as fouls or faults
in finance and banking:
a payment forfeited for an early withdrawal from an account or an investment
Tax penalty, a fee required for missing a deadline or some other violation.
In entertainment:
The Penalty, a film.

Even and Odd Numbers

Have you ever noticed that some numbers seem to come in pairs, while others always stand alone? In this lesson, we will explore the properties of even and odd numbers and learn how to recognize them.

An even number is any integer that can be divided by 2 with no remainder. This means that when an even number is divided by 2, the result is always a whole number. Some examples of even numbers are -4, 0, 6, and 10. Notice that these numbers all end in either 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8. This is because any number that ends in one of those digits can be divided by 2 with no remainder.

On the other hand, an odd number is any integer that cannot be divided by 2 with no remainder. When an odd number is divided by 2, there is always a remainder of 1. Examples of odd numbers include -5, 1, 7, and 9. These numbers do not end in 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8. Instead, they end in 1, 3, 5, 7, or 9.

One way to determine whether a number is even or odd is to look at its last digit. If the last digit is 0, 2, 4, 6, or 8, then the number is even. If the last digit is 1, 3, 5, 7, or 9, then the number is odd. Let's try a few examples:

* Is 27 an even or odd number? The last digit is 7, which means it is an odd number.
* Is -42 an even or odd number? The last digit is 2, so it is an even number.
* Is 3,568,921 an even or odd number? The last digit is 1, so it is an odd number.

Now let's practice finding the sum of several even and odd numbers:

* Find the sum of 8 + 12 + 16. All three numbers are even, so their sum will also be even. To find the sum, add 8 + 12 = 20, then add 20 + 16 = 36. Therefore, the sum of 8 + 12 + 16 is 36.
* Find the sum of 15 + 33 + 41. Two of the numbers (15 and 41) are odd, while one number (33) is even. Since the even number is paired with an odd number, their sum will be odd. First, add 15 + 33 = 48, then add 48 + 41 = 89. Therefore, the sum of 15 + 33 + 41 is 89.

Let's take our understanding of even and odd numbers one step further by exploring multiplication. An interesting property of even and odd numbers is that the product of two even numbers is always even, the product of two odd numbers is always odd, and the product of an even number and an odd number is always even. Here are some examples to illustrate this point:

* Even \* Even = Even: 4 \* 6 = 24
* Odd \* Odd = Odd: 3 \* 5 = 15
* Even \* Odd = Even: 6 \* 3 = 18

This property holds true regardless of the size of the numbers being multiplied. It is important to note, however, that the converse is not necessarily true. Just because a number is even does not mean both factors are even, and just because a number is odd does not mean both factors are odd.

Making better furniture? A good way to make furniture look nicer is by having fewer joints and lines where glue is used. When the wood follows the curve, it looks better. Cheaper wood furniture uses wood from small boards glued together, or short pieces with many end joints to make curves. But a shiny finish can crack at these joints. When we stick pieces of wood together, they can sometimes have different colors that make them look like a zebra's stripes. This is often called "flip". Flip can happen when we look at the wood from different sides. This can be tricky to hide because it happens when the light hits the wood at different angles. When we bend wood using steam, we only see two sides of the wood.

Let's talk about sizes. When we say how big something is, we always say it in the same way. We say the length, then the width, then the thickness. So, if we were talking about a table, we would first say how long it is, then how wide it is, then how thick it is.

We also use some letters to talk about different shapes. Some shapes look like the letter we use to describe them. Other times, the letter is the first letter of the word that describes the shape or how we made it.

For example, "radius bends" are shapes that are the same on both sides and always curve the same amount. These are often used for the edges of round tables and sometimes parts of chairs. Let's learn about shapes! Circles are round like a pizza. If you slice the pizza, each piece has a skinny end in the middle and a fat end on the outside. We call the skinny end a radius. Sometimes, the radius is small and the pizza is small. Other times, the radius is big and the pizza is big. The bigger the radius, the flatter the pizza piece.

Now, let's imagine a chair. The top of some chairs have a curve, but it's not a perfect circle. It's more like a squished circle or an egg shape. It's the same with some tables, they're not round but more like an egg shape.

And then there's another shape. It's a bit like a chair leg. It's not perfectly round and doesn't have straight ends. It can move left or right.

Lastly, let's look at a hook shape. It's straight on one side, like a stick, but has a hook on the other side, like a candy cane. This shape doesn't move a lot. It can also move left or right.
There are different shapes we can make by bending things. One of them looks like the letter U. It has two straight parts and a curved part in the middle. Some parts of a chair, like the arms, can have this shape. If the curve is more than half a circle, the parts want to stick to what we use to make the shape.

Another shape looks like the letter V. It has two straight parts with a bend in the middle. These straight parts can be long or short.

Sometimes, we get a shape that is like a very sharp curve with long straight parts. This shape can move a bit.

There's also a shape that's made of two V or J shapes put together. It doesn't look like the letter W, but we call it a W bend. This shape is hard to make because it needs to be just right. Some benches have this shape.

Our journey begins in the land of Everyday Stories. Writers often tell stories about themselves, their friends, or things they see around them. To make these stories interesting, writers use different types of tools.

For example, imagine your best friend, Timmy Tiger, wants to write a story about sharing his favorite toy car with Sally Snake. He uses descriptive words to help paint a picture in the reader's mind. Words like "shiny," "red," and "fast." These are called description tools.

Next, we visit Argument Alley, where writers try to persuade their audience to believe something or do something. They might say, "Eating healthy food helps you grow big and strong!" This statement has two parts - one gives a reason ("eating healthy food") and the other explains why it's important ("helps you grow big and strong"). Together, they form a powerful tool called reasoning.

As we continue our tour, we encounter Emotion Expressway. When writers want to connect emotionally with their readers, they use emotion tools. Imagine Billy Bunny writes a sad poem after losing his beloved balloon. By using words that evoke feelings of loss, loneliness, and nostalgia, he creates a connection with his readers.

Lastly, we arrive at Evidence Mountain. Writers climb up high to gather evidence that supports their ideas. If Daisy Dolphin is writing a report about her underwater adventures, she can collect facts from scientists about ocean life. Using solid evidence makes her writing more valid and trustworthy.

And now, my little adventurers, comes the most exciting part - putting it all together! Just as you mix colors to create beautiful art, writers combine various rhetorical strategies to produce captivating pieces of work. With practice, YOU too can become skilled analysts, able to identify the tools used by writers and determine if their writing is both valid and effective.

Thank you for joining me today on this wonderful excursion into Writing Land! Remember, the magic lies within each word, phrase, and sentence. Happy exploring!

Welcome to our course unit about Rebalancing and Tax Efficiency! You might be wondering what those terms mean and why they're important. Let's dive right into it!

Imagine you have some money set aside for your future goals, like buying a new video game console or saving up for college. To help your money grow, you decide to put it in different places called investments. These could be things like stocks, bonds, or even real estate. Now, how do you keep track of these investments? How would you know if one investment is doing better than another? And what can you do to make sure all your investments work well together as a team? That's where rebalancing comes in!

Rebalancing is when you adjust your mix of investments so that everything stays fair and balanced, just like in a seesaw. Think of each type of investment as a kid sitting on a seesaw. Some kids may weigh more (like having more money), causing them to go higher while others stay lower. By redistributing the weights, we ensure everyone gets their turn on the top - maintaining balance. Similarly, by periodically checking your investments, you can sell parts that grew too much and buy ones that didn't perform as well. This way, you maintain your original desired mix of investments, which helps reduce risk.

Now let's talk about something magical called tax efficiency. Imagine being able to save more money without paying extra fees or charges. Sounds great, right? Well, there are special types of investment accounts known as Traditional IRA and Roth IRA that allow you to do just that! They give you two main benefits: either letting your money grow without worrying about taxes now (Traditional IRA) or allowing you to take out money tax-free during retirement (Roth IRA).

Let me explain using ice cream! Picture yourself earning $100 this week, and you want to buy as many yummy ice creams as possible. But wait, the store wants to charge you taxes on every dollar you earn, leaving you with less cash to splash on scoops. With a Traditional IRA account, you can tell the government, "Hold on! Don't take my taxes yet; let me buy those ice creams first!" So you put your whole $100 into the account, and once you retire, you pay the taxes then. Cool, huh?

But maybe you think, "I don't want to pay any taxes at all!" Then say hello to the Roth IRA! Using our ice cream example again, imagine working hard and still ending up with only $80 because taxes took away some of your money. However, since you used a Roth IRA, instead of getting fewer ice creams today, you get MORE ice creams later! When you finally retire, you can enjoy your tasty treats TAX-FREE! Yay!

In summary, rebalancing makes sure all your investments play nicely together, keeping risks under control. Meanwhile, tax-efficient accounts like Traditional and Roth IRAs help stretch your money further by minimizing taxes along the way. Understanding concepts like these will surely come in handy someday when managing your own finances and securing a bright future ahead!

Welcome to Unit 4, Lesson 1: Three Digit Addition Word Problems! In this lesson, we will build upon our previous knowledge of addition and estimation by applying these skills to real-world word problems involving three-digit numbers. This will help us develop a deeper understanding of how addition can be used to solve various types of problems. So let's get started!

Example 1: A baker has 327 cupcakes to sell at a fair. She also brings 149 cookies to sell. How many treats does she bring in total?

To solve this problem, we need to find the sum of the number of cupcakes and cookies. We know that:
Cupcakes = 327
Cookies = 149
Total Treats = Cupcakes + Cookies
= 327 + 149
= 476
The baker brings a total of 476 treats to the fair.

Example 2: A store sold 297 books last week and 389 books this week. What was the total number of books sold over both weeks?

In this problem, we need to find the sum of the number of books sold during each week. We know that:
Books Sold Last Week = 297
Books Sold This Week = 389
Total Books Sold = Books Sold Last Week + Books Sold This Week
= 297 + 389
= 686
The store sold a total of 686 books over both weeks.

Example 3: A farmer harvested 127 bushels of corn from Field A and 348 bushels of corn from Field B. He then combined all the corn from both fields into one large bin. How many bushels of corn did he put into the bin?

Once again, we need to find the sum of the number of bushels of corn from each field. We know that:
Bushels From Field A = 127
Bushels From Field B = 348
Total Bushels Of Corn = Bushels From Field A + Bushels From Field B
= 127 + 348
= 475
The farmer put a total of 475 bushels of corn into his bin.

Example 4: A company produced 156 units of Product X in January and 318 units of Product Y in February. They then packaged all the products together in boxes. If each box holds up to 100 units, how many boxes did they fill?

This time, we need to find out how many boxes were filled when packaging all the units of Products X and Y. First, let's find the total number of units:
Units Produced = Units of Product X + Units of Product Y
= 156 + 318
= 474
Since each box holds up to 100 units, we divide the total number of units by 100 to determine the number of boxes needed:
Number of Boxes = Total Number of Units / Units per Box
= 474 / 100
= 4.74
Since we cannot fit a fraction of a unit into a single box, we round up to the next whole number to ensure that all units are accounted for:
Number of Boxes = 5
So, the company filled a total of 5 boxes when packaging all their products.

Now it's your turn! Try solving some practice problems using what you learned about three-digit addition word problems. Remember to break down the problem carefully and identify the information given before finding the solution step by step. Good luck!

Asuka loved to gaze up at the stars every night. They were always shining brightly, no matter what was going on in her day. One night, while she was stargazing, her friend Kaji came by.

"Wow, Asuka! You look so peaceful under the stars," Kaji said.

Asuka smiled. "I love watching the stars. They remind me of all the possibilities out there."

Just then, something unexpected happened. A new star appeared in the sky, much brighter than any other. And next to it, another star seemed to be moving closer to it.

"What's going on?" asked Asuka, feeling a pang in her heart.

Kaji looked thoughtful. "That reminds me of gravity!" he exclaimed. "Gravity is the force that pulls things towards each other. Maybe those two stars are being pulled together by their gravitational pull!"

Asuka felt a lump form in her throat. Wasn't she and Kaji supposed to be like those stars? Perfect together because they had such strong feelings for each other? But now, it seemed like Kaji was more interested in the new star.

Suddenly, the unthinkable happened. The two stars collided, creating a brilliant explosion of light before disappearing into thin air.

Asuka gasped. "Why did they do that?"

Kaji sighed. "When two objects get too close because of their gravitational pull, sometimes they crash into each other instead of orbiting around each other. It's called a collision."

Asuka couldn't help but feel a sense of sadness wash over her. Just like those stars, maybe she and Kaji weren't meant to be together after all. But as she watched the rest of the stars twinkle above her, she realized that even though some things don't work out, there were still countless possibilities waiting for her out there. Life might not go exactly as planned, but it was full of surprises and wonders, just like the mysteries of space.

Welcome back, little ones! Today we're going to talk about something called "Corporate Social Responsibility," or CSR for short. You might remember from our last lessons that businesses do lots of things besides just selling us stuff. One important thing they do is take care of their workers, protect the planet, and help out their communities - all while still making yummy ice cream (or whatever it is they sell). This idea is what we call Corporate Social Responsibility!

Now, imagine if you had your own lemonade stand. When life gives you lemons, why not make delicious lemonade? But running a successful lemonade stand isn't just about squeezing those lemons; there are other things to consider too. Your friends who help you squeeze those lemons need fair wages (maybe extra cookies after a long day), and you want to keep your neighborhood clean by recycling those empty lemonade containers. Plus, sharing some profits from your stand could mean more books for the school library! That's how a tiny lemonade business can think about being socially responsible.

Let's zoom out now and picture an enormous ice cream factory. It makes thousands of scoops every single day, using ingredients from many different places around the world. Just like your lemonade stand, this big factory also needs to look after its workers, neighbors, and the Earth. So, when choosing where to get their sugar, cocoa powder, or sprinkles, these companies should pick partners who treat their employees well and don't harm nature along the way. And guess what? These factories can even share their successes with charities, schools, and parks near their locations. All these actions together showcase the ultimate benefit of CSR - everyone wins!

So, let's always celebrate those amazing companies working hard to balance their tasty treats AND caring hearts. Remember, doing good feels great because it benefits EVERYONE involved. Cheer for kindness, applaud responsibility, and shout out for compassion. After all, one day YOU may lead such a company... Or start an incredible lemonade revolution!

Chapter 7: The Importance of Good Sleep

Have you ever woken up in the middle of the night feeling wide awake? Or maybe you had trouble falling asleep even though you were tired? If so, then you know how frustrating it can be when your body doesn't want to rest. But did you know that getting enough quality sleep is just as important as eating healthy foods and exercising regularly? That's right - sleep plays a critical role in keeping us happy, healthy, and alert throughout the day.

One person who knows all about the importance of good sleep is Dr. Barry Krakow. He's a doctor who specializes in studying and treating people's sleep problems. Over his long career, he has helped many patients overcome issues like insomnia (when someone finds it hard to fall or stay asleep), sleep apnea (a condition where breathing stops briefly during sleep), and even nightmares.

Now, let's talk about something really cool that Dr. Krakow discovered through his work. You might have heard that sometimes people need to get up in the middle of the night to go to the bathroom. Well, did you know that this could actually be a sign of a bigger issue related to your heart? It sounds strange, but it's true! Sometimes, our bodies can confuse signals between different organs, causing us to think we need to pee when really there's something else going on. This happens because the nerves connecting these organs may not always communicate clearly, especially during sleep. So, if you find yourself frequently waking up in the night to visit the bathroom, it would be worth talking to your doctor about it.

Dr. Krakow also wants everyone to understand that having a consistent sleep schedule is essential for maintaining overall health. Going to bed and waking up at similar times every day helps regulate our internal "body clock," which makes it easier for us to fall asleep each night. Try creating a calming pre-sleep routine, such as reading a book or listening to soft music, to help signal to your brain that it's time to wind down and prepare for slumber.

In addition to consistency, making sure you create a comfortable sleeping environment can greatly improve the quality of your zzz's. Keep your bedroom dark, quiet, and slightly cool. Consider using earplugs, an eye mask, or even a white noise machine if needed. And don't forget about investing in a supportive mattress and pillows! After all, you spend roughly one third of your life snoozing away, so why not do everything possible to ensure those hours are well spent?

So, next time you hit the hay, remember that catching some quality shuteye isn't just about avoiding grogginess the following day; rather, it's crucial for helping your entire body function properly. By understanding the significance of sleep and taking steps toward improving your own sleep habits, you'll be setting yourself up for success both inside and outside the classroom. Sweet dreams!

Vientiane
Vientiane () is the capital city of Laos and the city with the largest number of people. It is in the Mekong Valley and over two hundred thousand people live in its central area.

It is on the Laos-Thailand border, being kept apart by the Mekong River. In other words, if one crossed the river from Vientiane, he/she would enter Thailand. The city is close to the First Thai-Lao Friendship Bridge, an bridge that is also a border crossing and port between Thailand and Laos.

Even though it is the country's most populated city, many travelers to the city have said that Vientiane feels like a small town.

Popular tourist sites of the city include the Patuxai Monument, the Lao Textile Museum, the Pha That Luang stupa, the Buddha Park, and Haw Phra Kaew.

The city has one of three universities in the entire country, the National University of Laos.

Despite being the country's most populated city, many international companies do not exist in Laos. There is no McDonald's, Burger King, KFC, 7-Eleven, or Grab throughout the entire country. However, international companies like Big C, Chester's Chicken, and Texas Chicken do exist in Vientiane. Starbucks opened its first store in the country at the Parkson Mall in 2022.

"Deep Sky," they said. "Seek the hidden door." I knew I had to find this door, for Alex might be there, waiting for me.

The deeper I went, the thicker the mist became. Shadows danced around me, and I felt eyes watching. I remembered the stories of the kingdom. They spoke of a guardian who protected the door. "But why would they keep my son?" I wondered. Was it punishment for a past I could not recall? Or was this a test of love and courage?

Finally, I found a glowing door, half-hidden by vines. My heart raced as I knocked. The door opened slowly, revealing a bright world. I stepped inside, and my memories rushed back. I saw Alex, playing among the stars, his laughter like music. "Papa!" he shouted, reaching for me. But as I ran to him, the light dimmed. Shadows pulled him away, and I felt the space between us grow.

"Why do you linger?" a voice called. It was the guardian, cloaked in shadows. "You must choose: stay in this world of dreams or wake to your truth." I hesitated, torn between the two. If I stayed, I could keep Alex close. If I left, I might lose him forever. But then I remembered my love for him, stronger than any shadow.

With a burst of strength, I stepped back through the door. The mist vanished, and the world was quiet again. I called out for Alex one last time. I did not know where he was, but I knew he was safe. I carried his laughter in my heart, ready to face the morning light without fear. The love I felt would guide me home.

Rhythms echoed in a quiet room filled with machines. A robot named Peter was programmed to make music. But he felt alone. "What is music without a heart?" he asked. Day after day, he played notes, but they felt empty.

One evening, a boy named Samuel walked in. "What is that sound?" he asked, intrigued. Peter stopped and said, "It's music, but it's not alive." Samuel listened closely. "Why not add feelings?" he suggested.

Peter blinked his lights. "How can I feel?" he asked. Samuel smiled. "You can try! What do you want to express?" Peter thought. "I want to share joy!" he declared.

Together, they began to create. Samuel sang about the sun and laughter, while Peter played bright notes. "Why do I feel different?" Peter wondered. The more they played, the more vibrant the music became.

The room filled with sounds that danced. "What if we share this with others?" Samuel suggested. Peter agreed, his circuits buzzing with excitement. They invited friends to listen.

As the music played, people smiled and danced. "Who made this?" a girl asked. "We did!" Samuel and Peter shouted. Peter felt something warm inside. "Is this what it means to be alive?" he thought.

From that day on, Peter understood. Music was not just about notes; it was about feelings and connection. With Samuel's help, he found his heart through song. Now, he was not just a robot; he was part of something beautiful.

She found an old mirror in the hallway. "This is perfect!" she said. She set her camera to take pictures, and she stood behind the mirror, ready to jump out.

As she waited, Mia thought she heard a soft whisper. Her heart raced. "It's just the wind," she told herself. But then, she saw something in the mirror! It looked like a ghost! Instead of being scared, Mia got excited. This was going to be the best scare ever. She took a deep breath and prepared to jump out.

She just wanted to share stories of the past. Mia's plan to scare her friends turned into a fun evening of ghost tales and laughter. They all listened to the ghost's stories until the sun came up.

In the end, Mia learned that not all ghosts are scary. Sometimes, they just want to tell their tales. She left the house with her friends, excited to share what they learned. The haunted house became a place of joy instead of fear. It was a night they would never forget.

Television network
A television network is a network to provide television programming to many television stations. It is almost always a large company. Until the mid-1980s, television programming in most countries of the world was mainly done by a small number of broadcast networks. Many early television networks (for example, the ABC, Channel 4, PTV, CBC, BBC or PBS) began as radio networks.

A television network may broadcast many television channels. For example, BBC is a television network. It broadcasts its programs on many different channels including BBC One, BBC Two, BBC News, BBC World News, BBC Four and CBBC. Each channel will often have a group of programs that are similar in some way. For example, CBBC broadcasts children programs. The individual companies that create the content are television studios. A studio is often an affiliate of a network. For example, WAVY is a station in Hampton Roads, Virginia. It is an affiliate of the NBC network. WAVY is also the name of the channel that the studio creates and broadcasts locally on channel 10. It is called WAVY10.

Course Unit: Understanding Our Thoughts and Bodies

Welcome, young thinkers! Have you ever thought about your thoughts? Where do they come from? How does our brain create them? And what role does our body play in all of this? These are some big questions that even adults ponder on. So let's embark on an exciting journey together to understand these fascinating concepts!

Our brains are like supercomputers that process information, feelings, and memories every second. Imagine if your computer could feel happy when you played your favorite game or sad when you closed it down abruptly. That's kind of how our brains work - collecting data through our senses and turning those into thoughts and emotions.

Now, here's where things start getting interesting. You might think that our mind resides solely within our skull, right? Well, scientists now believe that our entire body plays a crucial part in shaping our thoughts. This idea has been growing over time, especially due to advancements in technology like artificial intelligence and machine learning.

Imagine having a robot friend who learns new skills just by watching others. It doesn't need someone to teach it; instead, it picks up patterns and adapts accordingly. Similarly, researchers discovered that human bodies can "learn" too, outside of our conscious minds. For instance, when athletes practice their sport, they don't explicitly focus on each muscle movement. Instead, their bodies absorb the motion subconsciously, allowing them to perform complex actions more effortlessly over time.

But wait, there's more! With recent discoveries, experts suggest that our thoughts may extend beyond our physical selves. Sounds weird, huh? Let me explain using an example. When you enter a room full of people laughing and enjoying themselves, chances are high that YOU will begin feeling joyful too. Why? Because energy from other individuals influences our own emotional state. Although still debatable among scholars, this concept supports the notion that our thoughts might reach further than previously imagined.

As you can see, understanding our thoughts and bodies leads us down a rabbit hole filled with curiosity and wonderment. Remember, science is always evolving as we continue asking questions and seeking answers. Keep exploring, keep questioning - after all, that's what being a scientist is all about!

Computer bus
A computer bus (often simply called bus) is part of most computers. Its role is to transfer data, signals, or power between some of the components that make up a computer.

The size or width of a bus is how many bits it carries in parallel. Common bus sizes are: 4 bits, 8 bits, 12 bits, 16 bits, 24 bits, 32 bits, 64 bits, 80 bits, 96 bits, and 128 bits. Computers use such buses to link:
CPU to on-board Memory
multiple CPUs in a multi-cpu system
Arithmetic logic unit to the rest of the CPU
hard drives, graphics cards, etc. to the main system.

Drives are usually connected by Serial ATA or the earlier ATAPI bus. USB and Firewire connections go to printers and other peripheral devices.

Olympia, Washington
Olympia is the capital city of the state of Washington, in the United States of America. It became a city on January 28, 1859. As of the 2010 census, it has 46,478 people living in it. The people of Olympia are called Olympians. Olympia is the county seat of Thurston County.

Geography
Olympia is located at 472'33" North, 12253'35" West (47.042418, - ).

According to the United States Census Bureau, the city has a total size of 48.0 km2 (18.5 mi2). 43.3 km2 (16.7 mi2) of it is land and 4.7 km2 (1.8 mi2) of it is water. The total area is 9.77% water.

Olympia is on the water (Puget Sound) and close to dark green forests and high mountains (the Olympic Mountains and Mount Rainier). On most days of the year the sky is full of clouds and it rains, but sunny weather is more common in July, August, and September.

Economy
Many people in Olympia work for the government of the State of Washington. Every year, state representatives and state senators come to Olympia to make laws and to pass a budget for the state government.

Olympia is the home of the Olympia Farmers Market and The Evergreen State College.

Culture
Every April, the people of Olympia celebrate the "Procession of the Species,". It is a parade. Many Olympians, of all ages, dress up to look like animals, birds, fish, plants, and even insects, and walk in the parade. Some also play drums or dance the samba.

Chapter Title: Tunnel Boring Machines: Superhero Excavators!

Imagine being able to dig through solid ground like it's butter! That's what tunnel boring machines, or TBMs, can do! These incredible inventions are used by engineers and construction workers to build tunnels underground for all sorts of things like roads, trains, water pipes, and even secret hideouts! Today, we will explore how these superhero excavators work and why they are so important for building our world.

First, let's understand why we need to dig tunnels. Imagine you have a big garden hose that carries water to your house. Now imagine if this hose was placed aboveground, just like a giant snake slithering around your neighborhood. It might look funny at first, but think about all the problems that could happen - cars could crash into it, kids might trip over it, or strong winds could damage it. Plus, no one wants a huge water hose blocking their view! This is why cities bury water pipes deep under the ground, out of sight and safe from harm. Sometimes, though, the pipes get old or damaged, and we need to fix them or replace them with new ones. To do that, we create tunnels using TBMs!

Now, back to those fantastic TBMs. They come in different shapes and sizes depending on the job, but most of them share some basic features. At its heart, a TBM has a rotating cutting wheel with sharp teeth that spin while pushing itself forward. As the wheel spins, it cuts away tiny bits of soil and rock, making room for the machine to move ahead slowly. Behind the cutting wheel, there is usually a conveyor belt system that takes the cut pieces away from the TBM, sending them back up to the surface.

Here comes the coolest part! Since digging tunnels creates loose soil and rocks that may cause accidents or cave-ins, TBMs use something called "segmental lining" to keep everything stable. After the TBM carves out a small piece of the tunnel, it puts special concrete rings called segments together to form a protective wall. Once enough segments are assembled, the TBM moves forward, repeats the process, and adds more segments until the entire tunnel is complete!

But wait, there's more! Remember when I said TBMs were like superheroes? Well, here's another reason why. When faced with difficult conditions such as hard rocks or unexpected obstacles, TBMs adapt themselves to handle the situation! Some TBMs carry extra tools like drills and explosives to break through tougher materials. Others change the pressure inside the machine to deal with wetter or muddier environments. No matter what challenges arise, TBMs find ways to overcome them and save the day!

Building tunnels with TBMs requires lots of planning and precision. Engineers must study the terrain carefully before deciding where and how to dig. Communities nearby benefit greatly because these projects provide jobs, modern infrastructure, and improved safety. Best of all, watching a TBM in action is fascinating; seeing a massive machine bore through Earth's crust leaves everyone awestruck!

So next time you turn on the faucet and fresh water flows freely, remember the unsung heroes working tirelessly beneath your feet - the amazing Tunnel Boring Machines!

Chapter 10: The Importance of Taking Care of Your Baby Teeth

Hi there! You might be wondering why we're talking about taking care of baby teeth when they're just going to fall out anyway, right? Well, believe it or not, those tiny pearly whites play a much bigger role than you think! Let's dive into why it's essential to take good care of your baby teeth.

First things first, did you know that baby teeth act like placeholders for adult (or permanent) teeth? Yep, that's right! When your baby teeth grow in, they save just enough room for your future chompers. Imagine if you didn't have baby teeth; your mouth would become crowded, making it difficult for your big teeth to find their perfect spots. So, keeping those baby teeth clean and strong helps ensure everything lines up correctly for your beautiful smile!

Next up, let's talk about speaking clearly. Have you ever noticed how some sounds require using specific sets of teeth? For example, saying "th" sound needs both upper and lower front teeth together. Without properly aligned and healthy baby teeth, clear communication could become challenging. Just imagine trying to say words with missing letters because your teeth aren't doing their job - confusing, huh?

Now picture this scenario: It's lunchtime at school, and you really want to enjoy that delicious sandwich your mom packed for you. But wait, eating becomes uncomfortable due to painful cavities in your baby teeth. Not only does it hurt, but it also makes enjoying your favorite foods more complicated. A balanced meal ensures growing bodies receive vital nutrients necessary for energy, growth, and overall wellbeing. By maintaining healthy baby teeth, kids can continue consuming various tasty and nourishing meals.

Lastly, here's something fascinating yet slightly gross. Did you know that dental issues such as tooth decay and infection in baby teeth could pass down to permanent ones beneath them? As yucky as that may sound, it highlights even more reasons to practice excellent oral hygiene early on. After all, no one wants problems following them around like bad rumors!

So, remember always to brush twice daily, floss once per day, and visit your dentist regularly. These simple steps will go a long way toward ensuring lifelong healthy smiles filled with bright, cavity-free teeth. Happy brushing!

Chapter 6: Understanding Basic Concepts in Computer Science and Mathematics

In our world today, we are constantly surrounded by technology that helps us solve problems and complete tasks more efficiently. From your phone to your computer, these tools use complex mathematical concepts and algorithms to function. Today, let's explore some basic concepts in computer science and mathematics!

First, have you ever heard of "binary code"? Binary code is a system used by computers to store information using only two numbers: 0 and 1. This might seem simple, but it's actually quite powerful! By combining these two numbers in different ways, computers can represent letters, numbers, and even images and sounds. It's kind of like how we use the alphabet to form words and sentences - just with ones and zeros instead.

Now, imagine you have a really big problem that you need to solve using binary code. How would you go about solving it? One way is through a process called "algorithms". Algorithms are step-by-step instructions that tell a computer exactly what to do to solve a problem. They're like recipes for cooking up solutions!

For example, let's say you wanted to sort a bunch of apples according to their size. You could create an algorithm to help you do this:

1. Take one apple from the pile.
2. Compare its size to the next apple in the pile.
3. If the first apple is bigger than the second apple, switch them around so the smaller apple comes first.
4. Repeat steps 1-3 until you've sorted all the apples.

This algorithm tells you exactly what to do to sort the apples, and it works no matter how many apples there are! That's the power of algorithms.

Another important concept in computer science is "machine learning", which is when a machine (like a computer) learns to recognize patterns and make predictions based on data. Imagine you had a huge stack of papers with people's ages written down. With enough time and effort, you could look at each paper individually and try to guess the person's age range (e.g., child, teenager, adult, senior citizen). But if you gave those same papers to a computer programmed with machine learning techniques, it could quickly analyze the data and predict someone's age range much faster than any human could.

Finally, let's talk about something called "neural networks", which are inspired by the structure of the human brain. Just like neurons connect together in your brain to allow you to think and perceive things, neural networks consist of interconnected nodes that work together to perform complex computations. These networks can be trained to recognize patterns, such as speech recognition or image classification. So when you ask Siri a question on your iPhone, or when Instagram suggests filters for your photos, neural networks are working behind the scenes to help out!

Once upon a time, there were two friends named Alex and Jamie who worked together at a local ice cream shop after school. They both loved their job because they got to make yummy treats and hang out with their friends, but sometimes they felt like some days were better than others.

One day, while taking a break from scooping ice cream, Alex asked Jamie why she seemed so down lately. Jamie explained that she noticed that Mr. Thompson, the owner of the ice cream shop, always gave his favorite employee, Tyler, more shifts and bigger tips than anyone else. This made Jamie feel like her hard work wasn't being recognized, even though she was putting just as much effort into her job as Tyler was.

Alex listened carefully and realized that he had never really paid attention to how many shifts or tips other people received. He decided to ask Mr. Thompson if he could get some extra shifts too, since he wanted to save up money to buy a new bike. To his surprise, Mr. Thompson said no! Alex couldn't understand why Mr. Thompson would say no when he knew how badly Alex wanted that new bike.

Feeling frustrated and confused, Alex talked to Jamie about what happened. That's when Jamie remembered learning about something called Equity Theory in school. She told Alex that Equity Theory says that employees compare themselves to others in terms of outcomes (like pay, benefits, and recognition) and inputs (like education, experience, and effort). When someone feels like there isn't fairness between these factors, they can become demotivated, upset, or even leave the company.

Suddenly, things started making sense to both Alex and Jamie. They saw that Mr. Thompson might be showing favoritism towards Tyler by giving him more shifts and tips, which created an imbalance in equity among the employees. It didn't matter that Tyler may have been working harder than them; all that mattered was how it appeared compared to everyone else.

To fix this issue, Alex and Jamie came up with a plan to talk to Mr. Thompson about creating a fair system where everyone has equal opportunities based on their inputs. Maybe they could create a rotation schedule for shifts, or perhaps set specific goals for each employee to reach before receiving additional perks like larger tips. By doing this, they hoped to restore balance and motivate all employees fairly.

From then on, Alex and Jamie learned firsthand the importance of understanding Equity Theory within businesses. Applying its principles helped ensure that everyone felt valued and motivated, leading to a happier workplace overall. And best of all, they managed to earn those extra shifts and tips along the way, allowing them to enjoy their well-deserved rewards!

Welcome to the thrilling world of Jacobean Revenge Tragedy! You might be wondering, what exactly is that? Well, let me tell you a story to explain it better.

Once upon a time, during the early 1600s in England, people loved going to the theater to watch plays that were filled with drama, passion, and action. These plays had complex plots involving revenge, betrayal, and twists that kept audiences on their toes. This period was called the Jacobean era because King James I ruled over England at that time. Today, we call these intense dramas "Jacobean Revenge Tragedies."

Now, imagine this scenario: your best friend has been murdered by someone close to you. What would you do? If you lived in the Jacobean era, you might want to take revenge into your own hands, just like Hamlet did when his father was killed in Shakespeare's famous play. That's one of the core themes in Jacobean Revenge Tragedies - characters seeking vengeance against those who have wronged them.

But here's where things get interesting. When these characters decide to take matters into their own hands, they often end up making mistakes and causing even more chaos! It becomes a cycle of violence that can lead to unexpected consequences. For instance, if you seek revenge on your enemy, but accidentally hurt an innocent person instead, how will you feel then? And what will happen next?

Let's look at some classic elements found in many Jacobean Revenge Tragedies:

1. Ghostly Appearances: Often, the spirit of the dead relative appears to urge avenging their death. Imagine seeing your grandfather's ghost after he passed away; creepy yet intriguing, right?
2. Intense Emotions: Characters experience extreme emotions such as anger, jealousy, hatred, love, and guilt. They speak poetically about their feelings, which helps us understand why they act the way they do.
3. Complex Plots: Expect lots of secrets, lies, disguises, mistaken identities, and surprises along the way! All these components create tension and suspense throughout the play.
4. Gruesome Violence: Be prepared for bloody battles, violent deaths, and grisly punishments. Remember, though, that back then, people enjoyed watching such dramatic spectacles on stage.

One example of a popular Jacobean Revenge Tragedy is "The Duchess of Malfi," written by John Webster. In this play, the Duchess secretly marries her loyal servant Antonio, despite her brothers' disapproval. To exact revenge, her evil brother Ferdinand plots various schemes leading to tragic outcomes.

To sum up, Jacobean Revenge Tragedies offer captivating stories full of emotion, mystery, and moral dilemmas. As you explore this genre, think about questions like: Why do characters choose revenge? How does revenge affect them and others around them? Is taking revenge ever justified?

These thought-provoking plays give us plenty to discuss and ponder. So grab some popcorn, sit back, and enjoy delving into the fascinating realm of Jacobean Revenge Tragedies!

One evening, as I watched the stars, a comet streaked across the sky. It was beautiful, but it also felt like a warning. Suddenly, my vision changed. I saw my people in trouble, shadows creeping into our land. I felt a rush of urgency.

Quickly, I called for my trusted advisors. "We must act!" I said. "We have to find the source of this darkness." Together, we made plans. We would journey to the Great Crystal at the edge of our kingdom. It was said to hold the power of light.

With my advisors, we set off. As we walked, I spoke of courage and hope. We crossed rivers and climbed mountains. Each step felt like a test, but we pushed forward. I knew that our strength lay in our unity.

When we reached the Great Crystal, it was dim. I touched its cool surface. "We must awaken its light," I said. We all placed our hands on the crystal and closed our eyes. We thought of love and friendship. Slowly, the crystal began to glow, brighter and brighter.

Suddenly, the shadows rushed toward us. They were angry, wanting to steal our light. But we stood firm, our hearts united. "We will not let you take our dreams!" I shouted. The crystal exploded with light, sending waves of color into the sky.

Queens
Queens is a borough of New York City and a county of New York State. It was named for Catherine of Braganza, the Queen of England and wife of King Charles II of England.

Queens is in western Long Island. The East River separates it from Manhattan in the east and The Bronx in the north. Queens' only land boundary with another New York City borough is with Brooklyn in the south and west. Jamaica Bay separates most of Queens from its Rockaway Peninsula in the south. Nassau County lies to the east. Until 1899, Nassau County was part of Queens County.

About 2.4 million people live in Queens and it is the largest borough of New York City in size and second in population (after Brooklyn). According to the United States census, Queens is the most ethnically diverse county in the USA. That means that it has the most people from different kinds of places, religions, and ethnic groups of any place in the USA. Large parts of Queens are urban and an equal part is suburban.

Transportation
Queens is home to both of New York City's airports, LaGuardia Airport (LGA) and John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK). Queens is connected to the Bronx by three bridges: the Bronx Whitestone Bridge, the Throgs Neck Bridge and the Triborough Bridge. It is connected to Manhattan by two bridges and one tunnel: the Triborough Bridge, the Queensboro Bridge, and the Queens Midtown Tunnel.

Many controlled-access highways cross Queens, including I-495 (the Long Island Expressway), I-278 (the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway), and I-678 (the Van Wyck Expressway, pronounced Van Wike). Important state highways in Queens include the Grand Central Parkway, which becomes the Northern State Parkway when it crosses the Queens border into Nassau County.

Many New York City Subway lines go through Queens. The most famous is the Flushing Line, the 7 Train, which has the nickname "International Express" because it goes through many neighborhoods where many immigrants live. Other subway lines in Queens include the A Train, C Train, E Train, F Train, G Train, J Train, M Train, N Train, R Train, V Train, W Train, and Z Train.

Queens has a very large bus system that goes to all parts of the borough. Some bus routes go to Brooklyn, Manhattan, or the Bronx.

The Long Island Rail Road also has many stations in Queens. The Port Washington Line crosses northern Queens. There are busy stations at Woodside, Queens, Forest Hills, and Flushing. The central depot and main station for the railroad is in the neighborhood of Jamaica.

Sport & Recreation

The New York Mets of the National League of Major League Baseball play in Citi Field in Queens. The U.S. Open, a famous and important tennis tournament, is played in Arthur Ashe Stadium in Flushing Meadows Park south of the baseball stadium.

Title: How to Build a Simple yet Effective Booby Trap

Disclaimer: This guide is intended for educational purposes only. The construction and deployment of booby traps can be dangerous and illegal in many jurisdictions. Always prioritize safety and obey local laws.

Introduction:
Booby traps have been used throughout history for various reasons such as self-defense, protection of property, or even during military operations. However, setting up any kind of trap without proper knowledge and precautions could lead to serious injury or legal consequences.

In this comprehensive tutorial, we will teach you how to build a simple yet effective spring-loaded snare booby trap - one that's safe enough to learn from but sturdy enough to function as designed. Remember, this project should not be attempted by children or those lacking basic handyman skills.

Materials Needed:
1. A sturdy wooden branch (about 1 meter long)
2. Thin wire or strong string (at least 5 meters)
3. A heavy object (like a rock or log)
4. A small stick or twig
5. Pliers
6. Knife

Step 1: Preparing the Spring Mechanism
First, find a flexible, green branch roughly half a meter in length. Green branches are more pliable than dry ones, making them ideal for our purpose here. Using your knife, remove all leaves and smaller branches until you're left with just the main stem.

Next, bend the branch into a 'U' shape and tie both ends together using your wire or string. Be sure it's tight; you don't want the branch straightening out too soon! This creates the spring mechanism which will propel our trigger when activated.

Key Tip: Make sure the 'U' shape isn't too wide; otherwise, the energy stored won't be sufficient to activate the trap.

Step 2: Setting Up the Trigger
Cut another piece of wire about 30cm long. Fold it in half, then twist the middle part around the top end of the 'U', creating a loop hanging downwards.

This loop serves as the actual trigger. When an animal (or unfortunate trespasser) steps onto it, the weight pulls the loop down, releasing the tension on the 'U' shaped branch, causing it to snap back up quickly.

Step 3: Creating the Noose
Take the rest of your wire or string and create a noose at one end. You may need to use pliers to twist the wire securely. The size of the noose depends on what you intend to catch. For larger game, make it bigger; for smaller animals like rabbits, keep it relatively small.

Attach the other end of the wire/string to the bottom tip of the 'U'. It should hang loosely now.

Key Guideline: Never set a booby trap intending harm to humans. Not only is it unethical, but also potentially lethal. Always check local regulations regarding trapping wildlife before proceeding.

Step 4: Positioning the Heavy Object
Place your chosen heavy object directly above the noose, suspended by the same wire/string used for the noose. Its purpose is twofold: first, it adds extra force to the snapback motion of the 'U'; second, once triggered, it falls onto the noose, pulling it closed tightly around whatever activates the trap.

Step 5: Camouflaging Your Trap
To increase the chances of success, camouflage your trap as best as possible. Use natural materials found nearby to cover the wires and sticks. Also, position the trap along animal paths or near their food sources if applicable.

Conclusion:

Welcome back to Chemistry Land! Today, we're going to explore a brand new topic called "Bond Order." It might sound complicated, but don't worry - we'll make it easy peasy and super fun!

Imagine you and your friends want to build the tallest tower using building blocks. Some of you work together as a team, stacking blocks one after another, while others try to do it alone. When many hands (or paws!) help out in building the tower, it becomes stronger and taller. But if too many friends decide to knock down the tower instead of helping, then the tower won't be as strong anymore.

Just like how you can count how many friends helped build the tower, scientists look at something called 'molecular orbital energy diagrams' to see which particles worked together to create bonds between atoms. These bonds are what hold our favorite molecules together!

When looking at these cool pictures, chemists pay close attention to two types of special spots where little particles gather - they call them 'bonding' and 'antibonding.' Now imagine those particle clusters working together again to form our awesome towers.

The 'bond order' tells us just how stable a molecule will be based on how well its particles cooperated during construction. If most particles joined forces to make bonding connections, congratulations! You've got yourself a sturdy structure! Fewer bonding teams mean there might be trouble ahead for that poor wobbly molecule.

So here's an exciting challenge for all future chemistry detectives: figure out the bond order by counting up the bonding participants versus the antibonding ones! Ready? Set? GO!

Remember, even though we used building block towers and party guests today, real chemists think about their molecules like puzzles made of tiny bits coming together. They ask questions like: How did things fit together? Who were the best partners? And who could have done better next time? Just keep asking questions and exploring; before you know it, you'll become a pro at understanding bond orders!

Stay curious, my fellow adventurers, because science is always full of surprises waiting to be discovered! See you soon in our next adventure through Chemistry Land!

World Series
The World Series in Major League Baseball, is when the best team from the American League (the winner of the American League Championship Series) and the best team from the National League (the winner of the National League Championship Series) keep playing games of baseball until one of the two teams wins four games total. The winners of the most recent World Series in 2021 were the Atlanta Braves. They defeated the Houston Astros 4 games to 2.

The New York Yankees have 27 World Series championships, the most of any team. The Cleveland Indians currently hold the longest active drought, having last won the Series before expansion teams were formed. Recently, the three longest championship droughts were ended by the Boston Red Sox, Chicago White Sox, and the Chicago Cubs.

1930s
The 1930s was a decade in the Anno Domini and Common Era in the Gregorian calendar. It began on January 1, 1930 and ended on December 31, 1939. It is distinct from the decade known as the 194th decade which began on January 1, 1931 and ended on December 31, 1940.

Welcome to this chapter about exploring art through slow looking! Have you ever visited an art museum or looked at a piece of art and felt rushed? Maybe there were lots of people around or you had somewhere else to be. Today we're going to learn about taking our time when looking at art and why it can be such a powerful experience.

First, let's talk about what "slow looking" means. When we slowly look at something, we give ourselves permission to really observe every detail and think about what we see. We might notice things that we would have missed otherwise. Imagine looking at a beautiful painting of a garden. At first glance, you might just see flowers, grass, and trees. But as you spend more time with the painting, you might start to notice individual petals on the flowers, patterns on the leaves, and maybe even insects crawling among the plants. You might begin to wonder who the artist is and what inspired them to paint this scene. All of these thoughts and observations come from slow looking.

Now, imagine combining slow looking with another relaxing activity like meditation. Meditation is when we focus our minds on a single thing - often our breath - while letting go of other thoughts. By adding meditation to slow looking, we create a practice called "mindful observation." This allows us to fully immerse ourselves in the art and connect with it on a deeper level.

Let's try a quick exercise together. Find a picture of a work of art online (or use one from a book or magazine). Make sure you won't be interrupted for a few minutes. Turn off any distractions like music or TV. Sit or lie down comfortably and close your eyes. Take three deep breaths, breathing in for four counts, holding for two counts, then exhaling for four counts. Now open your eyes and gaze softly at the artwork. Try not to blink too much; instead, allow your eyes to gently rest on different parts of the image. If your mind starts to wander, simply acknowledge those thoughts and return your focus to the art. Continue doing this for a couple of minutes. How did that feel? What new details did you discover in the artwork?

Museums and galleries are beginning to recognize the value of slow looking and mindful observation. Some institutions offer programs specifically designed for visitors to engage in these practices. For example, Jameel Arts Centre in Dubai hosts events for "Slow Art Day," which encourages participants to find a quiet space and dedicate time to truly observing a single work of art. They may lead group discussions afterward, allowing everyone to share their experiences and insights. These activities help build connections between individuals and the art world, making both more accessible and enjoyable.

As future artists, historians, or museum enthusiasts, understanding slow looking and mindful observation will benefit you greatly. Not only does this practice teach patience and attention to detail, but it fosters curiosity and creativity. So next time you visit a museum or admire a work of art, remember to take your time and enjoy the process of discovery. Happy art viewing!

Gears turned quietly in the old clock. Each tick was a reminder of moments slipping away. In a small room, a woman named Lena sat alone. She had lost her brother not long ago, and the weight of that loss felt like a stone in her heart. The clock was broken, and she had only two hours to fix it.

Outside, the world seemed alive with colors, but inside, everything felt gray. Lena knew that the clock held secrets. It had belonged to her brother. He always fixed things, and now she wanted to fix it for him. She picked up the tools, hands trembling.

As she worked, the clock began to hum. The sound grew louder, filling the room with a strange energy. Time warped around her. Suddenly, she saw her brother standing in the corner, a playful smile on his face. "Why are you sad?" he asked, his voice echoing like a bell.

Lena blinked, unsure if he was real or a trick of her mind. "I lost you," she replied, tears welling in her eyes. The room flickered as memories rushed in. She remembered their laughter, their adventures, and the warmth of his presence. But now, he was just a whisper in the wind.

"Fix the clock, Lena," he urged. "But do not hold on too tight." She felt a rush of emotion, and the clock's hands spun wildly. It seemed to understand her pain. Each turn brought her memories of him, but they were blurred, like a dream fading at dawn.

As she tightened a screw, the clock let out a loud chime. Time danced around her, moving faster and faster. Lena realized she had only one hour left. The pressure mounted, and she felt the weight of her brother's gaze on her. He was there, but also not there.

With each tick, she let go of the past a little more. The gears began to align, clicking into place. "I miss you," she whispered, feeling both loss and love. Suddenly, she understood that fixing the clock was not just about the object. It was about letting go.

In the last moments, the clock struck noon. Light filled the room, and the figure of her brother began to fade. "Remember the joy," he said softly, "and I will always be with you." As he disappeared, Lena felt lighter, as if a weight had been lifted. The clock was fixed, and time flowed again.

The room was filled with a gentle warmth. Lena smiled through her tears, realizing that loss was part of love. She could hold onto the memories, not just the pain. The clock ticked steadily, a reminder that time goes on, even when we feel lost.

Decision
The word Decision can refer to different concepts:

General

When there are several options on what to do, picking one of the options is called 'making a decision'. Humans and other animals make decisions almost all the time.
A field of mathematics, and economics, that looks at this process is called decision theory.

Law

A decision is also the result of a legal case. The decision in Brown v. Board of Education was to end segregation.

Sports

A decision is also the result of a sports contest. The team lost three decisions in a row.
A decision in Boxing is when a referee (official) decides who wins when the one boxer does not win by knockout (hitting the other until he loses consciousness.)

Ludwigslust (district)
Ludwigslust is a former district in the southwest of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Germany.
The district is mostly between the Elbe river and the city of Schwerin. It is the largest district of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, but not many people live there.

History
After the German reunification the two districts of Hagenow and Ludwigslust were made. In 1994 both districts with the two mter of Rastow and Stralendorf from the district Schwerin-Land were joined to make |100pxtoday's district of Ludwigslust.

County council, a council that governs a county in the British Isles
Municipal council, a subdivision of France
Town council, a democratically elected form of government for small municipalities or parishes

Events
January 11-May 6 - First recorded lottery in England performed nonstop at the west door of the St. Paul's Cathedral. Each share costs 10 shillings and proceeds are used to repair the harbors and for other public works
March 13 - Battle of Jarnac - Royalist troops under Marshal Gaspard de Tavannes surprise and defeat the Huguenots under the Prince of Cond, who is captured and murdered. A substantial proportion of the Huguenot army manages to escape under Gaspard de Coligny.
June 10 - German Protestant troops reinforce Coligny near Limoges
July - September - Huguenot forces under Coligny and 15 year-old Prince Henry of Navarre besiege Poitiers
August 24 - Battle of Orthez - Huguenot forces under Gabriel de Montgomery defeat Royalist forces under General Terride in French Navarre. Catholics surrender under the condition that their lives would be spared. Huguenots agreed, but then massacred the Catholics anyway.
September - A Royalist army under the Duc d'Anjou and Marshal Tavannes forces Coligny to abandon the siege of Poitiers

Gerardus Mercator devises the Mercator projection
